#7914. Two Ginger Brothers Became the First Documented Cases of Marfan Syndrome in Cats

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Cats come in all shapes and sizes. Some have legs that seem a little too long for their bodies, others have ears big enough to pick up satellite signals, and a few look like they haven't quite grown into themselves yet.

But when Gary and Shaggy were kittens, their disproportionately long limbs turned out to be more than an unusual-looking but perfectly charming physical trait. The two brothers would eventually become the first domestic cats confirmed to have Marfan syndrome through genetic testing; not exactly what any cat owner would expect when bringing home a pair of kittens.

As the cats grew, veterinarians identified abnormalities affecting their eyes and enlargement of the aorta, the major blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Researchers at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine and the Baker Institute for Animal Health worked with veterinary and genetic specialists to investigate what was going on.

Their long limbs were one clue. The eye abnormalities and enlarged aortas added two more. Slowly, the pieces of the puzzle began to fit together, pointing researchers toward Marfan syndrome, a rare inherited disorder far better known in human medicine than in veterinary practice. Genetic testing confirmed the connection, uncovering what made these two brothers so unusual.

Marfan syndrome affects connective tissue, the body's natural support system. This tissue helps give structure and strength to the bones, ligaments, skin, eyes, and blood vessels. When something goes wrong with this system, the effects can show up in several different ways.

In humans, the condition often causes unusually long limbs and fingers, a tall, slender build, eye abnormalities, and potentially serious cardiovascular complications.

Abraham Lincoln was famously tall and lanky, which has led to speculation that he may have had Marfan syndrome. No one can say for sure, though. Turns out, even Honest Abe left a few medical mysteries behind!

For Olympic volleyball player Flo Hyman, long limbs gave her an edge on the court. However, her life was tragically cut short, dying at age 31 from cardiac complications from Marfan syndrome.

One of the genes involved in Marfan syndrome is called FBN1. It contains the instructions for producing fibrillin-1, a protein that helps maintain the structure and function of connective tissues throughout the body.

When that gene doesn't work as it should, the effects can extend well beyond a person's or animal's appearance. As the gorgeous ginger duo, Gary and Shaggy, began showing signs similar to those seen in humans with Marfan syndrome, their veterinary team started to wonder if cats could also suffer from the same condition.

Genetic sequencing revealed that Gary and Shaggy both carried two altered copies of FBN1. In other words, they had inherited the mutation from both parents.

In humans, Marfan syndrome typically develops when a person inherits one disease-causing copy of the gene. Having two altered copies is exceptionally rare and can be associated with more severe disease.

So the brothers presented researchers with an interesting puzzle.

Their particular genetic variant didn't completely prevent the gene from functioning. Instead, it partially disrupted how the gene's instructions were processed, allowing some normal fibrillin-1 function to remain, which may explain why Gary and Shaggy survived into adulthood despite carrying two copies of the variant.

Their genetic instructions weren't simply switched on or off; it was something in between, which may help explain why the brothers developed the way they did.

Genes rarely behave like a tidy set of instructions. The effects of a genetic change depend on the specific variant involved and how it affects the resulting protein. Sometimes, a seemingly insignificant variation can have catastrophic consequences, altering the way the body functions.

The case of Gary and Shaggy is undeniably rare, and Marfan syndrome is unlikely to find its way onto the list of common feline diseases. However, in diagnosing and documenting the condition, veterinarians have something they didn't have before: a confirmed case of feline Marfan syndrome to help recognize, investigate, and compare with future cases.

These findings may help veterinary teams identify similar cases and better understand how particular FBN1 variants affect cats. They also demonstrate the value of bringing clinicians, genetic researchers, and pet parents together when a case doesn't fit neatly into an existing diagnosis.

Gary and Shaggy's shared genetic variant offered researchers a valuable opportunity to investigate the relationship between their physical features and the underlying condition.

Their owner, Nicole Desmond, also contributed to this process, and Cornell has highlighted the case as an example of how pet parents can collaborate with veterinary and genetic experts to advance knowledge that may eventually benefit other animals.

Even more importantly, Nicole loved the unique feline brothers with her whole heart. Vets did not expect either cat to survive for long, but they defied the odds. Gary was 6 years old when he passed away in July 2024, and in November 2025, at the incredible age of 7, Shaggy joined his brother across the rainbow bridge.

And that's one of the interesting things about veterinary medicine. Not every discovery starts with a large clinical trial or a disease affecting thousands of patients. Sometimes, it begins with two unusual kittens and a veterinary team willing to keep asking questions.

The rarity of this case means we donât necessarily have to think the worst when we see a long-legged kitten; itâs far more likely that theyâre simply long-limbed and not harboring a rare genetic disorder. However, it reminds us to pay attention to the bigger picture, bring unusual findings to the veterinarian's attention, and not automatically assume that two seemingly unrelated problems have nothing to do with each other.

Sometimes, a strange-looking kitten is simply a strange-looking kitten.

And sometimes, those extra-long legs are the first clue to a genetic story that researchers have never documented in cats before.

Dr. Paola Cuevas is the Senior In-House Veterinarian at Pangolia, the parent company of Catster. She has over 18 years of experience as a veterinarian and animal behaviorist. Paola's focus is on preventive medicine and animal welfare. Paola has a large range of skills in from diagnostic imaging to nutrition and clinical pathology. Paola enjoys sharing her extensive knowledge of animal training with our Catster readers and is always happy to answer reader questions as our in-house veterinarian.

The holidays are rushing in, but if you grow your own festive decorations you can create unique centerpieces and homegrown garlands that are the envy of all your neighbors

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The holiday season is fast approaching, bringing the annual scramble for festive boughs. wreaths, garlands, and mantelpiece greenery. But why buy store-bought greenery that will just end up in yard waste bags by January? Plastic greenery may be used again, but it doesn’t bring the same charm. Besides, there’s a far more rewarding alternative: growing your own living holiday decor outside your back door.

Growing plants that can help you see in the holiday season in style can deliver dual rewards. Through the year, these shrubs, trees, and aromatic herbs provide texture, wildlife shelter, and vibrant winter color. Come December, they supply an abundant, sustainable harvest of natural Christmas decorations in the form of lush foliage, pretty berries, and uplifting fragrance for seasonal wreaths, table runners, and gift wrapping.

Most of these perennial performers are resilient, adaptable, and low-maintenance once established. Bring authentic seasonal beauty indoors with these gorgeous double-duty beauties. These winter garden plants add effortless elegance, joy and character to your festive displays, and generally they need very little upkeep, freeing you up to enjoy the season. Here are 7 standout plants to add to your yard for easy homegrown holiday displays you can harvest for years to come.

Your USDA hardiness zone has some bearing on the plants you add for clippings that can festoon your festive garland and centerpieces. In mild and transitional zones, any hardy evergreens and deciduous shrubs planted now will establish strong roots over winter while top growth rests. In colder northern regions where frost arrives early, tender herbs thrive indoors in sunny containers, ready to move outside next spring.

Most evergreen conifers, hollies, and woodland shrubs thrive in slightly acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable drainage. Meanwhile, Mediterranean herbs demand sharp grit and full sun. When planting woody shrubs in November, dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball. Backfill with native soil amended with organic compost, and water deeply to settle any air pockets before the ground freezes.

Apply a 2-inch (5cm) layer of shredded bark mulch around the base, keeping it clear of the main stem, to insulate roots against freeze-thaw cycles. I like Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help lock in soil moisture and regulate soil temperature. In zones 6 and colder, verify that soil remains workable and unfrozen before planting. If hard freezes have already locked the earth, hold hardy specimens in a cold frame or pot until spring.

When harvesting for holiday arrangements, never strip entire limbs or harvest heavily from young shrubs during the first two years of establishment. Instead, take selective snips evenly from around the plant. Always cut just above an outward-facing bud or lateral branch, using sharp, sanitized bypass pruners to prevent winter disease.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

To keep cut greenery lush indoors, wait until you are ready to craft before harvesting, or submerge freshly cut stem ends in a bucket of cool water in an unheated garage for 24-48 hours to hydrate fully. Keep finished wreaths and garlands away from roaring fireplaces, radiators, and heating vents to prevent premature needle drop and fire hazards. Mist your arrangements lightly with water every few days. Hopefully the following plants will give you plenty of season’s greetings…

You must plant at least one pollinating male cultivar (such as Jersey Knight) within 40 feet of berry-producing female trees (Satyr Hill or Miss Helen) to guarantee fruit set. Harvest small, 8-12-inch (20-30cm) sprigs evenly around the tree using sharp pruners. Dip stems in water overnight before wiring into garlands. Note that holly berries are toxic to pets and humans if ingested, so display out of reach of dogs and toddlers. You can buy American Holly from Nature Hills at a discount if you hurry.

For winter drama, few shrubs rival winterberry holly. Unlike its evergreen cousins, this rugged native deciduous holly drops its leaves in fall to reveal bare branches densely studded with luminous, bright red berries that persist well into midwinter. Thriving across zones 3-9, winterberry (Ilex verticillata) is ideal for damp, low-lying, or poorly drained spots where most other woody ornamentals rot. It prefers full sun for maximum fruit production, as well as acidic, organic-rich soil.

Winterberry also requires male and female plants for pollination (and hence berries). Pair prolific female cultivars like Winter Red or compact Berry Poppins with a male pollinator such as Southern Gentleman or Mr. Poppins. Cut stems look magnificent in tall floor vases, outdoor porch planters, and minimalist wreaths paired with silver-blue cedar. Harvest selectively once leaves have fallen, leaving plenty of fruit for robins and cedar waxwings. If you fancy a golden variation on the classic winterberry, you can buy Yellow Winterberry Holly from Amazon.

When winter strips color from the yard, red twig dogwood (Cornus sericea) brings blazing crimson bark that looks electrifying against fresh snow. Hardy in zones 2-7, this vigorous native tolerates everything from boggy clay to average loam in full sun or light shade. Look for vibrant Cardinal or compact Arctic Fire, which stays under 4 feet (1.2m) tall and fits neatly into small suburban borders. You can currently buy Bailey Red Twigged Dogwood from Nature Hills at a staggering 40% discount.

The most dramatic bark develops on 1-2-year-old shoots, as older wood gradually turns brown. Cut out up to one third of the oldest, thickest stems down to the ground in late fall. This renewal pruning stimulates a flush of vivid new canes next spring, while providing structural crimson wands for your holiday decor. Weave flexible young stems into evergreen wreaths for classic contrast, or arrange upright branches in weighted urns alongside white pine and pinecones.

Junipers deliver unmistakable fragrance alongside feathery, silver-blue foliage studded with dusty, berry-like cones. Thriving in zones 3-9 depending on species, junipers range from low-spreading groundcovers (like Blue Rug) to graceful upright evergreens like Eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) and blue-tinged Rocky Mountain juniper (Wichita Blue). Plant in full sun and sharp, well-drained soil. Once established, junipers are drought-tolerant and shrug off winter winds. You can get Wichita Blue Juniper from Trees for a compact holiday-friendly choice.

Their supple boughs are tailor-made for weaving lush garlands over doorways, shaping rustic table runners, and layering texture into mixed evergreen wreaths. When harvesting branches, prune lightly from the outer tips and never cut back into old, bare interior wood. Dunk cut sprigs in cool water for 24 hours before crafting, and wear sleeves to guard against potential skin irritation from the resinous needles.

Bridging the gap between holiday decor and festive feasting, here comes rosemary. Its pine-scented foliage brings instant charm to winter tablescapes and mini wreaths, especially paired with dried orange slices and cinnamon sticks. Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) is reliably perennial outdoors in zones 8-10, where it thrives in lean alkaline soil. If you are in zone 7 or colder, grow upright cultivars like Tuscan Blue or Arp in terracotta containers. You can buy Arp Rosemary Indoor Christmas Plants from Plant Addicts. Just remember to transition plants outside when weather permits.

Move pots indoors to a bright, south-facing windowsill before hard fall freezes arrive, watering sparingly only when the top two inches (5cm) of soil feel dry. Harvesting sprigs in December encourages bushy branching, but never remove more than one-third of the plant at once. Any leftover trimmings from wreath-making sessions can be used in holiday roast potatoes, focaccia, and mulled cider. Win-win!

For a modern, frosted aesthetic that elevates traditional red-and-green palettes, try silver dollar eucalyptus (Eucalyptus cinerea). Prized by floral designers for its dusty leaves and camphor aroma, this fast-growing Australian native is hardy outside in zones 8-11. In cooler climates, grow it as a chic container specimen that can come into a cool, bright sunroom or frost-free conservatory before temperatures dip below 25°F (-4°C). You can buy Silver Dollar Eucalyptus Trees from Trees with a 20% discount if you quote the code at checkout.

Eucalyptus demands full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil. In late fall, selectively prune back overly long, whippy shoots by up to a third. This shapes the plant before winter rest, rewarding you with supple stems for cascading garlands, mantel swags, and vase displays. Unlike conifers that eventually shed, eucalyptus dries gracefully indoors. Just let the cut stems dry before using them in arrangements, hanging them upside down in a cool, dark room for 2 weeks.

Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) is quintessential holiday greenery. Instantly recognizable by its soft, feathery bundles of blue-green needles, this stately conifer thrives in zones 3-8. Plant in full sun or light shade in slightly acidic, well-drained soil. Give it generous space, too. Standard trees can soar 50-80 feet (15-24m) tall, but compact cultivars like Nana or Blue Shag suit smaller yards. You can get 30% off an American Beauties’ Eastern White Pine Trees from Nature Hills.

Growing white pine for holiday decor rewards patience. Allow newly planted trees 3-5 years to establish before harvesting, and never cut the central leader shoot, as it can ruin the tree's natural symmetry. When mature, snip 12-18-inch (30-45cm) lateral side tips around the lower and middle branches. You can weave its flexible stems into lush banister garlands and door wreaths, while its perfume fills the home.

Growing a holiday garden is a great way to get the most out of your plants, but it does require time and patience. Choose the right plants for your garden and help them get established strongly. Don’t rush the process and harvest too much too soon, and you’ll be rewarded with years of lush, natural décor.

#7911. 70+ Dogs Rescued From South Korean Meat Farm as 2027 Ban Approaches

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Nearly 30 dogs have arrived in New York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea. Their journey toward adoption is beginning, but with the country's ban still months away from taking full effect, the work is far from over.

A plane ride to New York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards. Neither, for that matter, was a soft bed, a full bowl of food, or the chance to be someone's beloved family member. After spending their lives confined to cages, even the simplest things may seem exciting and new.

On October 1, nearly 30 dogs were rescued from a dog-meat farm in Gangjin, South Korea, that once bred and slaughtered as many as 1,000 dogs each year. This was part of a larger rescue operation by Humane World for Animals that saved more than 70 dogs from the property.

For the organization, the operation marks its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea ahead of the country's ban, which takes full effect on February 7, 2027. Humane World for Animals has rescued nearly 3,000 dogs from farms since 2015, making this a significant milestone.

And yes, it's a reason to celebrate. But before we get too comfortable patting ourselves on the back, there's a much bigger picture to consider. Getting these dogs out was a huge victory, but there are still thousands at risk.

When the rescue team arrived at the farm in Gangjin, in South Korea's South Jeolla Province, they were met with disturbing scenes. Rows of rusting cages, abandoned collars scattered on the ground, and skeletal remains served as a gruesome reminder of the dogs that hadn't been so lucky.

It's a hard reality to come to terms with, especially if your own dog is currently hogging the sofa, demanding snacks, or staring at you as though you've ruined their life by being five minutes late with dinner. The minor dramas faced by our beloved pets are a world away from what these poor dogs endured.

Humane World for Animals has reported finding mixed breeds and dogs of different sizes during its rescue work. The survivors included Jindos, a breed native to South Korea, a husky mix, and smaller dogs, including a spitz mix. In other words, any dog could end up on the menu.

In this most recent rescue, a concerned citizen alerted a local animal protection group, which contacted Humane World for Animals and the authorities. Officials found that the farm had broken South Korea's Animal Protection Act. The farmer, a man in his 80s, agreed to hand over the dogs and promised not to take part in the dog-meat trade again.

More than 70 dogs were rescued. Nearly 30 travelled to New York, another 12 went to a rehabilitation center in Montreal, and some mothers and their puppies remained in South Korea because they were too young to fly safely.

Rescuing dogs from situations like this isn't as simple as just opening a cage and booking the next available flight. International transport requires veterinary checks, vaccinations, documentation, and careful consideration about which animals are fit to travel. The priority is getting them out safely, not rushing them onto a plane for the sake of a happy headline.

South Korea passed its Special Act on the Termination of Breeding, Slaughter, and Distribution of Dogs for Consumption in January 2024. Its key prohibitions will finally take full effect on February 7, 2027, making it illegal to breed, slaughter, or sell dogs or dog meat for human consumption. But the transition is already underway.

In May 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs reported that about 82% of the country's 1,537 registered dog-meat farms had closed. Over a thousand farms closed is something worth celebrating, but it means 272 farms are still operating.

Another consideration is that closing a farm doesn't automatically save the dogs living there. A business can shut down, the gates can close, and the paperwork can be signed, but where do all those dogs go?

According to Humane World for Animals, government figures indicate that of approximately 393,857 dogs counted on farms that had been closed, only 1,121 were adopted or transferred to public shelters. That's about 0.3%.

Itâs understood that most of these dogs were sent for slaughter or moved to other farms. So, while the closure of dog meat farms is good news, itâs not a true victory if these dogs are simply moved on to face the same fate. The ban is a huge step forward, but a law is only as good as its enforcement.

The real goal isn't just to close the farms. It's making sure the dogs are actually safe.

Getting out of the farm is the first big hurdle for these dogs. Now comes veterinary care, recovery, and the not-so-small task of learning how to live in a completely different world.

Humane World for Animalsâ rescue protocols include veterinary exams, vaccinations, respiratory screening when needed, and the health documents required for international travel. Each dog has their own needs. Some may need treatment for skin problems, wounds, dental disease, or nutritional deficiencies.

The second, and perhaps most challenging, hurdle for these dogs is adapting to a whole new way of life. Just because a dog has been saved doesn't automatically mean a dog feels safe.

Imagine never having lived in a home, then suddenly finding yourself surrounded by doors, stairs, strange noises, slippery floors, and humans who keep trying to show you how much they love you. Even a well-meaning hug could be overwhelming. And the vacuum cleaner? Let's just say it probably won't be winning any popularity contests.

These dogs may need to learn things many pets take for granted: how to explore a room, relax around people, or understand that a hand reaching toward them isn't something to fear. Some will be curious from the start. Others may prefer to watch from a safe distance. Neither response is wrong, and patience plus a little common sense go a long way.

A quiet place to rest, a predictable routine, and the freedom to explore without being pushed can help a dog settle in. Rewarding small steps with positive reinforcement builds confidence without turning every new experience into a test.

Adjusting to a new life takes time, and there's no need to rush it. A dog who hides under the table on day one isn't a failed adoption. A dog who isn't ready for cuddles isn't being ungrateful. Theyâre figuring things out, and they need time to decide that this strange new place might actually be safe. Building trust and confidence can be a slow process.

Those familiar with the process of adopting or fostering dogs, particularly those who may not have had the best start to life, may have heard of the 3-3-3 Rule for Dogs: 3 days, 3 weeks, 3 months. Itâs a simplified interpretation of the timeline many dogs tend to follow when adjusting to a new home environment.

The first 3 days are about decompression and resetting the nervous system. It might look like a dog that is timid, constantly moving, hiding, or even showing signs of aggression. Some dogs adjust quickly, while others may take a little longer than 3 days. The important thing to know is that this version of the dog is not usually a good representation of their true selves.

Over the first 3 weeks, dogs will start to gain confidence and explore their new world. They are often testing boundaries, becoming familiar with patterns, and learning how to trust. Being consistent and providing predictable routines is paramount to this process.

By the time 3 months have passed, most dogs will be feeling more settled. It may still take some time for their full personality to appear, but with every passing month, they become more confident, more trusting, and less anxious.

Sometimes progress looks like taking a treat from someone's hand. Sometimes it's finally falling asleep without startling at every sound. Those moments might not make a flashy before-and-after video, but for that dog, they're a big deal.

One more thing: fear and behavioural changes shouldn't automatically be dismissed as consequences of a dog's past. Pain, illness, and other medical problems can affect behaviour, too. If a dog seems persistently distressed or suddenly starts acting differently, a veterinary check is important. We don't want to assume it's trauma when there may be pain due to a treatable medical issue behind it.

A second chance isn't just getting a dog out of a cage. It's giving them the medical care, space, and time to discover that life can be safe, and maybe even pretty wonderful.

Humane World for Animals calls the Gangjin operation its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea. But that doesn't mean the work is over. The organization plans to continue monitoring the ban and supporting efforts to enforce it.

Closing farms is a huge win. Full stop. But making sure dogs aren't left behind, moved elsewhere, or subjected to illegal practices is part of making that win count. With the ban taking full effect in February 2027, the coming months will be crucial.

For the dogs already rescued, a new life is finally within reach. Veterinary care. Rehabilitation. A chance to find a home where the biggest worry is whether they get the good spot on the sofa. That's quite the upgrade.

Now, we turn our attention to the dogs still waiting in South Koreaâs remaining farms. Stopping the dog meat trade is a huge victory, but in many ways, itâs just the beginning. Saving these dogs is more than just stopping the slaughter. Itâs making sure they all get the happy ending they deserve.

#7910. Paws and Effect: The Reasons Behind a Cat’s Sudden Aggression

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

We all know that feline behavior can be somewhat unpredictable. Just when you think youâve got it all figured out, a cat is already three steps ahead of you. But thereâs a big difference between normal feline quirks and uncharacteristic aggression.

A cat that has always been gentle and suddenly starts lashing out may be reacting to something in its environment, changing hormones, pain, or a health problem. Aggression has many causes, from fear and frustration to competition with other cats. Understanding what has changed can help identify the cause and determine the best way to respond.

Unneutered male cats may fight over access to females, particularly when several cats are competing for mates in the same area. When a female cat is in heat, she may attract multiple males, making fights more likely.

Female cats can also behave differently during heat cycles. Many become unusually affectionate and demanding of attention, while others may become irritable or aggressive. Hormonal changes can also affect how they interact with other cats, particularly other females.

Spaying/neutering is an important aspect of taking care of a cat. Not only does it help to minimize aggression and friction between cats, but it also prevents unwanted litters and helps reduce the risk of certain diseases.

Pain can make even a normally friendly cat lash out. A cat may react aggressively if someone touches a sore area or approaches when it is feeling unwell.

Urinary tract disease can make a cat pretty miserable, and males in particular are vulnerable to urinary blockages, which are extremely painful and can become life-threatening. A cat that is straining to urinate or unable to pass urine needs emergency veterinary attention.

Infections, injuries, arthritis, and cancer are often painful but difficult to recognize from the outside. If aggression appears suddenly or seems linked to discomfort, a veterinary examination is an important first step.

A frightened cat may respond aggressively when startled, even if it is usually relaxed and friendly. A sudden noise, an unfamiliar person, or another threatening experience can trigger a defensive reaction.

Ongoing stress can also contribute to aggression. Cats that feel unsafe in their surroundings may remain on edge and react defensively to people or animals around them.

Every cat should have access to a quiet, comfortable place where it can retreat without being disturbed. Giving a frightened cat space can help it feel more secure.

Not every aggressive-looking interaction is driven by anger or fear. Play helps cats practise their hunting skills, and some become too rough when playing with people or other animals.

However, rough play should not be encouraged because biting and scratching can cause injuries. Rewarding gentle play and redirecting a cat toward appropriate toys can help it learn more acceptable ways to use its energy.

Cats can be protective of their territory, so the arrival of another animal may trigger aggression. The newcomer could be a new cat or dog in the household, or an outdoor cat that has started visiting the yard.

Sometimes, owners may not even realize another cat is nearby. Seeing or smelling an unfamiliar animal can leave a cat agitated, causing it to react to other pets or people.

Aggressive behavior plus inappropriate urination and scent-marking are not uncommon when a cat feels its territory is under threat.

A cat that becomes frustrated by something it cannot reach may take that frustration out on another target. This is known as redirected aggression.

For example, a cat might become agitated after seeing another cat outside, then lash out at a person or pet nearby. The target may have done nothing wrong and simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Giving an agitated cat time and space to calm down is safer than trying to handle it immediately.

Cats living together usually have established social relationships, and introducing a new pet tends to upset the status quo. A certain amount of fighting and posturing is to be expected as the cats adjust to the change, but escalating aggression or bullying of one cat should be addressed.

Introducing a new animal gradually can help reduce conflict. Cats should have time to become familiar with each other without being forced into close contact before they are ready.

Some cats seem to enjoy attention but suddenly bite or scratch once petting begins. A cat may become overstimulated by touch, or it may simply want to be near a person without being handled.

Watch for signs of discomfort, such as flattened ears or a flicking tail. If a cat seems agitated, stop petting and give it space. Treats can reward calm interactions when the cat is comfortable.

Aggression can be difficult for a household to manage, but many causes can be addressed with patience and the right approach. Rewarding calm behavior, avoiding known triggers, and providing a safe place to retreat can all help.

The first step is to work out why the cat is behaving differently. If the aggression is sudden, it may be linked to pain or illness, so you should always consult a veterinarian before treating it as a behavioral issue. Once medical causes are excluded, look for changes â both indoors and outside the home â that might be affecting your cat.

Simple steps like providing extra hiding places, calming aids, and adapting handling techniques can go a long way to reducing feline aggression.

#7909. Are Dogs the Secret to a Happier, Healthier Childhood?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Dogs have been a fixture of family life for thousands of years, and many people who grew up with one say they canât picture their childhood without them. Beyond the obvious benefits of companionship and fun, growing up with a dog has been shown to have positive effects on physical and emotional well-being; advantages that show up in how children handle friendships, feelings, and everyday challenges.

Of course, this doesnât mean that having a dog is right for everyone. Bringing a dog into your home is a big decision that affects budgets and daily routines for years to come, and the best outcomes tend to come from families who go in with open eyes.

For anyone considering life with a dog, here are a few ways they can improve a childâs life, and things to consider before adopting one.

Growing up around animals can lower the chance of developing allergies later on. Dogs, and all the things that come with living with them, expose children to a range of allergens, which helps build a more robust immune system. The key seems to be early exposure, which means the sooner a dog becomes part of a childâs world, the better.

Children who are close to their dogs tend to be more securely attached to their parents, and theyâre more likely to form strong friendships, too. Strong relationships in one part of a childâs life seem to go hand in hand with strong relationships in others. Kids who share more physical contact with their dogs, from cuddles to roughhousing, tend to get along better with their moms, dads, and friends.

Kids who grow up with a family dog tend to have lower rates of anxiety. The benefits reach well beyond childhood, too. Dogs can ease feelings of depression and anxiety in adults who went through childhood trauma, and they can reduce signs of post-traumatic stress, which is part of the reason theyâre so often brought into therapy.

A dog is a living, breathing creature with needs, and children who help care for one learn responsibility and dependability. A five-year-old canât take on every chore, but age-appropriate tasks are a great place to start. Young children spend much of their lives at the mercy of parents and teachers, so having a dog to look after can give them a real sense of empowerment and build self-esteem.

Caring for an animal from an early age also builds empathy, which supports emotional intelligence and helps a child grow into a more compassionate person. The lessons go on from there. Dogs model loyalty; training and bonding teach patience, and learning to read a dogâs body language and respect their boundaries teaches respect. When a family pet eventually passes away, children also learn about death and grieving.

Children with pets tend to have better self-esteem than children without them. The effect appears to be strongest as kids approach adolescence; an age when the emotional support of a companion animal may matter most.

Families with dogs tend to be more physically active than their peers, getting about 11 extra minutes of exercise a day. That may not sound like much, but it adds up to roughly 5.5 hours a month in a society that is growing more sedentary all the time.

For some children, the effect is far larger. Girls in particular gained around 52 minutes of light physical activity a day after a dog joined the family. The flip side was striking too, since girls who lost their pet saw their daily activity drop by 62 minutes.

Children tend to handle stressful moments better with a dog nearby. They feel happier and more at ease, and being able to touch the dog calms them even further. Simply having a furry companion close by seems to help kids feel steadier inside.

For all the upsides, adopting a dog isnât a decision to take lightly, and there are a few things every family needs to consider before racing out to get a four-legged friend.

Budget: Dogs depend on their owners for food, veterinary care, and emergencies, and a household budget that canât cover those costs is a reason to rethink the plan.

Age: Although many childhood benefits increase the earlier they start living with a dog, sometimes waiting until children are older is a good idea. St. Bernards make fantastic family pets, for example, but they can weigh as much as 180 pounds and can hurt a child accidentally. Small breeds have their own risks, since they can be fragile and prone to injury until kids learn boundaries and how to respect animals.

Lifestyle: A family that works long hours and spends every evening shuttling children to activities needs a plan for what the dog will be doing. Not every schedule has room for a pet, and that is perfectly fine, but a dog shouldnât be adopted without free time to spend with it.

Motivation: Children often beg for a dog, promising to walk, feed, and pick up after them.

Then, the novelty fades, and the adults end up with the bulk of the care. Although itâs a good idea to encourage children to take on some of the responsibility of looking after a dog, you should assume that youâll be the one doing most of the work â hope for the best, plan for the worst!

Growing up alongside a dog can bring real benefits, from fewer allergies and lower anxiety to stronger relationships and more time spent moving. But to enjoy the benefits of living with a dog, families need to have the time, money, and genuine desire to take care of one.

Growing up with a dog might not guarantee health and happiness, but itâs a pretty good place to start!

Just because it's your backyard doesn't mean you can burn whatever you like. Local ordinances and seasonal restrictions can complicate things.

Autumn leaves are the ornamental equivalent of spring flowers, nature’s fireworks show that excites and uplifts us. We love it when the green foliage of deciduous trees turns fiery shades and – leaf by leaf – drifts gracefully down to the ground. But the next act is unfortunate: mountains of fallen leaves and other fall debris that needs to be removed from the premises.

Raking up and carting away is one way to tackle fall cleanup, but it is tedious and time-consuming. Burning is a quicker, easier alternative – one match and the deed is done. But backyard burning is subject to a complicated patchwork of state laws, municipal ordinances, seasonal fire restrictions, and air-quality regulations. A fallen-leaf bonfire can result in fines or even a criminal complaint.

So is “burn, baby, burn” an appropriate way to deal with yard waste? I can't give a definitive yes or no, but as a former attorney, I will explain the general rules about the legality of burning yard waste and the consequences you might face if you do it wrong. It's exactly the kind of legal dilemma I cover in my Gardening Lawyer series. Here are the rules to check, along with safer alternatives for disposing of garden waste.

When a landscape issue has a legal component, you're unlikely to get a definitive yes-or-no answer. Instead, these issues depend on the applicable laws and ordinances. Whether you can legally burn yard waste in your backyard in the USA depends entirely on your state, county, and city ordinances, and current weather or fire-danger conditions. You’ll want to check with all of these authorities before burning, or ask a local landscape professional.

However, there are some general rules that usually apply. These give you a general idea of the restrictions that might be in place, what you can burn, whether burning is allowed, and what you can never burn.

The laws that restrict burning yard waste are far from uniform. More cities completely ban open burning of foliage all year long. These absolute prohibitions are based on community values like air quality issues. Nobody likes to breathe smoke, and burning green waste releases icky stuff: fine particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and toxic smoke.

Some states or counties allow you to burn dry leaves and brush, but with seasonal restrictions. These may specify certain months that burning is allowed, or it might ban burning entirely during dry seasons or high winds.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Other areas allow burning but control the size of the material to be burned (for example, permitting only a 6x6 foot (2x2 m) pile). Some laws impose setback requirements to keep the fires a safe distance from buildings and roads. Still others restrict when, during a day, piles can be burned. These can be seen as safety restrictions.

Other possible safety mandates include requiring that all fires be supervised by an adult during the entire burn, having a source of water near the fire, like a connected garden hose, and a requirement that the fire be wet down and the ashes stirred when the burn is done.

Even if your jurisdiction allows yard waste burning, that doesn’t mean you can burn anything and everything. If the law permits you to burn yard waste, there are always restrictions on the types of materials that can be burned. Generally, a homeowner living in an “okay-to-burn” jurisdiction can only burn dry, natural vegetation from plants on your property. This will include leaves, brush, limbs, grass clippings, and clean wood.

On the negative side, you should never expect to be permitted to burn personal garbage, paper, plastics, rubber, tires, painted or treated wood, construction debris, or chemicals of any kind. These can release dangerous dioxins and furans that settle into soil and local food chains.

The consequences for the Illegal burning of yard waste depend on the applicable laws. In general, thumbing your nose at burn bans or restrictions can lead to severe financial, legal, and environmental consequences.

The possible penalties fall into distinct categories:

Nobody wants to face these serious consequences of ignoring yard-debris burning restrictions. But you have to do something with all those leaves. What are your alternatives to burning?

If you shred fall leaves, small branches, and even grass cuttings, you can create an excellent compost. Spread this around your landscape. It will enrich your garden soil. It’s a good idea to invest in a shredder – like this Sun Joe Wood Chipper Shredder and Waste Shredding Machine – to speed up this process. You can also use shredded yard debris as eco-friendly mulch around the root area of trees and shrubs.

Many cities offer “compost” pickups the same day they take your garbage. In San Francisco, we get large green containers in which we can put any green-waste materials. They usually send these to a municipal recycling center.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

I remember when my mom brought home our first fosters. I was in fifth grade, and when my twin sister, Becca, and I came home from school, our mom walked us over to a box with three little neonatal kittens, just days old: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy. With closed eyes and little bodies running purely on instinct, they wriggled over one another, crying out to be fed. I watched as my mom gently picked them up, and as she did, she turned to us, smiling, and said, âtheyâre your responsibilityâ.

I was flooded with excitement and fear all at once. I knew nothing about caring for something so small. I watched in awe as my mom bottle-fed them one by one. The meowing subsided, and their little ears wiggled as they latched on and ate until their tiny bellies were full. The lesson had begun regardless of my fears. But feeding, I quickly learned, was just step one.

Soon after, we were stimulating each kitten to go potty, testing the temperature of their enclosure, wiping them clean, and getting them settled in for a post-bottle nap. So much happened so quickly, and they were so small and fragile. I told my mom I was nervous that I wouldnât be able to do what she did. She laughed and, with a grin, informed me I would have plenty of time to learn: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy would need to eat every 2 hours, even throughout the night. So we had lots of chances to practice and retain all the new skills she was showing us.

Over the next few weeks, we watched them grow and grow until they were ready to find their forever homes. As adoption day approached, it was incredibly hard. My sister and I begged our mom to let us keep the kittens. After all, we had raised them, and our love for them was undeniable. But she assured us that this was a good thing; letting them go meant we could help more animals in need. In the moment, however, I didnât understand. Instead, I cried myself to sleep holding the kittens. My kittens.

Then the day came, and even though the adopters were my friends, I bristled when they knocked at the door. But as they came in and met Amelia, Angel and Buddy, something magical happened: I watched my friends fall in love with them just like I had. They giggled at the clumsy way Buddy walked. Their hearts melted as they watched the girls cuddle in the sun. I was still scared to let the kittens go, but now part of me was excited, too. My friends saw them how I saw them. I had to trust that the little babies that we raised were on to bigger and better things. Things that would allow us to welcome another baby in need. But still, my heart broke - I had fallen in love with each of them, and saying goodbye terrified me.

There wasnât much time after they were adopted to worry about my fears, though. Before I knew it, we said hello to our next foster: a skittish and energetic 5-week-old boy we called Kipper. I thought maybe this time Iâd try to guard my heart, but Kipper stole it anyway. His silly antics and never-ending supply of energy made it impossible not to fall in love with him, too. Part of me hoped that maybe this time, Kipper could stay. But my mom held firm, and a few weeks later another friend came to us to adopt. I watched it play out all over again. I smiled as they swooned over this little precious kitten and all his quirks, just like I had.

This time, though I was still heartbroken, I felt a sense of understanding settle in, too. I remember thinking to myself, as Kipper fell asleep, purring, in my friendâs arms, âI wonder who we will get to help next?â

It didnât take long for that question to get its answer: Four tiny black-and-white kittens found in a hot tub and brought to our doorstep. Three were friendly; one, wellâ¦he was anything but! Cleo, Leo, and Brandy settled in beautifully, but Bindy just needed more.

More time, more attention, more understanding.

I felt drawn to him, and while my twin tended to the others, I found myself focused on Bindy. He would hide, hiss, spit, and bite. But really, he was just a little thing in a big world, and he was terrified. I worked with him every day, and slowly but surely, he made progress. When adoption day came around, however, we decided Bindy wasnât ready yet. He stayed behind to gain more confidence and, in time, became our first foster-fail.

Sometimes it was best for a foster to be adopted, but sometimes, they were already home.

Bindy eventually became the most loving cat I ever knew. He was my soul cat, and my best friend. And even though he stayed, I didnât avoid the heartbreak that came with saying goodbye; it just came many, many years later when old age finally took him. I learned a second lesson from Bindy then: there is no love without loss and, despite the pain, love would always be worth it.

So I continued to dive in, foster after foster. Heartbreak after heartbreak. Miracle after miracle. And it was always worth it; just like my mom said it would be. Iâm no longer the little girl learning from my mother; those lessons are now a part of me. Theyâre one of the things she left behind after a lifetime of love. My heart broke saying goodbye to her, too, but her teachings gave me a life thatâs filled to the brim with purpose. And paired with a passion inspired by my first foster fail, Bindy, I quickly developed a soft spot for the âspicyâ foster cats; and thatâs what I do now.

Currently, a euthanasia-list survivor is calling my home their safe haven. Just like Bindy, Simon wasterrified and aggressive, and he almost paid for it with his life. While Iâve been fostering him, however, Iâve gotten to know a completely different cat than the one in the shelter. A cat thatâs full of love and silly antics, whoâs eager to hold a conversation and meow for your attention. A cat who just needed a chance.

When his adoption day comes, I know my heart will break again; it always does. Itâs the price we pay for loving something, and Iâll pay that price over and over again because it means I get to watch someone adore him in all the ways I have, and more. The internet will go into an uproar demanding I keep him, but my momâs voice will sound clearly in my ear and keep me grounded:

âItâs a good thing. Letting them go means we can help others in need.â

So I'll say goodbye, knowing another Simon, Bindy, or Kipper is waiting for their chance to be loved. And as I walk back into the shelter, the lesson I began learning all those years ago in fifth grade remains true: Fostering Saves Lives.

#7905. War Dogs of History: Sergeant Stubby and the Birth of the American War Dog Legend

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

Stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in New Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

When the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

After surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

Stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

During the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

Conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

Stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a new generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

Stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Victoria and David Beckham’s tree uses golden-yellow bows instead of loads of ornaments. Experts explain how to copy it, from lights to bow spacing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bows are back and trending for Christmas 2026, as has been well and truly proven by Victoria and David Beckham.

Like trees, candy canes, and presents, bows are about as Christmassy as it gets. It’s the finishing touch on a really sparkly gift, the detail that truly brings out the beauty of a wreath or garlands, and it’s what makes a mantel look dressed for the holiday season.

O a Christmas tree, though? Why, it’s a very simple addition, but it can often prove itself to be the finishing touch that brings the whole thing to life.

Bows are popping up as the go-to Christmas tree ornament all over the place, from garden centers and social media, and it's all down to the likes of Kate Hudson and a whole host of other celebrities... including David and Victoria.

That's right; last Christmas saw the Beckhams decorate their traditional tree with golden-yellow bows rather than a massive collection of ornaments, and shared the results to Instagram.

Swipe to the second slide on the post below to check it out:

A post shared by Victoria Beckham (@victoriabeckham)

The vibe? Why, classy and unique (much as you'd expect from the stylish pair). It’s also way easier to copy than it looks, but it's important to remember that there are a few places where bow-trimmed trees tend do go wrong.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

To help you get it right, we consulted the pros. Here's what they had to say.

When trying to recreate the Beckhams' Christmas tree, most people start with the ribbon, which is a big mistake.

“Buy your lights before you buy your ribbon,” says Nadi Melam, founder and lead preservation artist at Florals Memories, who works with matching color to light. A golden-yellow bow can look orange once the tree is lit. “Warm light bulbs will add orange to anything they touch. Cool-white ones will remove any yellow.”

Interior designer Irena Cara, co-founder of Nova Wrap, recommends warm white as a general rule: “Use warm white lights and place them deep in the tree. Avoid tinsel and multicolored lights as they detract from the ribbon.”

Don't forget to do a test first. “Hold a strip of ribbon up to your lights before buying a full spool,” says Melam. “The wrong spool is your most expensive error.”

The key word here is restraint, and it’s what gives a bow tree like David and Victoria Beckham's tree that expertly designed look.

“Bows look planned when you select one ribbon color and one width,” says Melam. “You end up with too many choices if you use too many colors and widths. That’s what makes a tree look cluttered.”

Cara adds texture to the plan: “Velvet ribbon adds a nice textured element to a tree. Grosgrain and wired satin ribbon keep their shape and can also add nice detail to the tree.” Her limit is “no more than two finishes on the tree.”

While some Christmas trees look great with one oversized ribbon as per the above, those who want to emulate the Beckhams' Christmas tree need to get working on a few more bows than that.

In fact, Cara has a number in mind: “A tree is finished with 20 to 30 bows. They should be spaced about an arm’s length apart and staggered so they don’t form a straight line across the tree.”

Depth matters as much as spacing. “Place each bow deep within the tree, so the branches will embrace it,” says Melam. “If the bow is on the end of a branch, it will droop and move in the breeze.”

Cara’s main warning is about scale: “Decorating too small is the biggest faux pas. Tiny ornaments and thin ribbon get lost on a large tree.”

Do you ever feel completely satisfied when you decorate your Christmas tree only to get comfy on the sofa and realize you missed an entire side of it? “Look at your tree from all sides before you consider it finished,” says Melam.

Cara agrees: “A tree without decorations in the back and bottom of the tree looks unfinished.”

If the tree looks thin in places, definitely don’t make the mistake of adding more ornaments. “Add small evergreen sprigs into any gaps you see before you fill in more ornaments,” says Melam. “You create subtlety by making fewer design decisions and repeating those choices.”

Cara is clear that she’s a designer rather than a horticulturist, but she has noticed which trees hold up well. “The branches of a Fir, such as a Fraser or Nordmann, will keep an even shape and hold the needles better.”

A bow-led tree also helps the branches. “Heavier ornaments and a lot of ornaments on the tree cause the branches to break and bend over time, so place fewer, larger, and more considered ornaments on the tree.”

If you’re trying to be budget-conscious, bows are also a great idea as they’re a lot cheaper than a full set of ornaments. “Using a large, wide ribbon to make bows is cheaper than buying ornaments,” says Cara.

Melam’s advice is to put the money where it shows: “Spend on lights and high-quality ribbon, then use what you have to finish the job.” If you grow your own, she adds, “You can also use dried clippings from your garden as filler.”

Victoria and David Beckham don’t need a cluttered, crowded tree to make a big impression, and neither do you. Just pick the right lights, add a few golden ribbons, and you can get the same polished look in no time flat!

#7903. Impeach Pete Hegseth

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

He deserves it for his role in starting an unconstitutional war and perpetrating over 200 murders.

Outgoing GOP Representative Thomas Massie is planning to introduce an impeachment resolution against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Soon-to-be Democratic Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries says he's a "hard yes" on the idea. That makes it very likely it will happen. If not now, then when Democrats take control of Congress in January, after their big win in the midterm election. Hegseth richly deserves it, and should be convicted on at least two major charges: his role in starting an unconstitutional war and over 200 cases of outright murder.

On September 15, Rep. Massie outlined eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth (see here for his more detailed description). The two most compelling are these:

Article I - Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 2(c): Charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat. It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception….

Article V - Extrajudicial Killings: Charges Secretary Hegseth with replacing maritime law enforcement with unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers, resulting in at least 221 deaths. It also addresses denial of quarter, secondary strikes on survivors, failure to rescue shipwrecked persons, and the creation of artificial legal authorities for the campaign.

Massie's Article V is the single most damning, in my view. Hegseth is a principal architect of the Trump Administration's campaign of "drug boat" strikes in the Caribbean and the Pacific. It has now killed an estimated 244 people, virtually all of them civilians (Massie's September figure of 221 is now somewhat outdated).

I have previously written about why these strikes are illegal (see here and here). But don't take my word for it, or even that of other libertarian or left-liberal experts, like Brian Finucane. Take that of John Yoo, former Bush Administration official, and leading academic advocate of sweeping executive power over foreign policy and national security issues. If you illegally order the deliberate killing of civilians - especially outside the context of a war - that's outright murder. And that's exactly what Pete Hegseth has done.

This would be true even if those killed were all would-be drug dealers seeking to transport illegal drugs for sale in the US. I have previously explained why it is unjust and illegal to kill suspected drug dealers out of hand and why they are not the legal or moral equivalent of terrorists or enemy combatants in a war. As GOP Sen. Rand Paul pointed out when the drug boat strikes began, "The reason we have trials and we don't automatically assume guilt is what if we make a mistake and they happen to be people fleeing the Venezuelan dictator? … off our coast it isn't our policy just to blow people up … even the worst people in our country, they still get a trial." But, in fact, the evidence indicates most were not on their way to the US and many were not transporting drugs at all. Some, for example, were just fishermen.

The Constitution allows impeachment and removal of executive branch officials for "high crimes and misdemeanors." You don't have to be a lawyer or legal scholar to figure out that complicity in over 200 murders qualifies as a "high crime."

Hegseth is also a key architect of the disastrous Iran War. In previous writings, I have explained why that war is illegal, violating both the Constitution, and the War Powers Act of 1973. Such a war requires congressional authorization, and Trump and Hegseth did not even try to get it. The war's illegality is one of the main reasons for its failure to this point, as failure to secure the broad public support needed to get congressional authorization  ensured Trump lacked staying power to continue the fight effectively after the initial strikes didn't achieve a quick, decisive victory.

Initiating and waging an illegal war isn't a violation of criminal law (though perhaps it should be). But massive non-criminal illegal acts and abuses of power are impeachable under the history and original meaning of the Impeachment Clause of the Constitution. On that point, see analyses by Gene Healy of the Reason Foundation (formerly at the Cato Institute), and prominent conservative legal scholars Michael Stokes Paulsen (here, here, and here), and Keith Whittington. There are few bigger illegal abuses of power than starting a massive unconstitutional war.

In fairness, Trump and Hegseth are not alone in starting illegal wars. Barack Obama did it, too, with his unconstitutional wars against Libya and ISIS (which, for those keeping score, I condemned at the time). Obama likely deserved to be impeached, as well. But the fact that he got away with this illegality is no reason to spare Hegseth. To the contrary, past laxness is all the more reason to reestablish deterrence to prevent future wrongdoing. Furthermore, Trump and Hegseth's illegal war is on a much larger scale than Obama's were, and has had far worse results.

The only potentially valid objection to impeaching Hegseth is that it might fail, and backfire politically. But the Iran War is highly unpopular, and therefore impeachment on that basis is unlikely to backfire. The politics of the boat strikes is more debatable. The administration will surely try to defend them by arguing the victims deserved it because they were trying to smuggle dangerous drugs. But that can be countered by presenting the extensive evidence demonstrating that many were not on their way to the US or even transporting drugs at all. Testimony from members of the bereaved families of the victims can help make that point, and influence public opinion against Hegseth and the administration.

Hegseth is unpopular on Capitol Hill, which makes it potentially possible to secure the needed 11 or more GOP senators' votes required for conviction (the Democrats are going to have 54-56 senators in the next Congress, depending on the results of still-ongoing vote counts in close races in Alaska and Mississippi). But even if he gets acquitted, the process of impeachment and trial can send a useful signal, and further publicize the administration's massive criminality and wrongdoing.

Obviously, the ultimate perpetrator of these illegal acts is not Hegseth, but Trump. The former was following the latter's illegal orders (though he likely also helped influence Trump to give those orders in the first place). But sanctioning officials for obeying illegal orders is still important. That's one of the lessons of the Nuremberg trials. And, hopefully, the time will come for Trump to face sanctions for his many illegal actions, as well. As with Hegseth, the only plausible argument against impeaching him is political, not legal or moral.

Massie's impeachment resolution also outlines several other charges against Hegseth. I think most of them have merit, but are less significant than those covered above. I will not attempt to assess these other charges here.

UPDATE: Back in 2020, I critiqued the "slippery slope" argument against impeaching presidents for abuses of power that aren't technically crimes. My points apply with even greater force to any such argument against impeaching appointed officials, like Hegseth. In their case, there is no argument they have some kind of popular mandate from the electorate.

#7902. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.
