#7845. The Peaceful Second Amendment Revolution

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

How the right was restored from its nadir half a century ago

This speech was delivered during Wyoming Law Week at the University of Wyoming College of Law, October 13, 2026.

Ladies and gentlemen, cowboys and cowgirls, good evening.

The title of my presentation, "The Peaceful Second Amendment Revolution," is about a revolution in the original meaning of that word: a return to the original starting point, as when the earth completes a revolution around the sun.

The American Revolution began in that conservative sense. The Americans wanted the British to respect all their pre-existing rights, including the written right to arms from the 1689 English Bill of Rights.

Law Week is an appropriate time to reflect on the rule of law and the revolutionary role of lawyers, then and now.

Writing in 1789, after victory in the American Revolution, physician David Ramsay explained one reason for the Revolution: "The study of law was common and fashion­able." David Ramsay, 1 A History of the American Revolution 29 (Lester H. Cohen ed., Liberty Fund, 1990) (1789). According to Ramsay:

"No order of men has, in all ages, been more favourable to liberty, than lawyers. When they are not won over to the service of government, they are formidable adversaries to it. Professionally taught the rights of human nature, they keenly and quickly perceive every attack made upon them. While others judge of bad principles by the actual grievances they occasion, lawyers discover them at a distance, and trace future mischiefs from gilded innovations."

‍Ramsay pointed out that half of the First Continental Congress, in 1774, were lawyers.

"Bred in the habits of public speaking, they made a distinguished figure in the meetings of the people, and were particularly able to explain to them the tendency of the late acts of parlia­ment. Exerting their abilities and influence in the cause of their country, they were rewarded with its confidence."

We ought always feel gratitude to those lawyers, and other Americans, who defended and advanced natural rights during the American Revolution. Tonight is the story of how one of the rights which those lawyers and others had guaranteed in our Constitution was nearly obliterated during the last third of the twentieth century. And how the peaceful revolution that has restored the Second Amendment was the cooperative work of millions of Americans, especially lawyers, and among them, especially legal scholars.

Although the story does involve the recovery of the original meaning of Second Amendment, the story is also about living constitutionalism; the most important reason the right to keep and bear arms survived against the attempts to destroy it was that the right lives and thrives in the hearts and minds of the American people.

The U.S. Supreme Court decisions of District of Columbia v. Heller in 2008 and McDonald v. Chicago in 2010 were the opposite of cutting edge. Those decisions were lagging indicators. They were the long-term consequence of elections, of a generation of historical scholarship, and of the refusal of millions of ordinary people to accept that a right they had always exercised and cherished could be defined out of existence by unreasoned pronouncements.

During the nineteenth century, virtually all commentators and courts treated the right to keep and bear arms as a broad individual right, including for people not in the militia.

The most influential legal treatise of the early republic, St. George Tucker's American edition of Blackstone, described the Amendment as securing the rights of self-defense and resistance to tyranny.

Next came William Rawle's 1825 A View of the Constitution of the United States of America, which said that if either Congress or a state government, in "blind pursuit of inor­dinate power" should "attempt" "to disarm the people," "this amendment may be appealed to as a restraint on both."

The great Supreme Court Justice and prolific legal scholar Joseph Story wrote in 1840 that

"The right of the citizens to keep and bear arms has justly been considered, as the palladium of the liberties of a republic; since it offers a strong moral check against the usurpation and arbitrary power of rulers; and it will generally, even if these are successful in the first instance, enable the people to resist and triumph over them."

The preeminent constitutional writer of the latter 19th century was Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice and Michigan Law School Dean Thomas Cooley. In 1880 he explained that "The right is general." "[I]f the right were limited to those enrolled," in the militia, "the purpose of this guaranty might be defeated altogether by the action or neglect to act of the government it was meant to hold in check."

Congress agreed. When the former slave states attempted to keep the freedmen in de facto servitude by enacting Black Codes that forbade the freedmen to possess arms, or required them to obtain a license, the Reconstruction Congress in 1866 overrode President Andrew Johnson's veto and passed the Second Freedmen's Bureau Bill, guaranteeing the "consti­tutional right to bear arms" as among the "immunities and rights" of Americans. The Civil Rights Act and the Fourteenth Amendment were passed with a similar and oft-expressed intent.

The theory that the right to arms was actually not a right made its first substantial appearance in a 1905 Kansas Supreme Court decision, Salina v. Blaksley. The case involved a municipal ordinance against carrying a firearm while intoxicated; the ordinance was easy to uphold based on precedents from other states. But the Kansas court aimed to use the case to destroy the right. Section 4 of the 1859 Kansas Bill of Rights declared "that the people have the right to bear arms for their defense and security." Yet the Kansas court claimed that this provision, in the state constitution Bill of Rights, merely affirmed the inherent power to state government to conduct military activities. The Kansas court also claimed that the federal Second Amendment had the same, empty meaning.

The Kansas court could not cite a single authority for its radical propositions. For example, a Massachusetts case had said that the state constitution right to arms is not violated by requiring a permit for large armed parades. The Kansas court pretended that the Massachusetts court had declared that there is no right to arms.

Based on how the U.S. Supreme Court had misinterpreted the Fourteenth Amendment in The Slaughterhouse Cases and U.S. v. Cruikshank in the 1870s, the Second Amendment, like most of the rest of the Bill of Rights, was not considered applicable to the States in the latter 19th and 20th centuries. State courts varied in how strictly they enforced their state constitution right to arms.

In 1934, Congress passed the first major federal gun control law, the National Firearms Act, which required a hefty $200 tax and registration for a small subset of arms, including machine guns and short-barreled shotguns. The Supreme Court said in U.S. v. Miller that the short-barreled shotgun owned by a bootlegger had not been shown to be the sort of arm useful to a militia, and it upheld the National Firearms Act on that narrow ground. Notably, the Court was very interested in Miller's weapon, and did not even mention that Miller while bootlegging was not actively serving in the Arkansas militia.

The Supreme Court's decision was consistent with the most restrictive line of state constitution cases from the 19th century, all of which came from States of the Confederacy: every individual citizen had the right to arms, but only for the types of arms used in "civilized warfare." For example, rifles, swords, or large handguns, but not pocket pistols.

The First Circuit, in the 1942 Cases v. United States, said it would not follow Miller any further than Miller's particular holding about the short-barreled shotgun. According to Cases, the Miller rule, if generalized, would protect far too many weapons.

That same year, the Third Circuit in U.S. v. Tot asserted that the Second Amendment "was not adopted with individual rights in mind," and further asserted that the Supreme Court had said so in Miller.

Congress did not think so. Shortly before U.S. entry in World War II, the U.S. Congress passed the Property Requisition Act, to allow the executive branch to seize, with full compensation, property needed for the national defense. Except for firearms. The federal government could not seize or register firearms possessed "by any individual for his personal protection or sport." The government could not "impair or infringe in any manner the right of any individual to keep and bear arms." The committee report explained that right to arms protections were "[i]n view of the fact that certain totalitarian and dictatorial nations are now engaged in the willful and wholesale destruction of personal rights and liberties."

But things changed drastically starting in the late 1960s. First, by then the original public meaning of much of the Bill of Rights and of the Fourteenth Amendment had been long forgotten. Many original source documents were not available in any practical sense to federal or state court libraries. For example, David Young' 1997 book The Origin of Second Amendment would compile hundreds of original documents about the right to arms from 1787 to 1792; as of the 1960s or 1970s, most of these documents existed in archives, and were waiting to be rediscovered by scholars and published in modern anthologies. But not yet.

Beginning in the mid-1960s, surging violent crime rates and race riots all over America terrified the public. In 1963, President Kennedy was assassinated by a communist using a mail-order rifle; then in April 1968 Martin Luther King was assassinated by a racist using a rifle; and then in June Senator Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated by an anti-Jewish Jordanian immigrant using a cheap imported handgun.

Connecticut Senator Thomas Dodd was Chairman of the Senate Subcommittee on Juvenile Delinquency and in the early 1960s he had been criticizing violence on television and cinema. But under pressure from Hollywood and from advertisers, Dodd had shifted his focus to guns, and in 1968, after the second Kennedy assassination, he was able to pass the Gun Control Act of 1968. As amended, it is still the major federal gun control law.

The Act banned mail-order gun sales, outlawed the import of inexpensive pistols, and imposed many other controls. But it did not fulfill the objectives of President Lyndon Johnson and other advocates for national gun licensing or national gun registration.

Most notably, from the viewpoint of the federal courts, the Act greatly expanded the categories of persons who were forbidden by federal law to possess a firearm or ammunition. Prosecutorial resources for such crimes were also greatly augmented.

Soon, the federal courts were hearing many cases from convicted felons, whose desperate public defenders were arguing that prohibiting a convicted violent felon from possessing a firearm violated the Second Amendment.

In 1973, the Office of Legal Counsel under President Nixon, who personally opposed all firearms ownership by citizens, wrote a formal opinion that there is no personal constitutional right under the Second Amendment to own or use a gun.

The federal judges appointed by Presidents Johnson and Nixon tended to be hostile to gun ownership. So rather than simply upholding bans on gun possession by convicted violent felons, many federal courts denied that there was an individual Second Amendment right. Instead, the right was said to a "collective" right that no individual could exercise. This is similar to "collective property" in communist dictatorships, where property supposedly belongs to all the people, but in fact only to the government.

Or the right was said to a "States' right," although nobody who said so could articulate what this right was. Or why the authors of the U.S. Constitution, who repeatedly used the word "State" or "States" to identify states' rights, had momentarily forgotten when they were writing the Second Amendment, and had written "the People" when they actually meant "the States."

The judicial opinions were typically terse and contemptuous, often consisting of string cites of post-1968 federal cases, all of which traced back to Tot or Cases. The opinions dared not quote the Supreme Court's words in Miller that in the Second Amendment's militia, "ordinarily when called for service these men were expected to appear bearing arms supplied by them­selves and of the kind in common use at the time."

The purpose of the nullificatory lower court opinions was not to describe what the Second Amendment was. Rather, the effort was to declare by ipse dixit that there was no individual right. The effort reached its zenith of absurdity in a 1975 report of the American Bar Association asserting, "It is doubtful that the founding fathers had any intent in mind with regard to [the] meaning of this amendment." Ben R. Miller, The Legal Basis for Firearms Controls, 100 Ann. Rep. A.B.A. 1050, 1052 (1975).

So according to the ABA, the Second Amendment was essentially similar to the Beatles song "I am the Walrus," for which John Lennon wrote nonsense lyrics to get even with people who overanalyzed Beatles songs.

Man, you should have seen them kicking Edgar Allan Poe.

In 1974, two national groups were formed in the District of Columbia to ban handguns, although they later expanded their objectives to include long guns. The National Coalition to Ban Handguns is now known as the Coalition to Stop Gun Violence. The other was the National Council to Control Handguns, which after several name changes is today known as Brady.

The leader of the latter group explained the strategy to The New Yorker in 1976: "The first problem is to slow down the increasing number of handguns being produced and sold in this country. The second problem is to get handguns registered." Finally, make "totally illegal" "the possession of all handguns and all handgun ammunition," except for the government and a few exceptions, such as licensed collectors.

Shortly after Congress granted the District of Columbia home rule, the District Council in 1975 took the initiative and banned handguns and forbade residents from keeping any firearm loaded and assembled for self-defense inside the home.

In 1976, Massachusetts put a handgun confiscation measure on the ballot. Although early polling was favorable, the measure lost, 69% to 31%. It even lost in Boston. Although the Boston police chief was a fervent advocate, the rest of law enforcement, including police unions and police chiefs, was almost unanimously opposed. They pointed out the ban would not affect criminals but would disarm law-abiding citizens, including off-duty police.

After the landslide defeat, an official with the League of Women Voters (which had vigorously supported the ban) said, "I think a lot of voters have that idea that this was designed to get guns away from the criminals. That's not the real purpose."

In the opinion of the gun confiscation movement, the American people are not capable of keeping firearms in their home without eventually harming themselves.

Morton Grove, Illinois, banned handguns in 1981, and during the next several years, Chicago and five more nearby suburbs followed suit. But the reaction across the rest of the country was a wave of state preemption laws. Legislatures decided that cities would not be allowed to outlaw firearms the state itself permitted. Within a few years, the possibility of municipal gun bans had been eliminated in most states.

Prohibitionists tried next in California in 1982, with a ballot initiative for a "handgun freeze." Unlike the Massachusetts measure, the California freeze would allow current owners to keep their handguns.

The California initiative was defeated by a vote of 63% to 37%. Opposition to the freeze brought so many additional voters to the polls that they even carried the Republican to a 1% victory for Governor.

In 1993-94, President Clinton was enthusiastically supporting gun control, and so the confiscation lobbies tried ballot initiatives in three left-leaning cities in Wisconsin, one of the few states without preemption. After confiscation was defeated in Milwaukee, Kenosha, and even in Madison, the backlash led to the enactment of Wisconsin preemption, and then to a state constitution right to arms adopted with 73% voter support.

Nationally, President Clinton worked tirelessly on gun control, passing a major anti-crime bill September 1994 that included a 10-year ban on the sale or manufacture of many semiautomatic firearms and on standard magazines over 10 rounds.

In November 1994, Democrats lost control of the U.S. House for the first time since 1953. President Clinton said, "The NRA is the reason the Republicans control the House." A Conversation with President Clinton, Cleveland Plain Dealer, Jan. 14, 1995, at 11B. Clinton also blamed the NRA for the 1993 defeat of New Jersey Governor James Florio, who had signed a similar ban.

At the state level, the 1994 elections led to tremendous changes in state gun laws. State after state enacted standardized, objective Shall Issue licensing for handgun carry permits; new or enhanced preemption laws to eliminate local gun control; instant checks to replace state-level waiting periods for handgun purchases; range protection bills to prevent noise nuisance suits against shooting ranges; and other right to arms measures.

In 1999, the murders of 12 students and one teacher at Columbine High School south of Denver reinvigorated the gun control movement. Indeed, in many states and in Congress, the immediate aftermath of a mass shooting is the only opportunity for antigun activists to win legislative victories. A few weeks after Columbine, Vice President Al Gore cast the tie-breaking vote in the U.S. Senate for an amendment to a juvenile crime bill that would have given the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives the administrative power to shut down any or all gun shows in the United States.

The 2000 presidential election promised to be the great showdown on gun control. Like the election of 1800 for the First Amendment (when the Sedition Act was being used to silence Republican opposition to the Federalists), the 2000 election would decide the fate of the Second Amendment.

In response to a letter from a concerned citizen, Clinton's Solicitor General Seth Waxman articulated the DOJ's position that "the Second Amendment does not extend an individual right to keep and bear arms." Quoting the citizen's letter, Waxman concurred that the government believes that it "could 'take guns away from the public,' and 'restrict ownership of rifles, pistols and shotguns from all people.'" The NRA put Waxman's "take guns" quote on billboards in swing states.

President Clinton later wrote that the NRA had been the reason that his Vice-President Al Gore lost five swing states in the Southeast, and hence the election.

The Justice Department under President George W. Bush withdrew the old Nixon administration opinion. In its place came an Office of Legal Counsel opinion over 100 pages, affirming the individual right.

Bush won re-election by a close margin in 2004, contrasting his support of gun rights with Massachusetts Senator John Kerry, an ardent gun control advocate. That election would made the difference in the 5-4 decision in District of Columbia v. Heller, decided at the end of President Bush's second term in 2008. President Bush had nominated John Roberts and Samuel Alito; whereas the Democratic shortlist included former Solicitors General Seth Waxman and Walter Dellinger and D.C. Circuit Judges David Tatel and Merrick Garland, all of whom defended handgun bans.

State Constitution ballot measures are the highest possible means by which the people can express their views on what ought to be a right. Since 1978, 17 states by vote of the people have added or strengthened state constitution right-to-arms provisions. (In 2026, Arkansas.) Not a single proposed amendment to fortify the right has ever been defeated at the ballot box.

Starting in the 1970s, pollsters began asking Americans if they believed they had a constitutional right to arms, and large majorities always said yes.

But not the large majority of the scholarly and legal elites, starting in the 1960s. To many of them, the notion that an ordinary American had a right to own a firearm and use it for self-defense was unbearable. The idea could not even be considered.

Those who did dare consider it tended to be practicing lawyers, whose professional livelihood did not depend on the approval of law professors. Starting in the 1970s, Virginia attorney Stephen Halbrook did more than anyone else to found the field of firearms law. His career record in U.S. Supreme Court merits cases is five wins and zero loses, including Printz v. United States in 1997, one of the most important modern federalism decisions, and NRA v. Oak Park, the companion case to McDonald v. Chicago in 2010, making he Second Amendment enforceable against the States via the Fourteenth Amendment.

Author of the Thomson West treatise on Firearms Law, Halbrook has been a prolific author of law journal articles and books, especially on the history of the right to arms.

He has taken full advantage of the fact that, because every law school has at least one law review, law has many more scholarly journals than do most other disciplines, so there is much more room for publication of articles that do not conform to the conventional wisdom of the moment.

Next to Halbrook, the lawyer who did the most in the long term for the restoration of the Second Amendment was the late Don Kates. As a Yale Law Student, Kates had volunteered for the 1964 Freedom Summer, to provide support for rural Black Mississippians to register to vote. In late June, three civil rights workers were murdered.

Kates adopted the longstanding practices of the Black and White civil rights workers who lived in the South fulltime: carrying firearms for protection against the Ku Klux Klan and other violent white supremacists who were tacitly supported by local law enforcement. After graduation, Kates went to work for California Rural Legal Assistance, and was soon named poverty lawyer of the year by the National Legal Aid and Defender Association.

Kates began to specialize in firearms law, and he too became a prolific scholar. In 1983, the Michigan Law Review, including me as a student citechecker, published Kates' article "Handgun Prohibition and the Original Meaning of the Second Amendment."

The Kates article in the Michigan Law Review was the first article about the Second Amendment  that had appeared in what was then a top-5 law review since the early 20th century. Professor William Van Alstyne, who was an eminent constitutional law textbook author and very liberal, later recounted that "this pipsqueak Kates," who was not a law professor, had convinced many of the leading constitutional law professors that the Second Amendment really was an individual right.

But none dared express that idea in print. That is why Sanford Levinson, also a very eminent and very liberal constitutional law professor, titled his 1989 essay in the Yale Law Journal "The Embarrassing Second Amendment." He wrote:

"I cannot help but suspect that the best explanation for the absence of the Second Amendment from the legal consciousness of the elite bar, including that component found in the legal academy, is derived from a mixture of sheer opposition to the idea of private ownership of guns and the perhaps subconscious fear that altogether plausible, perhaps even 'winning,' interpretations of the Second Amendment would present real hurdles to those of us supporting prohibitory regulation."

Reassured by Levinson's grant of respectability and permission, many law scholars began to explore the unknown-to-them legal history of the Second Amendment. The large majority found the Second Amendment to guarantee a normal individual right. Other explorers  agreed that the Second Amendment was meant to be an individual right, but argued that the right no longer existed because conditions had changed; for example, the American people today are no longer virtuous and unified, as they supposedly were in 1791.

Besides Halbrook and Kates, there were many other lawyers and professors who played a role, including Arizona attorney David Hardy since 1974.

Federal courts often move slowly. It took until 2001 for a modern federal circuit panel, the Fifth Circuit in United States v. Emerson, to hold that the Second Amendment is an individual right.

The next Circuit to come around was the D.C. Circuit in 2007, whose decision striking the D.C. handgun ban would be affirmed by the Supreme Court the next year in Heller.

By the time Heller was being briefed in December 2007, even the gun ban groups had given up on the "collective right" theory that had once been hegemonic in elite circles. Only one amicus brief in support of the D.C. ban argued for the collective right theory at length, and it came from President Clinton's former Attorney General Janet Reno and some other former officials.

The Supreme Court in Heller ruled unanimously that the Second Amendment was an individual right. Justice Stevens' dissent expressly rejected the collective right. Instead, he described the Second Amendment as a narrow individual right that could only be asserted by individuals who were upholding a state's interest in its militia. That particular theory had been invented in 1989 by gun control attorney Dennis Henigan, who had studied the issue in enough depth to realize that the negation of an individual Second Amendment right was untenable.

The problem for Henigan and other supporters of the DC handgun ban was that the text of the Second Amendment guaranteed "the right of the People," and not "the right only of people actively serving in the militia." Since the 1990s, scholars had been calling the normal individual right for the general public "the standard model." The standard model was standard because it had been the standard model throughout the first century of the Second Amendment.

The standard model never forbade all gun control. In constitutional litigation over the Second Amendment or other liberties safeguarded by the Bill of Rights, the standard result is that the civil rights advocates and opponents each win sometimes and lose sometimes.

That is where the Second Amendment is today; as in the Early Republic and thereafter, there will always be disputes about what it means for the right to be "infringed." Many gun controls are not even challenged, and when there are challenges, the government usually wins. But not always, because the Second Amendment is today recognized as a meaningful and enforceable constitutional right that safeguards  natural right.

In the United States of America, the Rule of Law includes the government obeying the Constitution; the freedom of speech, including academic speech; free elections; and the leading role of liberty-minded lawyers in public life. All of these combined the rescue a fundamental right from a nadir half a century ago. The revolutionary restoration of the right to arms was accomplished peacefully, thanks to and because of the Rule of Law. This week, let us celebrate the Rule of Law, and let each of us honor it with our conduct every day of the year.

Further discussion, including citations, can be found in Kopel, The Great Gun Control War of the 20th Century--and its Lessons for Today, 39 Fordham Urban Law Journal 1257 (2012); and The Right to Arms in the Living Constitution, 2010 Cardozo Law Review de Novo 99.

David Kopel is research director at the Independence Institute.

#7844. The Best Benchtop Planers, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Glenda Taylor, Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Benchtop planers—box-shaped power tools that reduce board thickness while smoothing the surface—top many a woodcrafter’s wish list. They fine-tune the wood used to create cabinets, bookshelves, and more, replacing old-fashioned hand planes because they’re much faster and easier to use.

Like our readers, we wanted to know which of today’s popular models perform well in real workshop situations, so we tested them. We selected highly rated benchtop planers and started planing boards—hundreds of ’em! We also reached out to Jay Sanders, licensed contractor and owner of Castle Dream Construction, a home remodeling company based in Baltimore, Maryland, to get his insights on what to consider when shopping for one.

After testing, we liked the 15-amp DeWalt 13-Inch 3-Knife 2-Speed Thickness Planer the best. We chose it based on its built-in infeed and outfeed tables, fan-assisted chip ejection vacuums, and impressive speed.

Keep reading to find out how the following models earned a spot in this lineup of the best benchtop planers for DIYers and seasoned woodworkers.

Bottom line: Our tests reveal top benchtop planers for various needs, with DeWalt leading for overall performance and versatility.

Investing in the right benchtop planer is important for anyone who’s into woodworking. We put the top DIY and professional models through their paces and scrutinized each. The models that earned a spot in our lineup are among the best benchtop thickness planers available today, so one is likely to find a favored place in your workshop.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Board Capacity 5/5; Dust 4.7/5; Value 4.8/5

Those in the market for a high-capacity planer with plenty of features will want to consider the DeWalt 13-inch thickness planer. This benchtop planer can handle materials up to a 13-inch width capacity with a 6-inch length. This heavy planer weighs in at 92 pounds, and we found its weight was beneficial in keeping it in one place during operation. We put the planer on a reinforced work surface—this tool is too heavy for most portable-type bolt holes in the base.

We’re familiar with the high quality of many DeWalt tools, and this thickness planer is no exception. It boasts a powerful 15-amp motor and a three-blade cutterhead that spins at 10,000 revolutions per minute (rpm). It can be set to plane off as much as ⅛ inch of wood in a single pass. It comes standard with front and back stainless steel infeed and outfeed tables that help support the boards as they pass through the planer. A unique option on this benchtop planer is the ability to adjust the feed speed. A lever on the front let us select either 96 or 179 cuts per inch (cpi). At 95 cpi, the DeWalt planer pulled the boards through twice as quickly as when we selected 179 cpi, but the surface was slightly rougher. Interestingly, even at 96 cpi, we found the boards were smooth enough for most high-end woodworking. At 179 cpi, they felt as though they’d already been sanded. This is in large part because of the three straight blades in the DeWalt planer. Most of today’s planers have only two blades.

We planed dozens of boards with the DeWalt model: softwoods, including pine and cedar; and hardwoods, including ash, oak, and walnut. The DeWalt planed all of them smoothly, and we found little to no snipe on any of the boards. We attributed this benefit to an extension outfeed table that helps support the boards as they exit the machine. The benchtop planer has a fan-assisted chip-ejection port on the back of the machine that we connected to our dust-collection system. The chip-ejection fan is so powerful that when we walked behind the machine to grab the board as it passed through, the chips stung when they hit us. Impressive! And slightly painful. The downside is that the chip-ejection port is positioned just over the outfeed table, so the hose on our dust-collection system kept dipping down and interfering with the boards as they exited the planer. Our makeshift fix was to tie the hose up to keep it out of the way.

We believe this top-notch planer would be an asset in any DIYer or woodcrafter’s shop. It’s powerful, the feed speed is adjustable, and the ruler gauge is accurate. (We measured the planed boards with calipers to determine gauge accuracy.) The model comes with a “bump” on/off switch in the front that allowed us to shut the machine down simply by bumping the switch with our hand or arm. This is a safety feature in the event something goes wrong—such as a board getting caught sideways or an article of clothing getting drawn into the machine. Just a bump, and the DeWalt shuts down.

What our tester says: “I am a firm believer in ‘buy it once, use it forever,’ and the DeWalt DW735 feels like that kind of tool. Hardwood, softwood, fresh and sappy or old and dried boards, the finished faces always come out clean and smooth.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews writer and tester

See our full review: DeWalt 13-Inch 3-Knife 2-Speed Thickness Planer

Get the DeWalt benchtop planer at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

When selecting the best benchtop planers, Sanders considers several factors, including cutterhead type, power, and whether the benchtop planer comes with a table that supports the boards. We looked at all of these factors during the selection process, plus we considered how well each planer rated with experienced users. We also considered the brand to an extent. After all, manufacturers such as DeWalt, Makita, and Craftsman have top-notch reputations in the power tool industry. We didn’t stick with just those three; we also included additional highly rated models from other manufacturers.

We unboxed and set up the benchtop planers according to manufacturer specifications. Then, we started planing new wood, reclaimed wood, softwood boards, and hardwood boards. We paid special attention to how smooth the planers left the board surfaces and whether the machines left snipes (unwanted cuts in the last few inches of the board).

We analyzed overall performance and ease of use and awarded points based on a rubric. The better a planer performed, the higher the points. After testing, we averaged the points to help determine the best category and intended use.

Benchtop planers, also known as “thickness planers” because they reduce the thickness of a board, have rotating blades inside that shave off a thin layer of wood. Those who are interested in owning one but don’t have a lot of experience with this powerful tool will want to keep the following factors and features in mind when shopping.

A benchtop planer’s motor needs enough power to get the job done. How much is enough depends on specific projects.

If users work primarily with softer woods such as pine, cedar, and fir—for building country-style furniture or birdhouses, for example—a motor in the 1- to 1½-horsepower (hp) range might suit them well. A thickness planer doesn’t need much juice to shave a layer off the top of these materials.

However, if users are into high-end joinery or cabinetry, they’ll probably work with species such as oak, maple, and even walnut. These hard materials will require more from a planer to shave them down, so they’ll want to look for a 2 hp tool.

Perhaps even more important than horsepower is a planer’s motor rating—choose one with a 15-amp motor. Planers draw a lot of electricity, and Sanders suggests getting a powerful one. “Look for at least a 15-amp motor with multiple speed options,” he advises. A 15-amp motor helps ensure the machine can handle the task without breaking down. Smaller-amperage motors don’t have the power necessary for planing wood.

Thickness planer blades (or knives) come in different styles. “The three main options are straight knife, helical, and spiral/helix,” Sanders says. “The straight knife is the most affordable but produces more tear-out. Helical and spiral cut cleaner but cost more upfront. Spiral cutter heads are generally regarded as producing the best finish.”

Blades vary on straight-knife cutter models. Some are reversible, so when they become dull, the user can turn them over and use the other side. Others have only one sharp edge, but they can be manually sharpened with a standard sharpening stone, just like a kitchen knife. Reversible knives are disposable, meant to be tossed out after both sides wear down.

All the planers we tested came with cutterheads designed to accept straight blades.

Cutting depth refers to how much material a wood planer can remove in one pass. Generally speaking, the more powerful the planer, the more material it can remove in one pass and the larger the depth of cut.

Planers that can shave off up to ⅛ inch at a time are good for removing the surface of rough or weathered wood. Removing that much depth at once, however, isn’t always optimal. Generally, it’s usually best for the board—and for the machine—to err on the side of caution and plane off thinner amounts. The more wood a planer removes in a pass, the harder it must work, which can lead to overheating if the user is planing a lot of boards.

Many woodworkers will find little need to remove more than 1/16 inch per pass, and for fine-tuning boards, they will remove even less—1/32 or 1/64 inch. Don’t pass up a planer just because it doesn’t remove ⅛ inch per pass. It’s easy enough to set the planer at 1/16 inch and then run it through twice.

A thickness planer’s allowance indicates the widest (and tallest) board that can be passed through the tool. Manufacturers label most planers with ranges between 12 inches and 13 inches (plenty for most woodworking hobbyists), but this metric doesn’t tell the whole story.

For example, a 12-inch planer can handle a board 12 inches in width capacity, but that does not say how thick (i.e., tall) a piece of wood the planer can handle. This metric is quite helpful, so look for a model that can handle materials as thick as 5 or 6 inches to get the most use out of a wood planer.

Snipe refers to an undesirable line, which can sometimes be very noticeable, left on the top end of a board after planing. It’s the result of the wood planer removing more wood at the end of the board. As the end of the board clears the first set of rollers, gravity tends to pull the board downward, which puts pressure on the other end. When this happens, the cutterhead blades may remove slightly more wood at the very end. A snipe looks like a thin dip, usually less than 1/16 inch, located along the last couple inches of the board.

“Longer infeed and outfeed tables help support boards and minimize snipe,” Sanders explains. He adds that “36-inch to 44-inch tables are good for a benchtop planer.” Just make sure they fold down for storage. Snipe may be unavoidable to some degree, but some benchtop thickness planers do better than others at minimizing its effect. A good way to avoid snipe appearing on a  finished product is to leave boards longer than necessary by an inch or so when planning and then cut the sniped ends off before using the board for your project.

Shaving the intended amount of wood off your workpieces can be tedious. Bringing a hardwood board from a 1-inch thickness to a ⅝-inch thickness, for example, could take five or six passes. The user could measure the board’s thickness before each pass and adjust the cutterhead using a tape measure or a combination square, but that’s time-consuming.

Many of today’s benchtop planers have a built-in gauge that looks like a ruler attached to the side of the intake slot. The gauge will indicate the proposed board thickness as the user raises or lowers the planer’s carriage (the top part of the tool that moves up and down) via a hand crank.

Planer gauges typically show measurements in 1/16-inch increments, but some show measurements in 1/64-inch increments. Some experienced woodworkers don’t use the gauge at all but rather determine cutting depth with the tool’s hand crank. On a planer, a complete revolution of its hand crank equals 1/16 inch. Half a crank equals 1/32 inch, and a quarter of a crank equals 1/64 inch.

A depth stop is a feature that keeps the user from shaving off more than the machine’s maximum cutting depth. For example, if the planer has a maximum cutting depth of ⅛ inch, the depth stop will prevent the user from inserting any board more than ⅛ inch thicker than the thickness chosen on the gauge (ruler). The board simply will not go into the slot. In this way, users needn’t worry about taking off more than the maximum cutting depth because the depth stop won’t allow it.

Thickness planers create a good deal of dust and wood chips. These machines rip off and spit out tiny pieces of wood, and the floor under a thickness planer will resemble a child’s sandbox after only a few boards.

Many of today’s benchtop planers have dust ports that attach to a shop vacuum or dust-collection system to minimize the mess. These collection systems also do a good job of removing the dust from the machine before it can settle in the cutterhead, helping to maintain its usable life and cutting speed.

Different speeds apply to a benchtop planer: cutterhead speed, cutting speed, and feed speed.

Alongside other popular power tools, such as band saws, table saws, and wood lathes, benchtop thickness planers are a boon in a woodworking shop. If this is your first planer, you will probably have questions about the tool’s best use and operation. Ahead are answers to some of the most common questions about benchtop planers. If you still want more information about your benchtop planer, refer to the user’s manual or contact the manufacturer.

Similar to hand planes, benchtop planers reduce the thickness of a board. Woodcrafters can use them to create consistent thicknesses on several boards for woodworking purposes or to uncover the beauty hidden underneath reclaimed wood.

With the benchtop planer turned off, place a board in the intake feed slot. Lower the roller carriage (the top part of the planer) using the hand crank until it just touches the board. This is the starting point. Remove the board, and then use the crank to lower the roller carriage to the desired cutting depth (typically between 1/64 and ⅛ inch). The woodworker can use the ruler gauge to determine the cutting depth or use the crank rule of thumb—one full revolution of the crank equals 1/16 inch. Once the cutting height is decided, turn the planer on and slowly feed the board into the intake slot. The planer will do the rest—users don’t have to push the board.

Planers reduce the thickness of a board by shaving a uniform amount of wood off its surface. Jointers make the board flat by shaving away only the high spots, not the entire surface, as a planer does.

Wood planers can be some of the heaviest tools in your shop. Benchtop planers weigh an average of between 60 and 100 pounds, so it may be wise to keep it on a benchtop rather than moving it around.

#7840. Does the President's Removal Power Extend to the Voice of America?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The DC Circuit affirms an injunction barring the removal of VOA head Michael Abramowicz. Will the justices see the case the same way?

Trump v. Slaughter affirmed the President's presumptive power to remove principal officers (other than members of the Federal Reserve Board). But does this power also extend to inferior officers? And is it constitutional for Congress to effectively insulate some inferior officers from presidential removal?

Today, in Abramowitz v. Lake, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit affirmed a district court injunction barring the removal of Michael Abramowitz, the head of the Voice of America. In the process, it rejected the Department of Justice's arguments that the district court lacked jurisdiction to consider the case and held Congress may (as a practical matter) insulate inferior officers by presidential removal by vesting removal authority in the hands of an agency head that requires Senate confirmation.

Judge Pillard wrote for the panel, and was joined by Judges Srinivasan and Pan. Here is how she summarized the opinion.

Seeking to preserve the journalistic integrity of the news broadcasters within the U.S. Agency for Global Media, Congress empowered a separate agency, the International Broadcasting Advisory Board, with final authority over the hiring and firing of the broadcasters' heads-of-network. The leaders of the Agency for Global Media ignored that statute when they attempted unilaterally to fire Michael Abramowitz, the head of Voice of America. Abramowitz sued, and the district court permanently enjoined the Agency for Global Media from removing Abramowitz without the International Broadcasting Advisory Board's approval.

We affirm the injunction. The district court had jurisdiction to enforce the statutory requirements governing the Voice of America directorship. Those statutory requirements are consistent with Article II. And the district court had equitable power to enjoin defendants from effectuating the illegal termination.

While acknowledging that, as a general matter, Congress has channeled litigation concerning allegedly improper removal of government employees to the Merit Systems Protection Board under the Civil Service Reform Act, the panel concluded that this general rule does not apply to the VOA as "Congress gave no hint" that it sought to divest district courts of jurisdiction to hear cases such as this when it revised the statute governing VOA in 2021. The removal protection of the VOA head "is not a standard employment law," according to the D.C. Circuit, "but a durable barrier against any breach of the firewall protecting the journalistic integrity of Voice of America." Writes Judge Pillard: "Congress had no reason to channel Abramowitz's claim through the CSRA, and every reason not to."

On the merits, the panel concluded Congress lawfully insulated the head of the VOA--an inferior officer--from removal by the President by vesting authority to appoint and remove the head of VOA in the International Broadcasting Advisory Board (IBAB).

IBAB is a seven-member "separate independent agency," the members of which must be bipartisan and are subject to Senate confirmation. IBAB is the relevant department head, even though it does not directly supervise VOA, as that job is performed by the U.S. Agency for Global Media--an arrangement the panel concluded is lawful under Morrison v. Olson.

The Department of Justice argued this unconstitutionally constrains the President's removal power, but the court was unconvinced.

So long as the President has adequate control over the department head, and the department head can control the inferior officer (as is the case here), the President can transitively control the inferior officer. The department head's supervision "preserv[es] the chain of command in Article II." Braidwood, 606 U.S. at 754.

Yet the practical effect of the court's ruling is that there is nothing the President can do to replace the head of the VOA. Six of the seven IBAB seats are currently open (having been removed by President Trump in 2025). Thus the Board is inquorate, and lacks the ability to remove the head of the VOA (or do much else). And, should Congress refuse to confirm new IBAB members, the current VOA head will remain in place. The DC Circuit may conclude this arrangement formally leaves the President with "adequate control" over the Board, but what good is control over a department head that is incapable of acting?

I suspect the Administration will seek further review, ultimately in the Supreme Court.  The question is whether it files a petition for certiorari right away, or first seeks rehearing en banc. While there is no likelihood the full D.C. Circuit will disturb the panel ruling, a petition for rehearing en banc might generate a dissent that could help attract the justices' attention. This case would also give the justices the opportunity to revisit Morrison v. Olson and say more about the extent to which inferior officers may (or may not) be insulated from presidential removal.

NEXT: The Peaceful Second Amendment Revolution

Jonathan H. Adler (@jadler1969) is the Tazewell Taylor Professor of Law at the William & Mary Law School and a senior fellow at the Property and Environment Research Center.

#7838. 31 Vintage Christmas Ideas Worth Bringing Back This Year

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 2:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Festive feather trees, classic cocktails, and decorative popcorn garlands: Yesteryear’s Christmas revelers really knew how to embrace the holiday season. This year, add a festive touch of seasonal cheer to your home with these old-school traditions. These vintage Christmas decorations and comforting treats will impress any guest, and create lasting memories for years to come.

Christmas teas aren’t just for the British. This traditional activity, which came to America in the 1830s as part of the temperance movement, brought families together to converse while drinking a variety of teas at long communal tables. So, fire up the tea kettle, make some fancy finger sandwiches, and enjoy a warm mug of tea with your loved ones.

The first artificial Christmas tree, which was a feather tree, dates back to mid-19th-century Germany. The thin-branched trees became popular in America in the 1920s, when European immigrants carried their holiday traditions to their new homes. Add a feather tree to your holiday decor for a touch of whimsy and historical charm.

Best Choice’s 9-foot tree has over 2,000 branch tips, strong branches, and beautiful flocking. Read the review.

Classic cocktails have made a comeback in bars around the country. Learn how to make a few favorites so you’ll have something to keep yourself warm, and impress your guests, over the holidays. Good choices for winter include the hot toddy (made with a bracing spirit like brandy, rum, or whiskey mixed with honey, spices, and boiling water) and the Tom and Jerry (a concoction of eggnog, brandy, and rum). Pouring your potables into fancy cocktail glasses makes them even more festive.

Jell-O long ago lost its spot as the star of the dessert table, but we think it’s about time the jiggly treat made a comeback. Pull out one of your grandma’s old recipe books and have fun constructing your very own holiday Jell-O mold, sure to be a crowd-pleaser at the kids’ table this year.

When families in the 1950s and ’60s didn’t want to maintain real Christmas trees, they opted for aluminum versions instead. Nowadays, these shimmering trees can add a little sparkly elegance to your seasonal decor while giving a nod to a long-lost trend. National Tree Company’s red tinsel tree is fire resistant, 6 feet high and has a 20-inch base diameter.

Before people adorned their trees with lights and ornaments, they decorated them with homemade popcorn garlands. Strings of popped kernels were budget-friendly and simple to construct. This year, spend quality time with your kids, parents, or grandparents making your own vintage popcorn garland. Be sure to pop extra corn to munch on as you work!

In the past, people traditionally thanked their regular letter carriers by giving them a small Christmas gift. Though we don’t always have the chance to develop relationships with our letter carriers today, it’s still a nice idea to give them a token of appreciation around the holidays. Just remember that federal guidelines stipulate that postal employees can’t accept gifts worth more than $20.

Stockings overflow with chocolates and toys on Christmas morning, but in simpler times children were excited and grateful to find oranges in their stockings. Put an orange in your child’s stocking this year as a reminder of your family’s good fortune, and for a healthy dose of vitamin C.

Tinsel became popular in the United States in the 1950s as people sought a way to add shimmer to their Christmas trees without using Christmas lights, which were considered a fire hazard. Re-create this vintage trend and give your tree a shiny, icy look by draping strands of tinsel on the branches. (Skip this tradition if you have pets, because tinsel is a choking hazard for them.)

With roots in solstice celebrations of ancient times, caroling is one of the oldest holiday traditions in the world. Channel your jolly ancestors and spread holiday cheer by taking your family Christmas caroling this year. Don’t worry if your singing voice doesn’t rival Beyoncé’s—this tradition is more about having fun than showing off your vocal chops.

In the early 20th century, people relied on trains as a primary mode of transportation. It’s no wonder that toy versions of these all-important vehicles started appearing underneath Christmas trees during that time. Set up a track around your Christmas tree to take your holiday visitors back in time, or gift a toy train to young relatives.

With the convenience of Netflix and DVDs, it’s easy to forget that children used to have to wait all year for their favorite classic Christmas specials to air on TV, and how excited they’d get when that day finally rolled around. Re-create the joys of a less plugged-in era by looking up the air times of old favorites, such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” or “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” then whipping up a fresh batch of hot chocolate for a cozy night with the family.

Find a spot on the mantel for the classic figurines your family collected growing up, like Pixie Elves, Byers’ Choice Christmas Carolers, or Snowbabies. While the Elf on the Shelf might be the more common character right now, these guys were the original ones keeping watch over the house before Santa arrived.

If you don’t already have a Christmas village collection, consider starting one this year. The tradition of collecting miniature structures can be traced all the way back to the 17th century, but the charming ceramic houses and stores you know and love kicked off in the 1970s. Today, it’s easy to search up online sites and forums where Christmas village enthusiasts share their tips and tricks for creating elaborate setups.

We sing about it every year, but have you ever actually had a roasted chestnut? On a weekend afternoon or cozy evening, try your hand at roasting chestnuts—a stovetop will work just as well as an open fire for this.

Everything old is new again, and that includes ceramic Christmas trees. This ’70s Christmas decoration has roared back into style. If you don’t have one collecting dust in the basement, you can find the 15-inch Best Choice Products pre-lit ceramic Christmas tree, 18-inch Mr. Christmas ceramic tree, and others like them online.

If you have ever been to or seen photos of Dyker Heights Christmas lights, then you’re familiar with blow mold Christmas decorations. The playful plastic figurines first popped up on the market in the 1930s. Although many folks today like Christmas inflatables, we believe there’s enough room on the lawn for both.

Over the top, but worth it: BZB Goods’ Santa Claus with sleigh is 12 feet long and illuminated with internal lights.

While there are plenty of modern holiday hits to enjoy, set a retro mood by putting together a playlist with tracks from the likes of Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra. While music-streaming services like Spotify already have plenty of holiday playlists to choose from, you can also curate a selection that reminds you of Christmases past.

Snail mail is so retro! Virtual Christmas greetings get the job done, but they aren’t nearly as sentimental as old-fashioned handwritten cards. Crisp stationery and seasonal stamps never fail to spread holiday cheer. Buy a boxed card set, or take a picture with your kids (or pet!) and incorporate it into a personalized greeting for everyone on your mailing list.

While it’s convenient to pick up a freshly cut Christmas tree from a big-box store’s parking lot, the tradition doesn’t have quite the same sense of holiday magic as venturing into a snow-covered wood to choose the perfect type of Christmas tree for your home. Depending on where you live, there are likely Christmas tree farms in your area that allow you to choose and cut down your own Christmas tree.

In the Middle Ages, the Lord of Misrule was a figure who was appointed to take charge of planning the Christmas activities in royal courts and noble houses. But this tradition came with a twist: The “Lord” often planned holiday pranks and jests. Try out this historic practice in your home this holiday season by giving children turns being the Lord of Misrule for the day. Allow the “Lord” to decide which treats to eat after dinner, which holiday special to watch, or letting them arrange the Elf on the Shelf for the following day.

While today’s Christmas supper typically features turkey or ham as a main dish, goose was once the centerpiece of many holiday dinner tables. In fact, eating goose for Christmas is a tradition that dates back to ancient Greece. A goose may be tricky to track down, but it’s generally possible to order one in advance from a high-quality butcher.

Tiny warm white lights are most common nowadays—on the tree and outside—but why not decorate with some retro flair? The big, colorful light bulbs you remember from previous decades are now available ineco-friendly LED bulbs. The burst of color outlining your house will make your home stand out from everyone else’s on the block.

With 3-inch C9 LED bulbs, the indoor/outdoor C9 LED lights from Wintergreen 17-foot strings really dazzle when used to frame the roof,

Today, getting dressed up for Christmas dinner typically means showing up in pair of elastic-waist pants to accommodate second helpings of turkey. In photos of midcentury Christmases, however, you’ll likely see men in ties and women in chic dresses with nary a pair of sweatpants in sight. Update your holiday dress code this year to bring back some vintage holiday glamour.

Evoke a vintage Christmas vibe by watching some holiday classics this December. Introduce your family to some timeless black-and-white picks like Miracle on 34th Street, White Christmas, and It’s a Wonderful Life. If you’re already familiar with these classics, screen an underrated holiday flick like Christmas in Connecticut or I’ll Be Seeing You.

Christmas crackers first made an appearance in Victorian England and are still popular in the U.K., but aren’t common on American holiday tables. A cracker is a wrapped cardboard tube that makes a loud cracking sound when pulled at both ends. They typically contain paper crowns as well as a small trinket and a card containing a joke or a piece of trivia, all of which are great dinnertime icebreakers.

You’re probably familiar with the “12 Days of Christmas” tradition because of the popular yuletide carol, but it’s a tradition that has largely died out in North America. Christians traditionally celebrated from December 25 to January 5 or 6, and gave one another small gifts each day. Extend the holiday season in your home by keeping festivities alive until Twelfth Night and continue to enjoy Christmas treats and festive holiday movies.

Though in many ways Christmas has become commercialized, you can bring back the spirit of giving that the holiday season once held by lending a hand to your neighbors or community. Help an elderly neighbor hang Christmas lights, volunteer at a toy drive for underprivileged children, or spend a day working at a soup kitchen to spread holiday cheer to those who need it most.

The origin of bottle brush Christmas trees dates back to the 1940s when, as the story goes, Addis Housewares Company manufactured the trees on the same machines the company used to make toilet brushes. Addis never did confirm the truth of the tree’s manufacture, but we’ll never look at a toilet brush the same way again. Though vintage version of these faux-snow-covered trees are hard to come by, you can find reproductions at retailers like Target and Crate and Barrel.

#7837. The Hegseth Impeachment is Far From Over

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Republicans temporarily blocked it with a procedural maneuver. But it is highly likely to come back.

Today, House Republicans managed to block the impeachment of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, by voting 211-204 to send it to a committee for further "study." But this fight is likely to be far from over.

The Republicans may be able to effectively bottle up the impeachment in committee for the rest of the current Congress (which ends on January 3, 2027). But it will almost certainly come back in the new Democratic-controlled Congress. With approximately 260 seats in the new House, the Democrats (virtually all of whom support impeachment) should easily be able to vote to impeach. At that point, it will be harder to get the necessary 11 or more Republican votes needed to secure the required 2/3 majority to convict in the Senate (the Democrats will have 54 to 56 seats in the new Senate, depending on the outcome of still-incomplete vote counts in Alaska and Mississippi). But Hegseth will at least have to go through a trial focused on his role in the unconstitutional Iran War, and in the murder of over 200 people in "drug boat" strikes in the Caribbean and the Pacific, among other charges.

And, though it's a steep hill to climb, it is by no means impossible he might actually get convicted, as he is very unpopular on Capitol Hill (and elsewhere), and the evidence against him is strong. It is notable that House Republicans chose to use this procedural maneuver rather than just vote down the impeachment directly. It suggests they might not have had the votes to do the latter.

In previous posts, I explained in much more detail why Hegseth deserves to be impeached and convicted, and considered an excellent article on the subject by prominent conservative national security law expert Andrew McCarthy (who reaches similar conclusions).

It ain't over till it's over - and this one is far from that point.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7835. 13 Potted Plants You Can—and Should—Winter Indoors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:31 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plenty of gardeners place their houseplants outdoors for the summer and enjoy them indoors the rest of the year. So why not try a similar strategy, and save a little money while you’re at it, by bringing your favorite cold-tender plants inside when the temperature drops so they’ll be ready to grow again when spring and summer rolls around?

Before you bring your outdoor plants in for the winter, you’ll need to do a bit of preparation. Start by inspecting them for pests and treating, if necessary. Repot if a plant needs it, and cut down on (or eliminate) fertilizing. Some plants can simply be brought indoors as houseplants, others should be forced into dormancy for a few months of cool storage, and still others are best kept going by making rooted cuttings. The following are a few cold-tender plants that you can bring inside each winter and then continue to enjoy outside for many summers to come.

While some palm trees are hardy in the winters of the Deep South, most palms need help to survive winter temperatures, even only to 55 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit . It’s possible to cover and winterize some palms planted in the ground, but potted palms should come indoors (preferably to a bright, humid spot). Move palms to an indoor location that gets lots of light. Water them regularly to keep the soil moist until spring, and carry them back outdoors after nights warm back up to at least 50 or 60 degrees.

Leave cacti outdoors as late into the season as possible so that the combination of shorter days and cooler nights will stimulate a dormancy response. You’ll need to keep an eye on the thermometer and know the low-temperature threshold for your particular type of cactus. Some species may be able to withstand 20-degree temperatures, but others cannot. If unsure, move potted cacti indoors as soon as cold drops to about 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

Stop watering cacti 3 to 4 weeks before the move so the plants are dry, and check them carefully for pets like mealy bugs or mites. In general, cacti do best in a cool location with minimal water, as they go dormant. Transition them back outside in early spring, gradually introducing sunlight if the plants show any sign of burning.

Citrus trees can actively grow and flower in winter, and may also ripen fruit if they’re pollinated. Even without winter growth, it’s a good idea protect these plants during the chilly months. As the days get shorter, move potted citrus trees (typically, dwarf varieties of lime and lemon trees) to an interim space outdoors that gets some protection from the elements, like a porch with radiant heat, and cut back on watering.

Before the first frost, move the citrus tree into a brightly lit indoor room, ideally between 55 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Citrus plants are sensitive to the drying effects of air, so it’s best to position them away from heat vents and cold drafts. Provide supplemental humidity with a pebble tray or regular misting.

Move tropical hibiscus plants indoors when overnight temperatures reach the low 50s. Place them in a brightly lit room, and treat them like regular houseplants. Cut back on watering and fertilizing during these cooler months. Try to avoid heat vents and cold drafts, and put the plants on a pebble tray to boost the ambient humidity, if necessary. Prune tropical hibiscus three times during late fall and winter (October, December, and February) to maintain the plant’s shape.

Prune jasmine vines by at least 25 percent before bringing them in for winter, letting them adjust gradually by bringing them inside at night and slowly lengthening the time spent indoors. Some or all of the plant’s leaves will fall off, but new ones will grow again in time. Bring jasmine into a sunny room before frosty weather arrives, and keep it away from drying air vents and drafts. Use a pebble tray to boost humidity to about 30 percent.

Coleus plants are grown for their stunning foliage and adaptability to shade. The plants are annuals in most regions, though, since they do not like temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and cannot survive temperatures below freezing. Bring the potted plant indoors once nights hover near 50 degrees. Repot the plant if it is outgrowing its container.

Another option is to propagate coleus stems to use next spring. Cut a 6-inch healthy stem, remove low leaves, and dip the stem in a rooting hormone before planting it in a container with moist potting mix. Cover the container with a plastic bag for a few weeks and keep it in a warm and sunny spot; water regularly.

Aromatic rosemary is a favorite cooking herb for many fall and winter dishes. However, the plant does not always survive winters in USDA Zones 6 or lower. Start by planting a rosemary in a well-draining container. Bring potted rosemary indoors before the first freeze. Keep it in a cool location with fairly high humidity, but avoid overwatering; if its roots stay damp and cool, it can develop root rot.

Feel free to harvest from the plant, but never cut off more than about 20 percent of the foliage and avoid cutting into woody main stems. You also can propagate rosemary indoors at the end of the season with 4- to 6-inch cuttings from a stem with no flowers.

Elephant ears, or taro, is a tropical plant that can survive a light frost only; a true freeze will kill the tuber. Simply move potted elephant ears indoors to a cool bright location. For those grown in the ground, carefully dig up the elephant ear tuber when cool weather approaches and the foliage dies back (they won’t survive winter outdoors in USDA Zone 6 and lower). Cut stems down to about 4 to 6 inches, and gently wipe off excess dirt.

Place the tuber in a warm, dark location with good air circulation to dry out for a few days. Wrap the bulbs in paper or drop them in a paper bag and store them in a cool, dry, dark place. Check them periodically for rot (throw rotten ones away) and insect damage (treat with an insecticide). Beware that nearly all its parts are toxic to pets and people if ingested—we don’t recommend bringing it indoors if you have young children.

It is technically possible to bring Boston ferns indoors and overwinter them in their active state, but it gets very messy very quickly. Instead, let them rest. Put them in a cool, moderately light to dark location that will not freeze, like an unheated basement or garage.

Before bringing your fern inside, hose it down on a warm (60-degree Fahrenheit) day to spray away insects and loose leaves. Give it a light trim, and shake and ruffle the fronds to drop debris before carrying the plant to its indoor spot. Moisten dry soil as needed until spring. Don’t be alarmed if some leaves pale or drop.

Geranium is another plant that likes to sleep the winter away. Dig the plants out of the ground before the first freeze, and gently knock the soil off the roots. Allow the plants to dry in a cool, shady location for a couple of days. Place the plants upside down in a paper bag and close the top. Store them in a cool, dark location that stays between 55 and 60 degrees.

About 2 months before the last frost date, trim the stored geraniums and plant them in moist potting soil with two leaf nodes below the soil line. You also can propagate cuttings or bring potted geraniums indoors to a sunny window.

Thyme is a flavorful and aromatic perennial herb, but a tender one in regions 5 or lower. Plant culinary thyme in a container in spring, keeping it in a sunny, bright location with well-draining soil. Bring it indoors for winter before the first frost. If the herb’s roots are peeking though the bottom of the pot or it looks crowded, repot the thyme when you bring it in. It also can be divided easily.

Be sure to place the container near a sunny window with a western or southern exposure in a room that maintains a 60- to 70-degrees Fahrenheit temperature for most of the day. Prune or pinch off flowers to preserve the herb’s flavor. Water as needed, allowing the container dry out between watering. You can fertilize every week or two with a diluted solution of fish emulsion or liquid seaweed. Harvest sprigs as needed for winter dishes.

Although Musa basjoo, Musella lasiocarpa, and a few other banana trees are quite cold hardy, most will not tolerate extended freezing temperatures. Potted banana plants can be brought indoors to a bright, sunny room to spend the winter in a slowed active state. They can take up some space indoors, so you also can help them sleep through winter. As the weather cools, gradually reduce watering. Before the first frost, cut the plant to 6 inches in height and move it to a dark, cool location. Keep the soil just moist until the weather warms in the spring.

The stunning evergreen cordyline is hardy only in the warmest growing zones, but potted cordylines can be moved indoors when temperatures dip into the 60s. Place them in a spot with good ventilation and consistent indoor temperatures; avoid placing them near air vents or in drafty areas. Increase humidity around cordyline by situating it in a humid room or on a saucer filled with pebbles and water, and avoid fluoride-treated tap water. Although the plant does not require dormancy in winter, it does like a rest, so cut water some during fall and winter.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.
