In choosing the best water heater blankets among those currently on the market, we looked at two top factors: material and size. Our list of recommendations covers the most popular types of water heater blanks, including thick fiberglass options as well as thinner foam and foil options.

We also made sure to include a range of sizes on our list with options to cover most water heater shapes. For oddly shaped water heaters with awkward piping, we included recommendations for several easy-to-cut options that can fit snugly around even the most difficult water heater shapes or those in tight spaces.

Before shopping for a water heater blanket, read this section to understand the factors and features to keep in mind. This will help you make an informed decision.

When perusing water heater blankets, you’ll notice that there are a few different types available. This mostly comes down to the type of insulating material. Some are easier to work with during installation than others, as they often need to be trimmed to fit individual water heaters.

You may also find combinations of materials, such as fiberglass insulation with a foil face. This can offer the best of both worlds, as it uses a thick, insulating layer of air pockets and radiates heat back into the tank.

Water heaters, like most appliances, come in different sizes. The size of house and family and the number of sinks and showers all affect how large a water heater a home needs. While water heaters range between 30 and 98 gallons, 40-, 50-, and 60-gallon tanks are the common sizes used in homes.

Water heater blankets also come in similar sizes, so it’s important to find one that will work for your tank. If you have a 50-gallon tank, finding a water heater blanket to fit it should be no problem. Water heater blankets large enough to fit 98-gallon tanks, commonly found in commercial settings, may be harder to track down.

When it comes to materials such as fiberglass, cotton, and denim, the thicker the water heater blanket, the better it will be at insulating. A water heater located in a cool basement calls for a thicker blanket. Thicker blankets will do a better job of separating the cool air and the heat radiating from the tank than thinner ones.

Because foil works primarily by reflecting the heat instead of relying on an air-pocket barrier, it needn’t be thick to function efficiently. Most water heater blankets made with foil are less than ½ inch thick, which is another reason foil water heater blankets are so easy to work with.

Just like your home’s insulation, water heater blankets come in a variety of insulation ratings. These ratings are described as R-value, where the R stands for resistance. The higher the R-value, the more resistance the insulation has against heat transfer. Essentially, more is better.

The highest R-value you’re likely to find for a residential water heater blanket is R-11, but values of R-7 and R-8 are more common. To get the most from your investment, it’s best to use the water heater blanket with the highest R-value.

It’s important to keep in mind, though, that foil-type insulation rarely offers an R-value; R-values apply to fiberglass and other similar types of insulation.

Water heaters have burner assemblies that get very hot. The point of insulating a water heater is to save energy and money, not cause a fire. Different water heater blanket materials have varying degrees of fire resistance to combat that risk. While the most common designation is Class 1/Class A, it’s helpful to know which types are the most fire resistant.

If fire resistance is of utmost importance, a fiberglass or foil water heater blanket is the way to go. Some fiberglass or foil products aren’t fire rated, but that doesn’t mean they’re unsafe. Just be sure to keep the insulation clear of the burner by a few inches.

There are two types of water heaters: electric and gas. Electric water heaters have a heating element inside that energizes and heats the water that surrounds it. Gas water heaters have burners underneath that kick on to heat water through convection.

Fortunately, water heater blankets are interchangeable between the two water heater types. However, if you have a gas-powered heater, it’s crucial that the blanket doesn’t cover or otherwise obstruct the flue (aka exhaust) at the top. If you have an electric model, the blanket must not cover or obstruct its control box or access panel, typically located on the side of the tank. Also, be sure to cut the insulation back from the burner by at least 2 inches while installing.

For additional information about buying and using the best water heater blanket, consider the answers to these frequently asked questions.

A great water heater blanket will offer a blend of insulation value, cost-effectiveness, and fire resistance.

It depends on the size of your tank. Generally speaking, manufacturers label their water heater blankets according to the size of the tank they’ll cover. If you’re unsure, measure your tank’s height and circumference, and compare it to the measurements on the package.

Water heater blankets are low maintenance, but fiberglass, cotton, and denim can begin to smell and stop insulating if they get wet. It’s a good idea to check on your water heater blanket a few times a year to ensure it’s still in good condition.

Undamaged water heater blankets may far outlast a water heater. The average gas water heater lasts between 8 and 12 years, while the average electric water heater lasts 10 to 15 years. A water heater blanket kept in good condition will outlast a water heater without issue.

The most efficient way to install a water heater blanket is to measure the height and circumference of your tank before unrolling the product, allowing for an extra 2 inches for the circumference so you can overlap the product. Premeasuring allows you to swiftly cut the product to size using cutter or scissors. Wrap the tank with the blanket, and secure it in place with foil tape placed vertically along the seam. Cover the top of the tank with two half circles of material, and secure it in place with foil tape. Ensure that you cut openings for the venting hood, pressure relief valve, burner access cover, and wiring connection box. Make the holes about 2 inches larger than each opening to allow airflow.

Yes. Any steps you can take to keep your water hot without additional reheating of the water is worth it. The water heater blanket does just this and is an inexpensive purchase. In most cases, you should be able to recoup your investment when installing an insulator blanket.

Yes. When properly installed, hot water heater blankets are safe to use. The most important thing is to ensure proper airflow around all fixtures by cutting slightly larger openings around valves, hoods, burners, etc. Don’t forget that some blankets contain fiberglass, and those installing the product should wear safety goggles, a dust mask, gloves, and long sleeves, then carefully clean the area after installation to remove any stray fiberglass fibers.

If you’ve ever tried to start your car, but the battery was dead, or you found a tire was too low to drive on, you may have wished for a jump starter air compressor. These combo tools claim to be able to get you going again—so we decided to put 11 of the top models to the test on our own vehicles, and found 7 that we can recommend. DeWalt’s 1600A Jump Starter with Air Compressor took top honors in our tests, thanks to its quality build, internal alternator tester, and convenient pressure presets for accurate inflation.

These devices bring enough voltage and amperage to bring a dead battery back to life. They can also fill a low tire or pump up a leaky one until the driver can make it to a service station for repairs. Ahead, learn the most important factors to consider when choosing one of these combo units and find out how the following models earned a spot on our lineup of the best jump starters with air compressors.

Bottom line: Jump starters with air compressors are essential tools for emergencies, offering reliable performance and versatility. DeWalt leads the pack with its superior features.

There might be a lot to know about these versatile devices, but shopping for the best jump starter with an air compressor doesn’t have to be complicated. To help make the process even easier, these top-rated products are an excellent starting point. We performed hands-on testing with every model listed below to ensure they can meet the grade.

The DeWalt jump starter/compressor combo performed flawlessly in our hands-on tests, easily earning the title of the best overall model. This unit supplies enough juice to start depleted batteries and has a built-in alternator tester.

We got an alternator reading by connecting it to a vehicle’s battery terminals when the vehicle was idling. Since problems starting a vehicle can be due to a faulty alternator, this feature is a nice perk.

The clamps are large and grip the terminals firmly. We were able to get a reading of the current battery voltage. When we connected the terminals to a fully charged battery, the DeWalt indicated the voltage, which is a good way to see the battery’s current charge.

The compressor measured the existing pressure in the tires. We were able to preselect the amount of air we wanted to add, and the compressor inflated the tires to the exact pressure. This handy feature removes the guesswork, especially when inflating bicycle tires that can explode if too much pressure is applied. It took about 20 seconds to inflate bike tires and about 5 minutes to inflate a large pickup tire.

What our tester says: “The DeWalt jump starter was a dream to use—its multifunctionality and high-quality performance made jumping batteries and filling tires almost effortless.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the DeWalt jump starter with air compressor at Tractor Supply Co., Amazon, or The Home Depot.

Jump starters with air compressors can be incredibly versatile, and this model from DieHard definitely fits the bill. The lead-acid jump starter offers 950 peak amps for cranking over large diesel engines as well as reverse hookup protection to avoid damaging the expensive electrical components that are sometimes vulnerable during jumping. It also features two 12V ports and a USB port for charging devices.

The compressor produces up to 150 PSI of pressure and includes a digital gauge for presetting the pressure and checking the battery’s charge level. A built-in work light makes working on the side of the road in low light a bit less difficult as well. This DieHard model also includes three air nozzle adapters for filling sports equipment, pool floats, and other items.

The DieHard jump starter was more than capable of firing up an old Land Rover. It was easier to attach than other models as the cables were slightly longer than the compact versions. And just a flip of the switch turned the unit on for the jumping function. We found that the air compressor worked well, pumping up the tire faster than the other full-size models (about 5 minutes faster from 20 PSI to 36 PSI), though the gauge is in a strange place—it’s right behind the positive clamp. Also, the battery gauge on the front of the unit isn’t all that detailed, providing only broad ranges: 70 to 100 percent, 30 to 70 percent, and under 30 percent.

Get the DieHard jump starter with air compressor at Ace Hardware.

The Trekure jump starter fits a lot of energy into a small package, making it a good option for taking along on road trips. We didn’t have any problems jump-starting three different dead batteries, but the clamps are a little on the small side—we would have appreciated larger clamps.

This unit came with some battery charge, but once it was depleted by testing, it took about 6 hours to recharge. We liked its bright LED flashlight, which allowed us to see what we were doing after dark. The flashlight also doubles as a yellow flashing road flare that can be seen from a distance.

The inflator aired up our bicycle and car tires but didn’t have quite the oomph to fill up larger truck tires. But it’s simple to use—the display screen let us choose from images of a car, motorcycle, bike, or basketball for adjusting air pressure.

We like the Trekure for all-purpose 12-volt jump-starting, but we think it’s best suited for light-duty tire inflation. It comes in a handy case and includes two USB ports and a plug-in DC outlet for charging various devices in the car.

Get the Trekure jump starter with air compressor at Amazon.

Folks who value versatility will want to consider the Schumacher SJ1332 rechargeable power station. This device features 1,200A of cranking power, allowing it to start a massive 8-liter gas engine or a 6-liter diesel engine. It also features a 150 PSI air compressor with an analog gauge for pumping flat tires and a high-volume air port for filling air mattresses and pool floats.

The Schumacher features two 12-volt (V) charging ports, two standard 120V outlets, and a USB port for charging mobile devices. This allows it to charge several devices or act as an emergency power station if the power goes out in the home. Its cables wrap around the unit and clip onto the base for storage, and the compressor hose stores in a small compartment in the back.

We weren’t big fans of the tire pressure gauge, which was not lit and wasn’t very accurate (a difference of around 8 PSI), and it’s in a weird spot (on the back of the jump pack and obscured by the clamp). But otherwise, the unit had plenty of power to jump the car and it was easy to use. We liked the 120V outlets.

What our tester says: “The Schumacher was relatively easy to use to jump my Land Rover. The light was helpful and allowed me to identify the cables easily at night, and the buttons and controls were fairly intuitive.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Schumacher jump starter with air compressor at Amazon, Walmart, Blain’s Farm & Fleet, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

For an additional well-rounded jump starter, Stanley’s J5C09 portable power station could fit the bill. This jump starter features a lead-acid battery with up to 10,000A of cranking power for turning over large engines in gasoline and diesel vehicles alike. It also includes a 120 PSI compressor that can fill nearly any tire, with an illuminated analog gauge for monitoring the pressure in real-time.

This unit provides some additional built-in features worth noting. It offers a USB port for charging devices, a standard 12V port, a reverse polarity alarm to indicate improperly installed clamps, and a positionable work light for shedding light on the repair area.

During the test, the one feature that stood out the most was the air compressor. It was able to fill a tire in much less time than the other models (about 4 minutes), and the analog display was very accurate. It’s also easy to set up and use in the dark, plus it features extra-long cables to make reaching battery terminals easier. It also had plenty of power to kick the vehicle’s engine over. The positionable light is a nice touch as it allowed us to position the jump pack carefully without losing our light source. The light is a bit weak, however.

Get the Stanley jump starter with air compressor at MSC or Staples.

If you’re looking for a multi-function jump starter/compressor combo, check out this new model from JackPak. Right out of the box, we were impressed with this unit’s build quality—it’s solid, rugged, and comes with heavy-duty clamps.

Like the DeWalt that earned our best overall award, the JackPak shows how many volts the current vehicle battery has, which is great if there isn’t a voltmeter handy. We wish all the units came with this feature.

It supplied enough juice to jump all three dead batteries and took less than three hours to recharge. The compressor feature inflated our bike, car, and truck tires, but it took nearly 30 minutes to completely fill the truck tire. Still, the JackPak isn’t meant as a replacement for a commercial tire inflator, but it will get the job done when a service station isn’t nearby.

We liked the bright LED light on the JackPak, and it doubles as a powerbank for charging devices. It also features a low-power sleep mode that keeps its internal battery from discharging for up to 36 months.

Get the JackPack jump starter with air compressor at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

When a battery goes dead and a car is stuck in a parking lot or across town (or the side of the road), there’s a lot on the line. We know that, so we tested the jump starters with air compressors on our own depleted car and truck batteries and to inflate a range of tires.

We tested each product by jumping a dead car, truck, and riding mower batteries. We also used a multimeter to determine the voltage from the jump starters. We tested the jump starters over a 2-week period, connecting each one to the various battery terminals and then attempting to start the vehicle.

We also drained some of the air from bike, car, and truck tires to test the built-in compressors. For the inflation tests, we partially deflated bike, car, and truck tires and then timed how long it took each inflator to return the tires to the recommended pressure. During these inflation tests, we paid close attention to how easily the air chucks connected to the valve stems, whether they created a secure seal, and how well they held up through repeated use. We also considered whether the compressors operated consistently under pressure or showed signs of strain, as well as how intuitive and responsive the controls were throughout the process.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a jump starter/inflator did on a test or assessment, the higher the points. The products that excelled were given awards based on their strengths, while those that failed were removed from our lineup.

Carrying a jump starter with an air compressor means drivers can handle emergencies and repairs without calling for help (or when help isn’t available). And who doesn’t enjoy a little self-reliance? These devices include built-in jumper cables to clamp onto the positive and negative terminals of a dead battery. It sounds straightforward, but shopping for one of these devices requires a bit of background and know-how. The following sections will break down the most important considerations to keep in mind while shopping for a battery jumper with air compressor.

Jump starters equipped with air compressors include one of two battery types: lithium-ion and lead-acid.

The best jump starters with air compressors—and all portable jump starters, for that matter—have an onboard battery that provides ample power to start a vehicle or operate the compressor. In most cases, the battery size of these portable chargers is described in milliampere hours (mAh) or amp hours (Ah)—1,000mAh equals 1Ah.

Higher mAh or Ah ratings equals a larger capacity to store power, so higher ratings mean more batteries charged and tires inflated between recharges. Generally speaking, most portable jump starters use batteries between 10,000 and 35,000mAh. Remember that higher capacity batteries are heavy, and get heavier as the storage increases.

The purpose of a jump starter is to provide a vehicle with enough power to turn over and fire up the engine, then allow the vehicle’s alternator to continue charging the battery. The amount of power a jump starter needs to accomplish this task is determined by the engine.

Small gasoline engines, such as four-cylinder engines found in most cars (and progressively larger vehicles) don’t require much power. But larger eight-cylinder engines require a bit more. And, because of the extremely high compression ratios of diesel engines, large models found in heavy-duty pickups, RVs, and power equipment require even more power. In general, 1,000A or more will do the trick.

Many manufacturers today don’t explicitly list the amount of power provided by their chargers. Instead, they discuss the types of engines their chargers can handle. This is only a concern for diesel vehicles, as any jump starter will handle most gasoline engines.

While it might seem that jumper cables are all created equal, modern jump starters offer additional safety features. Today’s models protect a vehicle’s electrical system and the person using the cables from sparking or reverse polarity, which happens when the user connects the clamps to the wrong terminals—something that’s very easy to do in the dark. Reverse polarity can wreak havoc on the sensitive electronics in today’s vehicles, so this is a crucial feature.

These units will detect the reverse polarity or contact between the clamps and prevent the unit from expelling stored energy through them. Often, a small light or audible alarm will alert the user so you can understand what’s occurring and why the jump starter isn’t charging the vehicle.

When choosing the best jump starter with an air compressor, there is some variance in the amount of pounds per square inch (PSI) offered by these models. Most models produce around 100 PSI—more than enough for any road vehicle’s tires. Most vehicle tires require just 30 to 40 PSI.

Some models offer 150 PSI or more, which is as much pressure as a traditional home air compressor. Are they necessary for typical vehicle repairs? No. But it might take these compressors less time to boost up a tire on the side of the road, so they could be worth the consideration and splurge.

Several additional features might make a portable jump starter with an air compressor a bit more attractive to consumers.

Even with all of this background on choosing the best jump starter with air compressor, you might have questions. The following section is a collection of some of the most frequently asked questions about battery jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.stions about jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.

This depends on the vehicle, with smaller engines requiring just a few hundred amps and larger engines requiring 1,000 or more amps. Consider erring on the side of caution and choosing a car battery jump starter from this guide, as they all boast at least 1,000A.

Many units include their own AC adapters for charging via an outlet in a home garage. Others might have plugs to attach a standard extension cord for charging. Some also feature 12V ports for charging in a vehicle.

Most manufacturers suggest charging a jump starter with an air compressor every 30 days to ensure it’s in good working order.

Let your vehicle run for 15 to 30 minutes to allow the battery to recharge.

Yes, but it’s a good idea to take it indoors during extreme hot or cold weather.

You can expect to get 3 to 5 years of service, depending on quality and usage.

No, it shouldn’t if it is used correctly. If you’re worried about that, look for a unit that offers reverse polarity protection.

#7829. 13 Retailers You Never Knew Would Recycle Your Old Stuff

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 10, 2026 11:43 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As consumers, we create a massive amount of waste, filling up landfills with all of the products we’ve used and thrown away. While most people have a recycling bin along with their trash bin, they might not realize that many stores they frequent offer exceptional recycling programs for the items that can’t go in the recycling container.

These major retailers have robust recycling programs that can refurbish and reuse your old clothes, smartphones, rechargeable batteries, or furniture. And, for items that aren’t reusable, the retailers partner with recycling companies that can break them down into their base components to create a variety of other products.

“These sort of recycling programs are of huge importance,” says Paula Napolitano, product sales manager at Wisetek, a major Ireland-based distributor of refurbished and recycled electronics. “Last year there were around 59 million metric tons of e-waste generated globally, which is hugely impacting the environment. If large amounts of old electronics are allowed to build up in landfills, they can eventually begin to leach toxic materials into the soil, which may seriously harm the surrounding environment,” Napolitano says.

While lowering the impact you have on the local landfill is reason enough to hand off unwanted furniture, bedsheets, tablets, or rechargeable batteries to these retailers, you might be surprised to know that many of these companies offer additional incentives in the form of coupons, gift cards, and trade-in deals. Ahead, learn more about some of the top retailers who will take your unwanted stuff.

The big-box appliance and electronics giant is a leader in recycling, reusing, or repurposing, to the tune of 2.7 billion pounds of e-waste and appliances since 2009. You can drop off old electronics like computers, smartphones, radios, and more at any of Best Buy’s more than 1,000 locations and receive special promotions off certain products in the store. You can even earn gift cards for those items that still have value. Best Buy will also haul old TVs, fitness equipment, and appliances away for a nominal fee when you buy new ones.

“You can recycle up to three items per household per day,” says Alejandra Valeriano, public relations representative for Best Buy. “For $199.99, we’ll haul away and recycle up to a total of two large products (including TVs, major appliances, all-in-one computers and monitors), along with an unlimited number of select smaller products,” Valeriano says. Best Buy partners with Electronic Recyclers International, which breaks down electronics into materials that can be repurposed for use in everything from fiber optic cables to airplanes.

Few retailers have as robust a recycling program as The Home Depot. Consumers can access their comprehensive recycling web page that explains how to recycle everything from plastic plant pots to florescent tube lights. The company partners with nonprofit recycling company The Battery Network (formerly Call2Recycle) to recycle a variety of battery types, including those for power tools, EVs, and e-bikes. In 2024, The Home Depot recycled approximately 1 million pounds of rechargeable batteries. The retailer also collects plastic bags for composite manufacturer Trex, which uses them to make fencing and decking.

Not only will Staples recycle your old office supplies and electronics, they’ll pay you for it. Since 2012, Staples has recycled nearly 188 million pounds of technology. “Staples wants to make recycling easier for everyone across the U.S.,” says Mike Sauchuk, senior director of recycling and sustainability of Staples. “There are many items out there that we use every day that can be recycled, but it can be challenging to find a place to recycle them. That’s where Staples steps in. We offer free recycling for many hard-to-recycle items like technology, writing instruments, phone cases, and more. There’s no more waiting for your town’s local recycling day or event. At Staples, it’s recycling day every day.”

Through the Staples Rewards program, you can earn $5 back in rewards when you recycle tech and $2 back on every recycled ink or toner cartridge brought to one of the store’s more than 1,000 locations. In addition, the retailer will take unwanted electronics and worn-out rechargeable batteries for free.

Like other retailers, Walmart will take used cell phones, Bluetooth speakers, laptops, gaming consoles, tablets, and other devices through its trade-in program. Simply input info about the device on the Walmart website, get an offer for it, then ship it for free via FedEx or UPS Ground using a preprinted label. You receive an instant Walmart gift card for your efforts.

The presence of mercury, cadmium, lithium, and lead in car batteries ranks these vital components of cars and trucks among the more harmful products for the environment. Advance Auto Parts knows this, and therefore the company offers a nice incentive for bringing in your old battery once it dies. Take the worn-out battery to any Advance store and you’ll get a $10 gift card, which you can put toward the cost of a new battery or anything else in the store. The old batteries are then used to manufacture new ones.

While Apple’s products might be on the more expensive side when it comes to consumer electronics, they hold some of their value. That’s because the company makes it easy to cash in on that old iPhone, iPad, Macbook, or Apple Watch by allowing owners of the devices to trade their electronics in at an Apple Store or online. In return, Apple gives the customer store credit (Apple will also recycle other brands of electronics for free).

If the device is in good shape, it will be refurbished and resold. Those that can’t be reused go to one of Apple’s recycling partners, where they are broken down and recycled. Many iPhones end up with Daisy, Apple’s disassembly robot, which is designed to recover a device’s usable parts.

Habitat for Humanity’s ReStore has more than 900 locations nationwide, all of which will take appliances, furniture, various household items, and even building materials. Habitat then resells these items in its store and uses the proceeds to build affordable homes for families. “New and gently used items donated to a Habitat ReStore are resold to the community at a fraction of retail prices and help to support Habitat for Humanity’s vision of a world where everyone has a decent place to live,” says Jared Williams, communications manager at Habitat for Humanity International.

According to Williams, “Habitat ReStores tend to accept both new and gently used household items and building materials, which can include a wide variety of products.” He adds that donations come from all kinds of sources, “from neighbors completing home projects to restaurants after a remodel.” Habitat might not offer you a gift card for your stuff, but you can take tax deductions for your donations, since Habitat is a nonprofit organization.

RELATED: Don’t Throw Your Old Christmas Lights in the Trash—Do This Instead

Ever wonder where the used products Amazon sells come from? The online retailing behemoth accepts your old electronics and devices, including Bluetooth speakers and headphones, home security devices, wireless routers, and gaming systems. The company will even reward you with gift cards for gently used electronics that it can refurbish and resell. Amazon also takes some products that are no longer functioning. The company will recycle a variety of electronic devices for free, even covering the cost of shipping them to Amazon via UPS.

Bedding, unmatched socks, old T-shirts—clothing retailer H&M will take all linens as part of the company’s recycling program. Since 2013, H&M has collected more than 172,000 tons of textiles. The items were either cleaned and reused as second-hand clothing, turned into other products such as cleaning rags, or recycled into materials like insulation. When you drop off a bag of used clothing at H&M, the company will give you a coupon toward your next purchase at their store.

More than 1 billion HP ink and toner cartridges have been recycled by customers through the company’s HP Planet Partners program. The program aims to give a second life to HP’s end-of-life equipment and printing supplies and to reduce the environmental impact of electronic waste and greenhouse gas emissions. Simply drop off your HP ink and toner supplies at a location near you, mail them back, or request a pickup if you have a large quantity of supplies to give back.

Calling all coffee enthusiasts! If you own a Nespresso machine, you might be familiar with the company’s recycling program. Fill a Nespresso recycling bag (available for free at any Nespresso store) with your used capsules and drop them off at one of the 122,000-plus collection points around the world. The aluminum from the pods is recycled into items such as bicycles, computers, and soda cans, while the used coffee grounds create compost or green energy.

Kroger recognizes that most shoppers throw out plastic grocery bags and packaging after shopping, so they’ve put a special system in place for customers to take your discarded grocery bags and packaging and recycle them responsibly. The retail giant provides convenient drop-off bins to recycle plastic. The grocery chain has recycled more than 180 million pounds of plastic and aims to eliminate single-use plastic grocery bags in all of their stores by 2025.

Williams-Sonoma has a variety of initiatives dedicated to creating a more circular economy. The company works with donation programs like Good360 to give away returned and unsold products to local nonprofit organizations and others. They are also exploring rental and resale business models to give a second life to products like bedding, curtains, throws, pillows, linens, and more.

#7828. 5 Smart Tips for Soundproofing Windows

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Gretchen Heber, Bob Vila, Manasa Reddigari

Updated Nov 10, 2026 12:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Whether it’s highway traffic, loud neighbors, or birds chirping, if you don’t have sound proof windows, some noise from the outside world is bound to disrupt your daily activities, especially if the racket intrudes when you’re in a bedroom or other area intended as a sanctuary or work space. While you can’t control what goes on outside, you can block (or at least reduce) the noise by soundproofing windows using these techniques. Whether you implement one of these strategies or a combination thereof, you may find that soundproofing windows is your secret to attaining inner peace.

Soundproofing windows in your home can help you dampen noise for better sleep, and block out ambient noise in your home office. Window inserts are probably the most effective options, but they are expensive—they’ll set you back $300 to $800 per insert. Replacing older single-pane windows with updated double-pane windows, which cost $350 to $900 (and sometimes more) is another effective solution, albeit another big investment. A more affordable way to soundproof windows is to seal window gaps with acoustic caulk, which costs just $10 to $20. Sound-reducing window treatments, which start at about $20 each, are another cost-effective way to go.

If you live in an environment with heavy noise pollution, such as honking car horns, wailing sirens, or music blasting from next door, utilizing soundproofing window inserts is the most effective way to reduce the cacophony. These glass inserts are installed in the window frame a few inches in front of the interior face of your existing window. The air space between the insert and the window keeps most sound vibrations from passing through the glass, resulting in greater noise-reduction benefits than double-pane windows alone (more on these ahead). The most effective inserts are made of laminated glass, a thick glass consisting of two layers of glass with an intervening layer of plastic that effectively blocks vibrations. Some companies that make these inserts include Indow, Soundproof Windows, and CitiQuiet.

On the Sound Transmission Class (STC) scale that reflects the decibel reduction in noise volume that a window provides, soundproof windows typically measure between 48 and 54—the higher the STC, the greater the noise-reduction benefit. At the upper end, this means that a 98-decibel (db) outside noise (e.g., a motorcycle engine) is heard at only 44 db indoors (98 minus 54), which is no louder than a typical indoor conversation. You’ll get more noise reduction benefits by installing an insert in front of a single-pane window than you would with a double-pane window. This is because the STC of a double-pane window is often higher to begin with, so an insert won’t increase its overall STC as substantially. An insert for one window typically costs between $350 and $800 installed, which is less than or equal to the cost of the next option for soundproofing windows: a window replacement.

If you experience moderate outdoor noise pollution, such as the occasional lawn mower or a passing car, you may wish to replace single-pane windows with double-pane windows. Single-pane pane windows, often found in homes 15 years old or older, have just a single piece of glass in the window frame, while double-pane windows, the standard in newer homes, consist of two pieces of glass with air between them. Single-pane windows provide no air barrier between the outside and the glass, so they permit virtually all outdoor sounds to vibrate through the glass, resulting in a noisy interior.

Single-pane windows have an STC of between 26 and 28, which is only a little over half that of soundproof windows. At the upper end of this range, the window would reduce the noise volume of a passing car (70 db) to 42 db (70 minus 28). In contrast, the air space between the individual panes of a double-pane window helps halt the vibration of outdoor sounds through the glass, resulting in greater noise reduction benefit translating to an STC of 26 to 35. Compared with a single-pane window with an STC of 28, a double-pane window measuring in at 35 would reduce the noise volume of a passing car to only 35 db—offering a 7-decibel greater reduction in noise than the single-pane window (70 minus 35). While this may not seem like much, to the listener, a 7-db difference results in a perceived volume reduction of around 87 percent. Replacing one single-pane window with a double-pane equivalent will run you $350 to $900.

RELATED: Soundproofing a Room: The Two Best Ways to Dampen Noise Without Tearing Down Your Walls

Small gaps between a window frame and an interior wall can let outdoor noise into your home and keep your windows from performing at their STC rating. A simple way to seal these gaps is to fill them with an acoustic caulk, such as Green Glue Acoustical Caulk. This noiseproof, latex-based product reduces sound transmission and maintains windows’ STC but still allows you to open and close the windows.

Applying acoustic caulk is the easiest and most inexpensive way to soundproof windows. If there is already silicone caulk around the window frame, remove it with a putty knife. Cut a quarter-inch opening in the tip of the acoustic caulk tube with a utility knife, load the tube into a caulking gun, and pull the gun’s trigger to apply a thin bead of caulk in the gap between the interior window frame and interior wall.

Acoustic caulk readily bonds with most window frame and wall materials, including wood and drywall. More flexible than regular silicone caulk, acoustic caulk won’t shrink or form new cracks over time as you operate your windows; it’s also ultra-durable, lasting for several years before it requires re-caulking. Though you’ll most often find it white, acoustic caulk is available in a variety of hues. Some products turn clear as they dry, while others remain their original color but can be painted to match the color of interior walls.

To soften noise as well as reduce harsh glare, hang sound-dampening curtains. PONY DANCE’s blackout curtains, which were the top overall pick in our tested guide to the best soundproof curtains, are a top-quality option. Sound-dampening curtains, which usually cost $20 to $60 per panel, are made of a thick, heavy fabric such as velvet, and are typically lined with vinyl or a similar material that absorbs sound. These curtains also minimize echoes. Because they dampen but do not block sound entirely, they’re better suited for light noise pollution that may interrupt sleep, such as crickets or birds chirping, than they are for dampening the sound of heavy street traffic.

Many of these window treatments also serve as quality blackout curtains, which have a foam backing that helps block out light. Curtains that absorb sound and block light are great options for soundproofing bedrooms and other spaces designed for sleep and relaxation. They are especially popular with people who work night-shift hours and sleep during the day.

These lightweight linen blackout curtains reduced sound by 5 decibels in our hands-on testing. See our full review.

Cellular shades, also known as honeycomb shades, consist of rows of cells or hexagonal tubes of fabric stacked on top of each other. These shades serve several purposes: They block out light, prevent indoor heat gain in the summer and retain heat in winter, and absorb sound that vibrates into a room to reduce the echo. While single-cell shades have a single layer of cells and absorb limited sound, double-cell shades (such as those by First Rate Blinds) have two layers of cells and thus absorb more sound. Like sound-dampening curtains, they’re best suited for people who experience low levels of noise pollution.

Whether you live in an urban apartment where the noise of blaring horns is enough to drive you mad, or in a rural neighborhood where early-rising roosters create a cacophony, sometimes you just need relief from the racket. Addressing deficiencies in your windows’ soundproofing is one way to do that.

You may elect to replace your windows altogether, or you might choose to layer in some sound-blocking elements. Either way, relief from exterior racket isn’t too difficult to find. As for that drum kit your in-laws bought for the kids, you’re on your own there, though soundproofing your doors might be a good start.

The most affordable way to soundproof your windows is to caulk them with acoustic caulk. Remove any existing silicone caulk and recaulk with a product that is specifically designed to block window noise. A tube of acoustic caulk costs about $20. Window treatments are another economical way to soundproof your windows.

If you have single-pane windows or have no soundproofing materials in place, the sound of the wind blowing through the trees may be loud enough to permeate the windows. Or, you could be hearing wind whistling into the house, entering through gaps between window sashes and other parts of the window housing, such as the sill, jambs, or casing.

You can’t purchase 100 percent soundproof windows; they don’t exist. Noise-reduction windows can block up to 90 to 95 percent of sound.

Curb appeal does not have to be solely cosmetic. See which good-looking projects we are prioritizing to make homes safer, more energy-efficient, and weather resistant.

#7827. Prosecution for Alleged Threats to ICE Officer's Children (Sent to Officer's Wife) Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

In U.S. v. Alexander, decided yesterday by Judge Paul Engelmayer (S.D.N.Y.), the criminal complaint (which yielded an indictment) alleges:

[O]n or about August 20, 2025, [Alexander] sent threatening electronic messages via a social media application … to the spouse ("Victim-1") of a U.S. Immigrations [sic] and Customs Enforcement ("ICE") deportation officer ("Officer-1"). The first message stated, "Are these your kids you had with your Nazi murder rapist husband. They will get it too. Never think that his whiteness will protect them." The second message consisted of a photograph of Victim-1's and Officer-1's children….

Defendant argued her speech was protected the First Amendment, but the court declined to dismiss the indictment:

Section 875(c) makes it a crime to transmit in interstate commerce "any communication containing any threat to kidnap any person or any threat to injure the person of another." … Only "true threats" are outside the First Amendment's scope and thus are punishable under § 875(c). The Supreme Court has described "true threats" of violence unprotected by the First Amendment as "'serious expression[s]' conveying that a speaker means to 'commit an act of unlawful violence.'" "True threats" are distinguished from "jests, 'hyperbole,' or other statements that when taken in context do not convey a real possibility that violence will follow." …

Whether Alexander's alleged message to the victim contains a "true threat" to injure is a question for the jury. There is no basis for the Court to determine that the conduct, necessarily, cannot so qualify, and to dismiss the Indictment on that ground….

The court acknowledged that, "[i]n a rare case, a court may conclude 'as a matter of law' that 'no reasonable jury could find that the alleged communication constitutes a threat or a true threat,'" but concluded that this wasn't such a case:

… Alexander posits a non-threatening construction. She urges that the key phrase ("[t]hey will get it too"), read in light of the next sentence ("[n]ever think that his whiteness will protect them"), is not a threat to injure the children. Rather, she argues, the message conveys that the "children will not be insulated from the harsh governmental policies associated with their father's work." Alexander argues that the message "contained no threat," in that it was "so clearly non-threatening that no reasonable jury could find otherwise." U.S. v. Joudeh (M.D. Fla. 2026) (citation omitted). She likens her case to Joudeh, supra, in which an online communication was held, on a motion to dismiss, necessarily to fall short of a true threat.

Joudeh is readily distinguished. There, the defendant was charged with violating § 875(c) for transmitting an "online comment" that read, "I wish someone would in alive him." On the motion to dismiss, the district court credited (as the Government argued) that "in alive" was a mistype of "unalive," a euphemism for "kill." The court nonetheless found that "no reasonable jury could consider this broad, non-detailed wish to be a threat." Instead, it held, the communication reflected "a vague desire that someone was no longer alive." The court therefore dismissed the indictment on the ground that the statement did "not express an intent to commit harm in the past, present, or future, and there [was] no other context to explain how this statement could possibly be threatening"—it was "simply not a threat." In recognizing that a message conveying merely "a vague desire" that harm would befall someone was not a true threat, the court tracked the Second Circuit's case law in this area, which likewise distinguishes expressions of "abstract desire" from "true threats." U.S. v. Turner (2d Cir. 2013) ("Turner did not merely advocate law violation or express an abstract desire for the deaths of Judges Easterbrook, Bauer, and Posner.").

That principle, however, does not avail Alexander. The message she sent the victim—that "[t]hey will get it too"—is instead like the statements held in Turner to qualify as "true threats" because they expressed an intent to commit harm. These were that certain federal judges "deserve to be killed"; that "[i]f they are allowed to get away with this by surviving, other Judges will act the same way"; and that "[t]hese Judges deserve to be made such an example of as to send a message to the entire judiciary: Obey the Constitution or die."

Significant, too, Alexander attached a photograph of the victim's minor children, establishing her knowledge of their identity, and she sent the message directly to the victim, rather than posting it in a forum where the victim might not alert to it. On the basis of limited materials at hand—the message and attachment—a reasonable jury could find Alexander's statement to the victim that her children "will get it" to express an intent to do physical harm to them, not a mere "vague" desire that the children be injured, and thus to "constitute[ ] a threat or a true threat." …

Moreover, contrary to Alexander's premise, § 875(c) does not require that the defendant "specifically intend to carry out the threat." And to the extent that Alexander defends that the statement was too euphemistic and/or insufficiently specific to support a conviction, the case law is against her….

[W]ithout an evidentiary record, it is premature for the Court to assess whether, as Alexander argues, her message could only be understood as non-threatening commentary protected by the First Amendment…. [T]hat argument "reduces to a question of evidentiary sufficiency, i.e., was the evidence sufficient to prove 'true threats' falling outside First Amendment protection?" Conceivably, the trial evidence may support that Alexander "engaged solely in protected speech … [b]ut this is a matter of proof that cannot be resolved at this stage of the proceedings." …

{At trial, the parties will be at liberty to offer additional admissible evidence as to the context of this message, which may inform a jury's assessment of whether it was a true threat. In this case, the Government proffered at a pretrial conference and in briefing that the ICE official to whom the victim is married was doxxed—i.e., his personal information was publicly shared—roughly contemporaneously with the charged communication.

The defense, meanwhile, notes that the communication occurred on the same day that the New York Times published an article documenting the separation of immigrant families, and in particular ICE's deportation of a six-year-old girl and her mother. For purposes of this decision, the Court does not consider these proffers, but is mindful that evidence speaking to Alexander's motivations could be received and could bear on the "true threat" inquiry.}

Patrick J. Gallagher represents the government.

UPDATE 11/11/26 10:34 am: I originally erroneously said in the post title the threats alleged in the indictment were to the officer's husband and children; of course, they were sent to the officer's wife (listed as the victim in the indictment) and threatened the children. I've corrected the title accordingly; my apologies for the mistake.

Ever since someone put a club and stone together to make the first axe, it has remained a handy tool that has made life easier. Sure, you could fire up a chainsaw to do many things that an axe can do — like chopping wood for fuel, creating wood sculptures, prepping building materials, and clearing land, but an axe doesn’t require any fuel, is way easier to transport, and quieter.

While it may be one of the original tools that humans used, it’s still a tool that comes with risks and it’s important to know how to use an axe safely. It’s also crucial to know the differences among the various axes so you know which one will best suit your needs and how to use it safely and with the right technique.

It’s helpful to know the names for the main parts of an axe so that it’s easier to compare various models, and decide which type is right for your needs. Here are some key axe parts:

It’s not hard to imagine how things can go really wrong when using an axe. In addition to practicing with the axe so you feel confident using it, there are guidelines you should follow to stay safe.

While it may seem like power is the most important part of successful axe-swinging, control and technique have greater influence on success. Even though the weight of the axe helps increase the force, trying to swing an axe that’s too heavy for your abilities is never a good idea. You’ll have better success if you reach for an axe that’s a comfortable weight.

No matter the task, the technique for using an axe is similar.

Most felling strokes are diagonal, but some are horizontal to create a notch in the tree so it will fall. Always position your body (or halt your swing) so that the follow-through does not hit your body. And never stand in the path of where the tree may fall.

The Fiskars X27 is 36 inches long and weighs 6.3 pounds; requires strength to wield but cuts decisively. Read the review.

Limbing can be more dangerous than felling because you are dealing with smaller pieces and a great deal of sharp force near your body. Often, limbing happens while you are standing on a fallen tree. But if you aren’t, make sure there is ample distance between you and the arc of the axe swing. It’s usually easiest to start at the bottom of the tree and work your way to the top branches, swinging in the direction of the top of the tree as you go.

After a downed tree is limbed, it’s ready to be bucked into transportable lengths. Make sure the log won’t roll before you begin. Then, stand on the log and strike the axe below and between your feet.

Cutting logs along the grain is called splitting. A split log dries out faster, and will be ready quicker for a fireplace or fire pit. After placing a log vertically on a chopping block, aim at the face and swing the axe to make contact.

A competitive activity that’s become popular in recent years, axe throwing is usually done in a controlled space. While standing with your nondominant leg forward and at least 12 feet away from the target, pull the axe back over your head. With arms slightly bent, release the axe forward. Just like in golf, follow-through is essential.

Your axe will stay in great shape for a long time with proper care and maintenance. It only takes a few minutes after each use to keep it in fine shape. Plus, it will benefit from oiling and sharpening once a year.

Safely using an axe depends on careful planning about where and when you use the tool. It’s essential to select the right axe based on the task. And it takes practice to know how to hold an axe and how to swing an axe with ease. Never attempt to swing an axe if you feel nervous, if it’s dark out, or if people or pets are within your swing zone.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

Boost comfort in the rooms that need it most this winter with Stelpro’s efficient and stylish supplemental heating options.

As frigid temperatures set in, it’s common to notice the weak spots in your home heating system. From an undersized bathroom fan heater that barely warms up the room to a garage nobody uses starting in November, these cold spots can quickly lead to frustration and inconvenience. Fortunately, fixing these problems is easier than you might expect, thanks to the latest in electric heating solutions. Modern units feature sleeker profiles, compact footprints, and high-performance heating capabilities that outperform older models.

To keep every room comfortable when winter arrives, consider upgrades such as baseboard heaters, discreet wall fan heaters, and special garage heaters, depending on the specific issue you are trying to address.

Do you have one room in your house that is always cooler than the rest? Whether this is a result of location in the home, lack of adequate insulation, drafts, or another factor, you can fix the issue by installing a baseboard heater. This supplemental heating system can quickly transform a room into a much cozier space.

But we’re not talking about the baseboard heaters from years ago that were bulky and unattractive. There are now sleeker models designed with aesthetics in mind, such as the Stelpro Prima Electric Baseboard Heater. These long, narrow units are installed along the base of walls, often under windows, and use electricity to heat up elements in the unit to warm the air as it rises and radiates heat into the entire room.

Here are some of the benefits of choosing modern electric baseboard heaters:

Stelpro’s Prima model is sought after for its elegance, discretion, and efficiency. It is designed with a distinctive format that adapts to various applications without compromising on performance. Additionally, it heats as efficiently as a standard baseboard unit, but the heat generated is more concentrated, so warm air radiates into the room more quickly.

Available in several colors, the unit is also impact-resistant with a reinforced front panel. And thanks to its safe and innovative housing design that prevents fingers from touching the heating elements, it’s easy to clean and maintain. Finally, this model is fast and easy to install, making it a smart choice for updating any room in your house.

This top-of-the-line baseboard heater is as efficient and safe as it is beautiful, with a modern look sure to enhance any room’s decor.

It’s never pleasant stepping onto a chilly floor or taking a shower when your bathroom tends to be the coldest room in the house during winter. This is actually quite common since bathrooms often contain cold, hard materials like ceramic tiles and metal fixtures and typically are built without adequate ductwork. Also, using your bathroom exhaust fan too much can actually make the space feel colder; fans remove moisture quickly, which also removes warm air out of the room.

The best way to warm up your bathroom is to install an electric wall-mounted fan heater such as Stelpro’s Sonoma Style Wall Fan Heater. The main advantage of this type of heater is that it doesn’t take up any valuable floor space, which is important in small bathrooms. The Sonoma is especially discreet, seamlessly blending in with the room’s décor given no visible screws and a smooth cover. It has a modern, slim look with air inlet on the sides to hide internal mechanical parts, not to mention an impact-resistant façade that makes it a safe and sustainable choice. The unit is compact but still has strong performance, from 1,000 to 1,500 watts of heating power, depending on the model.

This heating unit is known for optimal comfort and ease of use. It contains an element that produces instant heat, while the exceptionally quiet fan ensures a quick rise in temperature. In addition, hot air flows out from the bottom of the unit to provide good heat distribution throughout the room. You can choose a model to be paired with a wall thermostat or one with a two-button built-in electronic thermostat to increase energy savings. Finally, Stelpro’s fan heaters can be used to retrofit most competitors’ units.

Ideal for bathrooms, the Sonoma Style fan heater is the new standard for those who need a quiet but fast heating solution.

If you use your garage for more than just parking cars—such as for a workshop or gym—then it’s important to keep the temperature comfortable, no matter how cold it gets outside. Garages aren’t designed to stay warm, as they typically have bare concrete floors and lack insulation. By installing a special type of heater made for garages, you can continue using this space throughout the colder months. Plus, it will protect your tools, paint, and other home supplies from getting ruined by being stored in icy temperatures.

Even if you try running a portable space heater, the temperature inside the garage probably won’t rise more than a few degrees. That’s why installing an electric heating unit like Stelpro’s Spider Ceiling Fan Heater is the best way to ensure you can continue using your garage all year long. Designed specifically for residential garage environments, the Spider’s combination of optimal performance, instant heat using 4,000W of heating power, quiet operation, and stylish red and stainless steel finishes will be a great addition to any garage.

The Spider heater is purposely compact and mounts on the ceiling, so it can heat the entire garage without taking up valuable floor or wall space that you can instead use to hang tools, bicycles, and other garage-friendly items. Finally, you’ll be able to conveniently control this heater using an electronic wall thermostat (not included).

Designed specifically for garage environments, the Spider’s combination of optimal performance, instant heat, and distinct design are a surefire hit.

#7823. Indirectly Inciting "Followers to Flood" Business "with False Reviews, Calls, and Emails" May Be Tortious

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Couture v. Noshirvan, decided Tuesday by Judge Kyle Dudek (M.D. Fla.):

[T]he story begins with a viral video of a parking-lot argument. Convinced that one of the women [Couture] had broken the law, Noshirvan set out to uncover her identity. He deployed a "sock puppet" social media account, posing as a concerned bystander to gain her trust. The ruse worked, and Couture unwittingly confirmed her involvement. Armed with that info, Noshirvan published a TikTok video broadcasting both Couture's name and her employer—Garramone Plastic Surgery.

Noshirvan's followers quickly took to the comments with ideas for how to retaliate. One suggested to "schedule appointments and not show up[.]" Another pitched calling Garramone Plastic Surgery to ask about Couture. And two users went so far as to agree that "we are now working on reviews for his business[.]" Just as the comments suggested, Garramone Plastic Surgery received emails, voicemails, and fictitious reviews….

Apparently having endured enough of this negative publicity, patients cancelled their scheduled procedures, a physician left the practice, and Garramone Plastic Surgery hired security personnel and installed an enhanced security system. Garramone Plastic Surgery now seeks to recover those damages….

The court held that Garramone's tortious interference claim against Noshirvan could go forward:

To succeed on a claim for tortious interference under Florida law, the plaintiff must prove: "(1) the existence of a business relationship, not necessarily evidence[d] by an enforceable contract; (2) knowledge of the relationship on the part of the defendant; (3) an intentional and unjustified interference with the relationship by the defendant; and (4) damage[s.]" …

There is no shortage of evidence showing both protected business relationships and Noshirvan's knowledge of them. Garramone Plastic Surgery's testimony highlights interference with its existing patients and with Dr. Allison Yee, an associate physician who left the practice amid the fallout. Florida law does not require Noshirvan to know these individuals by name. He merely had to know the business relationships existed. The targeted nature of the online attack—especially the bogus reviews planted on the Yelp and Google pages—is more than enough for a jury to infer that Noshirvan knew he was interfering with the practice's clientele.

Further, there is evidence of competent damages. Garramone Plastic Surgery testified that it lost about $900,000 in non-surgical procedures and $130,000 in surgical procedures. Then there are the costs Garramone Plastic Surgery incurred for security personnel and a security surveillance system. …

What is not clear though, is whether there was intentional, unjustified interference…. But Noshirvan's intent in making his posts is best left for the jury. A reasonable jury could conclude Noshirvan's intent was to harass and target Garramone Plastic Surgery. [Plaintiff's theory is that] {Noshirvan incited his followers to flood Garramone Plastic Surgery with false reviews, calls, and emails.} … A reasonable jury could also conclude, however, that Noshirvan's intent was just to harass and target Couture.

The court also concluded that Noshirvan couldn't use 47 U.S.C. § 230 to avoid liability:

Section 230 protects a "provider or user of an interactive computer service" from being treated as the "publisher or speaker" of information provided by another. While there is admittedly little case law regarding users of interactive computer services, a user or provider is still responsible for their own encouragement of, or material contribution to, unlawful content. See, e.g., Elliott v. Donegan (E.D.N.Y. 2022); Doe #1 v. MG Freesites, LTD (N.D. Ala. 2022). Noshirvan published multiple videos on his social media accounts specifically identifying Garramone Plastic Surgery. The videos can be interpreted as a call to action for his followers—especially given Noshirvan's comments that he had done this to numerous people before. Noshirvan cannot escape liability by focusing on the reviews, calls, and emails. After all, it is his own publication that a reasonable jury could conclude sparked them….

But the court concluded that, though Garramone's incitement theory might support a tortious interference claim, it couldn't support a civil conspiracy claim, which requires enough evidence of an "agreement" to do something unlawful:

An agreement can be express or implied. But where a party lacks direct evidence of a conspiracy, circumstantial evidence only establishes an agreement where it "outweighs all reasonable inferences to the contrary."

Garramone Plastic Surgery cannot show an agreement exists…. Garramone Plastic Surgery … claims direct incitement, but the evidence falls short. Noshirvan certainly gave his audience the practice's name, but he did not issue the marching orders to attack its reviews. That call to action came from someone else—a user named @motherofrockets. Garramone Plastic Surgery does provide a post where Noshirvan suggested calling businesses around the practice. But that post is a far cry from launching a targeted harassment campaign against Garramone Plastic Surgery, which is the conduct at issue. There is simply not enough evidence for a jury to conclude Noshirvan directed his followers' actions.

Garramone Plastic Surgery separately leans on indirect incitement, claiming that alone is enough to prove a conspiracy. But that argument expands Florida civil conspiracy liability beyond its breaking point…. When courts find an actionable agreement, there is often at least some direct communication between the conspirators. That crucial link is missing here….

The record here certainly shows that Noshirvan's followers committed wrongful acts. It may even show that he knew his followers were bound to respond with this sort of misconduct. But the Court declines to endorse a rule that anticipating bad behavior creates a conspiracy, at least not without some Florida law in support.

In conducting its own research, the Court could find only one case involving social media. See Conradis v. Buonocore (M.D. Fla. 2021). It offers no meaningful support to Garramone Plastic Surgery because the defendant directly encouraged and recruited third parties to engage in a specific act. At bottom, Garramone Plastic Surgery has failed to prove an actionable agreement between Noshirvan and his followers….

UPDATE 11/11/26 12:19 pm: Note that plaintiff alleges that Noshirvan created the videos because someone paid him money to do that, not out of political or moral conviction; but this particular opinion did not seem to turn on this distinction.

NEXT: Prosecution for Alleged Threats to ICE Officer's Children (Sent to Officer's Wife) Can Go Forward

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7820. Why Not Seek the Win/Win?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"Why not seek the win/win?" Justice Brett Kavanaugh posed that question to Colorado's attorney during last week's oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a case involving Catholic preschools and the state's nondiscrimination requirements. His question raises a broader issue: Why is compromise so difficult in conflicts between religious freedom and LGBTQ rights?

Some background: Colorado operates a universal preschool program that provides public funding for children attending participating schools, including religious schools. But participating schools must agree not to discriminate on several grounds, including sexual orientation and gender identity. Catholic preschools argue that these requirements interfere with their religious mission, which includes teaching Catholic doctrine about marriage and requiring families to support that teaching. Colorado maintains that religious schools may participate, but must comply with the same nondiscrimination requirements as other schools.

During oral argument, Kavanaugh noted that approximately 2,000 preschools participate in Colorado's program, while only 34 Catholic preschools are involved in the dispute. The record does not identify any family headed by a same-sex couple that has sought admission for a child to one of these schools and been rejected. Why couldn't Colorado accommodate these schools while ensuring that other families had ample preschool options?

Colorado's attorney responded that equal access to publicly funded education requires more than the availability of alternative schools. The Catholic schools have a principled position as well. Why should they have to compromise their religious identity to participate in a generally available public program? They aren't asking Colorado to endorse Catholic doctrine, only to permit them to maintain their religious mission.

So why is compromise so elusive? St Mary illustrates a dynamic I wrote about in an article several years ago on Masterpiece Cakeshop, another Colorado religious freedom controversy. I argued that conflicts over religious freedom and LGBTQ rights reflect profound cultural divisions in American society. These controversies implicate competing understandings of identity, dignity, and equality.

For traditional religious believers, marriage and sexuality implicate fundamental religious convictions. Requiring religious schools to disregard those convictions in their admissions policies seems like an intrusion on religious autonomy. For supporters of LGBTQ rights, allowing publicly funded schools to exclude children because of their parents' relationships seems like a denial of equal dignity and citizenship. Each side regards the other's position as demanding a concession on something fundamental. Besides, each side may think it has compromised enough. Colorado doesn't prohibit religious instruction in funded schools; the schools don't ask Colorado to endorse their position on same-sex marriage.

This isn't the first time the Court has confronted such a problem. About a decade ago in Zubik v. Burwell, Justice Elena Kagan explored possible accommodations in a contraception mandate controversy, and the Court subsequently sought additional briefing on a compromise.

Kavanaugh's question makes practical sense. The difficulty is that the parties don't understand the controversy primarily in practical terms. Each sees fundamental principles at stake. The Court will resolve the legal dispute in St. Mary. But it cannot resolve the deeper social divisions that make compromises in these cases so difficult.

I discuss these questions in a new episode of Legal Spirits, available here.

NEXT: Indirectly Inciting "Followers to Flood" Business "with False Reviews, Calls, and Emails" May Be Tortious

Mark Movsesian is the Frederick A. Whitney Professor of Contract Law and the Director of the Center for Law and Religion at St. John's University School of Law. He writes and teaches in law and religion, contracts and international and comparative law.

Hydroponic systems, which allow plants to grow in water rather than soil, are popular because they offer a way to produce a bounty of plants in a relatively small area in an indoor garden. These systems also tend to be user-friendly, so even newbie growers are likely to succeed. We recently tested eight popular models, spending several months setting them up and evaluating their various features while growing a range of plants.

We also evaluated each tested hydroponics system for its ease of use, value, functionality, appearance, and build quality. With these factors in mind, our favorite is Ahopegarden’s 10-Pod Aeroponics Growing Kit. It offers the flexibility to grow almost any type of plant, is easy to set up, and provides a good value for the money.

To qualify as one of our top picks, we required each hydroponic system to have a water circulation system to keep the water fresh. When evaluating all-inclusive systems, we looked for bright grow lights that could be adjusted in height as the plants grow taller. While this system can be used to produce any type of plant, the adjustable light reaches a maximum height of 14.6 inches, so users will need to select plant varieties that won’t exceed this.

We added grow domes to our plant pods and selected the “vegetable” button on the top of the light panel, which put the grow light on the appropriate timer.

We love this system’s flexibility. It’s also on the smaller side, so it’s easy to find a spot for it, even in cramped spaces. Our biggest concern is that there isn’t much spacing between the pods, so depending on the plant, it can get crowded.

We appreciate that the two included extension arms allow for plants up to 18.5 inches tall. This hydroponics grow kit was one of our favorite, easy-to-use indoor gardens. Our only complaint is that it’s a little pricey considering there is only room for three plant pods.

Get the Click & Grow hydroponics system at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 4.5/5; Build Quality 3/5; Value 3.5/5

Even newbies can stretch their green thumb with this system from leading hydroponic systems manufacturer AeroGarden. The Harvest 2.0 indoor herb garden provides everything necessary to care for its six growing stations. We loved the simple setup: Gardeners simply insert plant pods, add water and plant food, plug in the unit, and it’s ready to grow. Humidity caps to help germinate seeds when starting the system are included.

This hydroponics growing system comes with six plastic pots and six seed plugs that are preseeded (Italian basil, Thai basil, parsley, dill, thyme, and mint) and ready to go. Liquid plant nutrients are also included. For convenience, the Harvest automates both lighting and water circulation. The system turns the LED grow lights on for 15 hours per day, though users can turn the lights on and off manually as well. Water circulation is automatic, and the unit features both a low-water and a time-to-add-nutrients indicator to take the guesswork out of indoor hydroponics.

One downside to this indoor hydroponic garden is that it lacks an adjustable light timer—the lights simply come on for 15 hours a day, then turn off until the cycle starts again. The height of the light hood is limited, too. It only offers about 12 inches for plants to grow, which may prove too short for the herbs. Our dill and our basil, for instance, were damaged because they grew too tall and pressed against the hot light before we could harvest them.

Plantaform’s Smart Indoor Garden is a fogponics system that turns a fertilizer and water mixture into fog, delivering nutrients to the plant’s root system. It comes with 15 pods, a lettuce mix plant pack, germination domes, and plant food. Six other plant pack varieties are available for purchase separately.

When we received the Plantaform grow kit, we were impressed by its quality, futuristic look. While it’s a bit larger, at about two feet tall and almost two feet in diameter, we positioned it in the middle of our dining room table. The instructions for setting it up weren’t quite as clear as those for other growing systems we tried. However, once we figured out what to do, it only took about fifteen minutes to get everything set up.

Our lettuce seeds sprouted within a few days, and we were able to remove the germination domes. We then relied on the app to inform us when to add water and nutrients and harvest the plants. Unfortunately, the app malfunctioned a few times, telling us to harvest at one week and then again at two weeks when the plants were still tiny.
