#7796. Judge Richard Posner, RIP

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, a founder of law and economics, and an enormously influential judge.

Judge Richard Posner passed away yesterday. Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, one of the founders of the field of law and economics, and probably the most influential lower-court federal judge of the last several decades. His contributions across a wide range of fields are so great, that no obituary can possibly do them justice.

As a longtime professor at the University of Chicago Law School, Posner was a pioneer of the application of economics to legal issues. His book Economic Analysis of Law, (which has gone through numerous editions since the first one in 1973), was and is the best overview of the field. His classic articles on antitrust law, regulation, the economics of common law, and many related issues were pathbreaking applications of economics to law that continue to influence economists, legal scholars, and policymakers even many decades later.

In addition to his many contributions to law and economics, Posner also published enormously influential books and articles on a dizzying array of other issues. I can only mention a few here. His book Sex and Reason is a tremendously insightful analysis of legal regulation of intimate relationships. How Judges Think and Reflections on Judging shed light on a variety of issues relating to judicial behavior, and legal philosophy. Law and Literature is one of the greatest books on the depiction of law in classic literary works. This list of pathbreaking Posner works can be extended almost endlessly!

Posner became a federal appellate judge in 1981 (appointed to the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit). There, he became perhaps the most influential federal lower court judge of his time, writing a variety of widely cited opinions. He was famous in legal circles for drafting almost all of his opinions himself, rarely relying on law clerks to do it.

A few of my own experiences with Posner and his work may shed some small additional light on the man and his achievements.

As a first-year law student, I was required to take an early-morning Contracts class. Not being a morning person, I periodically overslept and missed class (Posner, I'm sure, would never have done such a thing!). As a result, I was confused about some issues when final exam time came around. The class textbook was only of limited help in clearing up my confusion. So I decided to read the contracts chapter of Economic Analysis of Law. In a relatively few pages, Posner made everything much clearer, and I came to a much better understanding of a wide range of contracts issues than I had before, from studying the much longer textbook. Thanks to Posner, I did much better on the exam than I had any right to expect. He had a gift for distilling complex issues of law and public policy and making them readily understandable even to late-sleeping slackers!

A few years later, I was a law clerk for a federal appellate judge. Usually, when courts cite legal precedents, they do not indicate the name of the judge who wrote the decision. But my judge - who is more conservative than Posner and has a very different judicial philosophy - made clear that, when citing a Posner opinion, I should make sure to indicate Posner was the author. It's a small, but telling, indication of the respect Posner commanded from jurists across the political and jurisprudential spectrum.

Early in my academic career, I was co-editor of the Supreme Court Economic Review. One of the more difficult duties of academic journal editors is dealing with peer reviewers, who often procrastinate,  submit inadequate reviews, or both. One time, on a Friday afternoon, I e-mailed Posner an article submission, asking him to review it. Due to his simultaneous work as legal scholar and judge, Posner was almost certainly much busier than most of our other reviewers. Still, on Saturday morning, I woke up to find a message from Posner in my e-mail inbox. I expected the message would indicate whether he accepted the assignment or not. But instead, I found an extremely thorough and insightful review of the article I had sent him - one of the best peer review reports I have ever seen. In addition to his many other achievements and talents, Posner was extraordinarily hard-working and efficient. He made most of the rest of us seem lazy and indolent by comparison.

I was privileged to know Posner over a period of many years, though we interacted only occasionally. Most of my professional writings related to his work were critical, as in the case of my review of his book Law, Pragmatism, and Democracy, (to which he wrote a solid response,  and I in turn did a short rejoinder), and my criticism (in my book The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain) of his defense of the Supreme Court's controversial ruling in Kelo v. City of New London.

In retrospect, I fear these writings did not always sufficiently convey the enormous respect - even awe - that I had for Posner's many achievements. But I did support his longstanding campaign to get rid of the Bluebook, the ridiculously overcomplicated system of legal citation. In general, I am not a fan of book-burning. But I was happy to follow Posner in making an exception for the Bluebook! For a time, we even collaborated on an effort to persuade law journal editors to rethink the system.

Much, much more can be said. No words of mine can even come close to doing justice to Judge Posner's many achievements, or to his generosity to students and younger colleagues, of which my own experiences with him were just small examples. Thus, I will close by offering my profound condolences to those of his friends, family, and colleagues, who might read this post.

UPDATE: For more on Judge Posner's life and achievements, see this obituary on the University of Chicago Law School website.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7795. The Right Types of Christmas Lights for Indoor and Outdoor Holiday Displays

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Deirdre Mundorf, Updated by Margaret Foley

Updated Nov 12, 2026 11:41 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Each year, as the holiday season approaches, homeowners prepare to deck their homes in sparkling lights. They pull tangled strings from their attics and garages and then, after rushing to the store for replacement bulbs, fuses, or even more lights, they get to work. But if they’re starting fresh in a new house or trying to change up their holiday decor, they have some lighting decisions to make: What kind of Christmas lights should they use? What are the best Christmas lights for the roof? Which lights should are best for the mantel?

More than 150 million strings of Christmas lights are sold in the U.S. every year. Homeowners certainly have a lot to choose from. This guide is the place to start. Here you’ll find some Christmas light basics, a review of the most common types of lights, and suggestions for the best uses for each type.

First, decide whether you want LED or incandescent lights. The choice largely comes down to cost, energy efficiency, and aesthetics.

Since their introduction in the late 1990s, LED Christmas lights have become increasingly popular. In 2024, LED lights accounted for more than 90 percent of holiday string light sales, and for good reason. LED Christmas lights are far more energy efficient and last significantly longer than incandescent bulbs, going strong for upwards of 50,000 hours. Additionally, LED bulbs are brighter and stay cooler than incandescent bulbs. Also worth noting: While you can generally connect only three or so incandescent light strings together, you can link together many more LED strings, depending on their wattage. This can be a big help if you’re installing lights along an expansive roof or trimming an especially large tree.

LEDs do, however, have some significant negatives. For starters, they cost more than incandescents. However, because they last longer and are more energy efficient, the higher expense can be offset over time by lower utility costs and savings from not having to replace the lights as frequently. Another drawback: Some homeowners simply don’t like the look of LEDs, finding the light too harsh and their colors too cool. While newer LEDs have a greater range of color temperature and improved color rendering, some shoppers still prefer the cozier look of incandescents.

Best For: Those willing to pay a higher upfront cost in return for energy efficiency and a vibrant display.

Our Recommendation: Connectable 240 LED Twinkle Fairy Light String at Amazon for $17.99These LED wide-angle indoor/outdoor lights extend to a length of 88 feet, offer 13 lighting modes, and are available in a range of colors.

Incandescent lights are typically less expensive than LEDs and emit a warmer, softer glow. However, incandescent bulbs burn out faster, are less durable, and consume a lot more electricity than LED bulbs.

Best For: Creating a nostalgic display with a warmer, cozier glow.

Our Recommendation: Home Accents Holiday 300 Incandescent Mini String Lights at The Home Depot for $9.98Even if one of the bulbs burns out, this 68-foot strand of 300 mini incandescent lights will stay lit; available in white and multicolor.

Holiday lights are rated for outdoor use, indoor use only, or indoor/outdoor use.

In a 2026 survey by Thumbtack, over half of respondents plan to hang holiday lights outdoors this year. If you’re part of this majority, be sure that you’re using outdoor-rated holiday lights for your outdoor Christmas light installations. These lights are more weather-resistant, have thicker wiring, and are made of more durable materials than indoor Christmas lights. Other tips for selecting and hanging outdoor lights include:

The Balsam Hill classic spruce tree is well-made, easy to set up, and sturdy enough to hang heavy ornaments. See our full review.

Christmas lights can be powered by electricity, batteries, solar energy, or even USB. Your budget and access to electrical outlets will help you determine which power sources are best for your situation.

Plug-in lights are any type of light that plugs into an electrical socket. This is the traditional way of powering Christmas lights.

For plug-in lights, you need a nearby electrical outlet or an extension cord. Once plugged in, the lights stay on as long as there’s power. There’s no need to worry about dead batteries or the solar charge depleting.

Best For: Creating dependable, long-lasting holiday light displays near a power outlet or where an extension cord can be used.

Our Recommendation: Prextex 100-Count White Christmas Lights at Amazon for $8.99This 20-foot incandescent light string has 100 warm white lights with a waterproof design suitable for indoor or outdoor use.

Some holiday lights rely on battery power, often using AA batteries. These sets are great solutions in situations where cords could pose a tripping hazard. where you want to keep the power source hidden, or where there are no electrical outlets nearby—for instance, if you want to add lights to a Christmas wreath on an entry door.

The lifespan of battery-operated lights can vary depending on the number of lights on the strand, whether the bulbs are LED or incandescent, the quality of the batteries, and other factors. While some lights may stay lit for more than 100 hours before requiring new batteries, others will need fresh batteries after only a few hours.

Best For: Displaying lights where no power outlets are available or where cords either aren’t wanted or can’t be used.

Our Recommendation: Loende Battery-Operated String Lights at Amazon for $12.99These classic-looking LED string lights are available in white, clear, and multicolor. The 50-light, 18-foot string features eight lighting modes and an automatic timer.

Solar-powered Christmas lights offer an eco-friendly solution for holiday decorations. Rather than consuming electricity, these lights are powered by sunlight through a connected solar panel. Solar Christmas lights are often comparably priced to their plug-in LED counterparts.

Though they’re eco-friendly, be forewarned that the lights may not stay lit very long at night if the solar panel doesn’t receive enough sunlight during the day. Also, if you’re planning a large display, the individual solar panels of each light strand could leave your lawn looking cluttered.

Best For: Small outdoor areas that get a lot of sunlight, such as sunny pathways, small sections of fence, and shrubs.

Our Recommendation: Joomer Solar Christmas Lights 2 Pack at Amazon for $19.99 Available in white and multicolor as well as several single-color options, this two-pack totals 400 LED lights and 144 feet and is safe for indoor and outdoor use. The strands offer eight lighting modes, and a 6-hour charge during the day will power the lights for more than 8 hours.

Plug these lights into a laptop, power bank, USB power adapter, or anywhere else you find a USB port. They’re handy for brightening up bedrooms, backyards, campsites, and other spots where a USB port is the most convenient power option.

Best For: Any space where a USB port is the most easily accessible power source for spreading some holiday cheer.

Our Recommendation: Green Convenience 100 LED USB or Battery String Lights at Amazon for $9.99This 33-foot indoor/outdoor holiday light string can be powered with either batteries or USB, offers eight lighting modes, comes with a remote control and timer function, and is available in white or multicolor.

Once you’ve decided whether you want LED or incandescent lights and have figured out how you’ll power them, it’s time to choose the best Christmas lights to suit your holiday decor. Here’s a rundown of the most common string and bulb styles and some of their best uses.

These small cylindrical bulbs with pointy tips are the most common holiday string lights. They’re available with both LED and incandescent bulbs and are sold for both indoor and outdoor use. Though they’re probably the most popular types of Christmas tree lights, mini string lights are also great for highlighting the mantel, wrapping around columns and banisters, and draping over entryways and windows. These are the light strings you’ll find crowding the shelves at the best places to find Christmas lights.

There are two main types of mini lights: M5 bulbs and T5 bulbs. Their shapes are similar, but T5 bulbs have a pointier tip, while M5 bulbs have a more rounded tip and textured sides.

Best For: Decorating Christmas trees and hanging over windows and entryways.

Our Recommendation: Minetom LED Christmas Mini Lights, Warm White at Amazon for $16.99Give a warm glow to your Christmas tree, bushes, columns, and more with this 75-foot string of 200 indoor/outdoor mini lights that offers eight lighting modes.

For a vintage look, nothing beats classic, colorful C6, C7, and C9 bulbs. Their rounded, conical shape evokes the homey Christmas trees in movies like It’s a Wonderful Life and A Christmas Story.

These days, C-type bulbs are available in both incandescent and LED light strings and in a range of colors. Use the smaller C6 (1⅛ inches tall) or C7 bulbs (1½ inches tall) indoors to give the Christmas tree or mantel a retro vibe, or outside on smaller trees and architectural features. The larger C9 bulbs (2½ inches tall) are best used outside to frame the roof or windows, or to wrap larger trees and shrubs.

C6 and C7, Best For: Lighting retro-style Christmas trees and smaller landscaping features.

Our Recommendation: Dazzle Bright C6 Christmas String Lights at Amazon for $16.99This set of indoor/outdoor C6 Christmas lights has 100 multicolor LED bulbs and eight lighting modes; UL-certified, and can be used indoors or outdoors.

Our Recommendation: Minetom C7 Christmas String Lights at Amazon for $33.99This 50-foot string has 52 C7 bulbs that are transparent, warm white, and give a vintage glow.

C9, Best For: Illuminating a large roofline.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen 25 C9 Multicolor LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $22.99This 17-foot string of faceted, indoor/outdoor C9 LED bulbs is expandable (you can safely connect up to 90 sets), long-lasting, and even dimmable.

Also known as 5mm lights, these bulbs have a concave lens that spreads extremely bright light in all directions. Because they’re compact, they don’t snag as easily as larger lights, so they’re often the bulb of choice for wrapping tree trunks and branches. Don’t let their small size fool you—these lights can easily illuminate large spaces.

Best For: Wrapping branches, bushes, or trees.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen Lighting Multicolor 5mm LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $24.99Available in white, single-color, and a variety of color combinations, this 24-foot strand of 70 LEDs is backed by a 3-year seasonal warranty—and you can string together 44 sets.

Strings of icicle lights have short, vertical strands of mini lights (or actual icicle-shaped bulbs) hanging down at intervals, “dripping” like icicles. They’re available in both LED and incandescent, and although white icicle lights are most popular, they’re also available in multicolor and single-color strands.

Best For: Installing on eaves to mimic dripping icicles.

Our Recommendation: Knonew Christmas Icicle Lights at Amazon for $69.99This 99-foot string of icicle lights features 228 vertical drops, eight modes, and a built-in timer. Also available in multicolor and single-color strands.

Pathway lights are mounted on stakes that can be driven into the ground along walkways, driveways, or garden beds to enhance safety and spread holiday joy. These eye-catching outdoor decorations are typically plug-in or solar-powered and available in fanciful shapes like candy canes, jolly Santas, and Christmas bulbs.

Best For: Lining front walkways or driveways.

Our Recommendation: Brightown C9 Christmas String Lights LED Pathway Lights at Amazon for $32.99With 20 C9 bulbs on a 25.7-foot string, these plug-in LED pathway lights will brighten up walkways and garden beds. They’re also available in faceted and multicolor styles.

Add a bright, modern, geometric touch to your outdoor decor with durable, flexible rope lights. They’re easy to bend around railings and columns, and some strands offer color-changing or chasing effects.

Best For: Wrapping tree trunks and banisters, and accenting architectural features.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen Lighting 18-Foot LED Warm White Rope Lights at Amazon for $27.99The kit includes an 18-foot length of rope with 216 LED bulbs, mounting clips, three splice connectors, and end caps. Connect up to 15 kits; available in multicolor and various color combinations as well as single-color options.

Net lights are light strings that have been connected into a grid. They’re a hassle-free way to create a uniform blanket of light on bushes and hedges. Similarly, trunk lights are nets designed to wrap around the trunk of a tree. Both products can really speed up holiday decorating.

To make sure you’re buying the right size, first measure the square footage (surface area) of the shrub you’d like to cover. Net lights generally range from 4 to 10 feet long and 2 to 5 feet wide, although they can run much larger.

Best For: Covering shrubs and hedges with lights.

Our Recommendation: Meteds 120 LED Christmas Net Lights at Amazon for $23.39The warm white bulbs in this 6-by-4-foot net light will give your shrub a romantic glow, but it’s also available in cool white as well as three colorful options. Connect up to 10 sets.

Many of the LED light options in this list are available with color-changing features, where bulbs produce many different hues, or “chasing” features, where bulbs cycle on and off in patterns that create the illusion of lights moving along the string. These technological wonders may be the most fun and interactive types of Christmas tree lighting, and whether they’re used indoors or out, they give the homeowner the ability to customize or reimagine their holiday decorating scheme at a moment’s notice, often using a remote or an app.

Best For: Creating dynamic, customizable holiday light displays, indoors and outside.

Our Recommendation: Twinkly Strings Smart LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $74.99Once you’ve mapped your light display to the company’s app, you can select one of the app’s preset light effects or create your own, with 16 million colors to choose from.

The colors you choose set the tone for your holiday light display: the classy, subdued sparkle of a warm white, the exuberance of a multicolor string, or the uniform glow of a single hue. Consider some of these popular choices.

For the Christmas tree: Plan on at least 100 lights per vertical foot of tree, more if the tree is especially wide or if you like a really bright tree.

For shrubs: Net lights are the fastest and easiest way to illuminate bushes. Just measure the approximate surface area of the bush and purchase a net light that will cover it. If you’re using string lights, figure 50 lights per square foot.

For the exterior: Decide where you want to install lights. Do you want them just along the eaves, or would you like to outline windows, railings, and other architectural features? Measure the total linear feet you intend to cover, add 10 percent to account for corners, plug-in space, and irregularities, and then divide by the length of your light strands (for example, 25 feet or 50 feet) to determine how many you’ll need.

For wrapping columns/tree trunks: The number of lights needed will vary depending on the circumference and height of the column, the desired vertical spacing of the lights, and the distance between lights on the string (for mini lights, the standard is 4 or 6 inches). To make things easier, check online for calculators.

#7793. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7791. How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a new car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

Use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin says. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

Vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”

Even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical issues with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

(also referred to as Y.R.J.), a Child, Trial Court Cause No. 323-107644-18, 323rd District Court, Tarrant County, Texas (Honorable Alexander Han Kim / Judge Alex Kim). Cornyn's judiciary committee staff under Chief Counsel Matt Johnson and later Chief Counsel Noah Phillips. Elliot has spoken at the Texas Chapter Conference, and routinely attends Texas FedSoc happy hours and other gatherings.

Elliot is deeply respected by members of the Texas conservative legal movement. This evening, he attended the Texas FedSoc gathering at the Mayflower and we are all pulling for him. He would make a stellar judge and fill a seat that cannot be left empty.

#7789. How to Get Stink Bugs Out of Your House

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 12, 2026 12:57 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys) is a stowaway from Asia that entered the U.S. sometime in the 1990s. Adult stink bugs are approximately the size of a dime and easily recognized by their shield shape, mottled gray-brown coloring, and alternating light and dark bands on their antennae and abdomen. They can also, of course, be identified by the unpleasant odor they release, often described as a strong cilantro-like smell, when they are threatened or squashed. (Not everyone is sensitive to the smell, so it’s possible to have an infestation even if you don’t perceive the odor.)

As of 2021, the brown marmorated stink bug had been found in 47 states, and it’s earned a rep as an agricultural villain, feeding on upward of 60 different species of fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants. But its habits have also made it a notable household nuisance.

Outdoors, stink bugs are attracted to a wide range of plants. But when the weather turns cold and they start searching for a place to spend the winter, they, like so many other bugs, seek the warmth and shelter of your home. In these colder months, they enter a dormant phase during which they’re inactive, neither feeding nor reproducing. In fact, they’re model insect houseguests: They don’t move around much, damage structures or clothing, reproduce, or bite people or animals. Stink bugs are not poisonous, and they won’t raid the pantry.

Stink bugs do, however, have some big drawbacks, including their noxious odor. Unfortunately, they also release a pheromone that attracts other stink bugs, which means they can gather in numbers reaching into the hundreds or even thousands.

While dormant, stink bugs may move around slowly, if at all. You are most likely to notice them in the fall, when they’re coming indoors, or in early spring as they head back outside to mate. David Price, associate certified entomologist and director of technical services at Mosquito Joe, a Neighborly company, “They do not leave behind any visible indications they have chosen your home, other than their physical appearance.” This means that you might not know you have a stink bug infestation until you actually see a bug, dead or alive.

Commercial insecticides may kill off some of the stink bugs in your house, but these toxic chemicals are generally ineffective and don’t offer a long-term solution. “Their shield provides them with protection against many insecticides,” Price says. Even after treatment, bugs can migrate from other areas of the house or emerge from cracks and crevices, including gaps around baseboards and molding. Insecticides do nothing to prevent more bugs from coming in, either. If you’re trying to figure out how to eliminate stink bugs, the most effective approaches are physical removal and deterrence.

For physical removal, focus on areas where stink bugs tend to congregate. Price notes that they typically gather in the “attic, or voids around windows,” and they’re attracted to light-colored surfaces and the sunny side of a house. Stink bugs are also known to tuck themselves into folds of curtains, hole up in crevices, and seek out quiet spots like crawl spaces.

You can use either a regular vacuum or a wet/dry vacuum, but use just the hose. Steer clear of attachments that might crush the bugs. You will need to clean out the vacuum when done. While the smell will eventually wear off, if your home is subject to frequent infestations, you may want to invest in a dedicated vacuum or handheld vac. Another option: Slip a knee-high stocking over the vacuum hose, secure it with a rubber band, and stuff the toe of the stocking down the hose so the stink bugs will be captured in the stocking instead of the vacuum canister.

If you are sweeping up stink bugs with a broom, it’s a good idea to sweep or dump them directly into a bucket of soapy water. Dispose of the bugs outside the house in a tied plastic bag.

A direct hit with a stream of soapy water from a spray bottle should kill a stink bug. It takes just a few teaspoons of dish soap in a spray bottle filled with water.

Trapping stink bugs when they’re on the move is an inexpensive but effective strategy, especially in the spring, when the brighter, longer days signal that it’s time for them to head outside and mate.

The Flowtron bug zapper has an electrified grid that is effective at killing insects, though its design may not be for everyone. Read the review.

A spritz of hair spray can paralyze a stink bug so you can either drop it in a bucket of soapy water or simply take it outside. Take care using this method near upholstery, leather, and other surfaces that could be damaged by hair spray.

Stink bugs are attracted to light, including the blue UV light that bug zappers use. While not the most effective method, a quality bug zapper can be a useful ally. Note that entomologists and others concerned with the environment discourage the use of zappers, which kill both good and bad bugs.

If you’ve successfully eliminated stink bugs from your home, you’ll continue to have problems if you can’t prevent more bugs from coming in. The key to keeping stink bugs out is to seal common entry points.

Fill cracks around windows and doors, both indoors and out, with exterior caulk.

Check around plumbing pipes, AC lines, cables, electrical conduits, and other pipes that pass through the exterior walls of your home. Seal up gaps, indoors and out, with plumber’s putty, sealant, spray foam, or another appropriate filler.

Periodically, and certainly before fall kicks in, check your home’s siding for gaps and holes. Caulk gaps as needed.

Make sure there are no openings to the outside (check for daylight showing through). Also, look for cracks in the walls.

When possible, remove window air conditioners at summer’s end. If they must stay in all year, seal up any gaps around the unit and cover it before the weather turns colder.

Check weatherstripping around doors for wear and tear, such as missing pieces and other damage. Replace weatherstripping as necessary.

Look for rips and tears in window or door screens, and repair or replace damaged screens promptly. Invest in screens if some of your windows or doors don’t have them.

Screen gable vents, eave vents, and other openings to prevent stink bugs from gaining access.

All of the sealing methods rank high in advice for how to deter stink bugs from invading your house. A bonus method is use of various essential oils, especially clove, lemongrass, spearmint, and ylang-ylang, which can discourage stink bugs from coming in. Combine about 10 or so drops of the essential oil of your choice (or a combination of a few oils) with water in a spray bottle, and spray windowsills, window frames, doorways, and other common entry points regularly in fall. Another option is to mix a few teaspoons of garlic powder with a few cups of water and spray the solution around entry points.

These removal and deterrence strategies can help control a modest infestation, but if you’ve tried all of these and your home is still overwhelmed by hundreds of stink bugs, you need a pro. Pest control companies can employ multiple techniques to stop an infestation, including vacuuming, applying specialized dusts and powders, and sealing off or treating entry points. They also can provide advice on preventing future infestations.

Keeping a home properly sealed prevents stink bugs from entering. It’s important to check the perimeter and openings annually, and seal or weatherstrip as needed.

Rake up debris and edible vegetation around your home’s foundation, keep wood piles and compost heaps well away from the house, and consider turning off interior and exterior lights near entrances when possible.

Although this is a common belief, killing a stink bug does not attract others.

Yes, you can flush stink bugs down the toilet. Flushing is a good way to get rid of them without giving them a chance to release their scent.

Vacuuming is the fastest and most efficient way to remove stink bugs. For easy disposal, use a vacuum with a bag.

#7787. What the Heck Happened To Regular Gear Shifts?

Why ate regular gear shifts being replaced by increasingly impractical buttons and screens? Here's the deal.

You sit down in the driver’s seat of your car, push the start button, and then reach for the gear lever. Except it’s not there. The console has ten cup holders and three phone charging ports, but no gear shift. Nothing above it on the dash either: that’s also lever-lackin’. Upon the column like an old school pickup? Nope.

There was a time when shifting gears was one of the most fundamental parts of driving. You reached for a lever, moved it into position, and felt a mechanical connection between your hand and the machinery responsible for making the car move. Whether you drove a three-on-the-tree sedan, a four-speed muscle car, or a truck with a modern automatic, there was a lever involved in changing gears.

Then automakers decided that shifting gears was probably too much work.

Today’s vehicles increasingly replace conventional gear selectors with things that are decidedly not gear selectors. Rotary knobs, push buttons, electronic switches, touchscreen menus, and all manner of non-levers are now in vogue.

The question is simple: What happened to gear shifts, and why did automakers decide that one of the most recognizable controls in an automobile needed reinventing?

Early automobiles required direct mechanical connections between the driver’s controls and the transmission. Whether automatic or manual, gearboxes used levers and linkages to move internal components into position to make the vehicle drive. The gear lever was a functional necessity.

As automatic transmissions became more common in the 1960s, the familiar PRND (Park, Reverse, Neutral, Drive) arrangement became standard. Whether mounted on the steering column or the center console, the selector offered a straightforward interface with an obvious purpose. And it was usually physically connected to what it was doing in the transmission.

The mechanical connection also provided useful feedback. Moving a lever into Drive felt different from selecting Reverse or Park. The driver could often determine the selected gear by feel without looking down at the shifter.

Msst recently, however, electronic controls began replacing mechanical linkages. Known as shift-by-wire, these systems communicate the driver’s selection electronically rather than relying on a direct physical connection between the selector and transmission. By the 2010s this was the norm in consumer vehicles and the disconnection between driver and machine began in earnest.

This technology offered automakers more freedom in where and how they placed gear controls. It also opened the door to an increasingly strange assortment of alternatives. With the advent of increasingly smartphone-on-wheels designs, making the gear shift a radical part of design is now all the rage.

Once a conventional mechanical linkage was no longer necessary, designers gained considerable freedom. A rotary dial could perform the same function as a traditional lever. A collection of buttons could accomplish the same task. A small electronic toggle could select Drive or Reverse without occupying much space.

Some manufacturers embraced the change enthusiastically.

Jaguar Land Rover became particularly associated with rotary gear selectors, including the rising dial used in certain Jaguar and Land Rover models. Chrysler experimented with rotary selectors in vehicles such as the Ram 1500 (quickly finding out that many truck owners hate them), while Ford and other manufacturers introduced electronic switches and compact selectors across portions of their lineups. Honda famously went to push buttons that were immediately compared to the (questionable, short-lived) push-button shifting American Motors used in the 1950s.

Mercedes-Benz moved many gear selectors to a steering-column stalk, freeing space on the center console. Not wanting to be left behind, Hyundai did the same, but with bulkier shifters located down low on the column. Others kept a traditional-appearing shifter, but made it barely move and difficult to shift into neutral (Nissan) or manual control (Subaru).

The reasoning isn’t entirely unreasonable. A conventional shifter can consume valuable cabin space, particularly in vehicles with complex center consoles. Replacing it with a dial or switch can free room for storage, cupholders, charging pads, and other amenities.

Electronic selectors can also reduce the number of mechanical components required between the cabin and transmission.

But there is a difference between making a control smaller and making it better.

A conventional lever communicates something to the driver through its position and movement. A rotary dial or momentary switch often depends on a display or indicator to communicate the selected gear. The control becomes less self-explanatory, and the driver may need to look down to confirm what the vehicle is doing.

That isn’t necessarily a deal-breaker, but it raises an obvious question: What problem was the new design solving for the person behind the wheel? This question often goes unanswered.

Automotive interiors have become battlegrounds for designers seeking to make each new model feel more modern than the last. Large screens, minimalist dashboards, floating center consoles, and increasingly elaborate ambient lighting have become selling points. Traditional physical controls can appear old-fashioned in comparison.

And despite design trends toward “minimalism” in vehicle cabins, prospective buyers are expecting more. We want cup holders capable of increasingly large volumes. We want phone chargers so we don’t have to plug anything in. We want a place to put a purse. An extra drink. Our miscellaneous devices. Car keys. A picture of grandma.

Despite design trends pushing toward minimalism, American car buyers are anything but minimal with the amount of stuff we expect to fit in our cars. A current, full-sized pickup truck will have no fewer than six drink holders within the driver’s reach. Because that’s what focus groups demand. Holes in the center console for a purse? Yep, also demanded in most SUVs and minivans. Two or more wireless phone chargers? Also requested. Set-and-forget climate controls? Thumbs up there too. Plugs for dash cams, a place for the air freshener that isn’t the rearview, a way to get into the center storage bin from at least four of the vehicle’s seating positions, six ways to put… You get the idea. We want a lot. While being minimal. Because that aesthetic is in.

So the conventional gear lever became an option that could be eliminated to make more space for other stuff, while achieving a minimalist look. And so the gear shift… Well, shifted to somewhere else.

Some of the alternatives make no sense whatsoever.

The problem isn’t that electronic shifters are inherently bad. It’s that automakers sometimes appear to treat novelty as an improvement in itself.  A control that performs the same task in a less intuitive way hasn’t necessarily advanced automotive technology. It may simply have changed the shape of the inconvenience.

Much of the more recent change has come thanks to electric vehicles accelerating the transformation.

Most battery-electric vehicles don’t use conventional multi-gear transmissions. Their electric motors can deliver useful torque across a broad operating range, allowing many EVs to operate with a single fixed reduction gear rather than the multiple forward ratios common in gasoline-powered vehicles.

Drivers still need to select Park, Reverse, Neutral, and Drive, but there is less reason to retain a traditional transmission selector designed around a conventional automatic gearbox.

Add in that many EVs have been just experimental smartphones with wheels, and things get even dicier. Early adopters of a new technology are usually happy to accept all kinds of radical changes and inconveniences for the privilege of being first. And so gear shifters got radicalized in electric cars.

Some EVs use steering-column stalks. Others employ center-console switches, small toggles, or touchscreen controls. The absence of a conventional transmission also gives designers more freedom when arranging the cabin. Things could be sleeker, thinner, lower, and above all.. Whiter. Every early EV seemed to have a white interior with a complete absence of useful buttons or switches. Giant TV-sized screens dominated the interior instead.

However, electrification doesn’t automatically justify every unusual design. An EV still needs a clear, accessible way to select a direction of travel. The motor may be simpler than a conventional powertrain, but the driver’s task remains fundamentally the same: choose where the vehicle should go.

Slowly, as EVs gained mainstream appeal, those “old school” controls began to return. Today, the best-selling electrics for any given carmaker are usually the ones that are cars that happen to be electric rather than being electric for EV sake.

Probably not everywhere, but it isn’t disappearing entirely. In fact, it’s making a bit of a comeback. It’s the traditional manual transmission that is becoming rarer than an uncirculated wheat penny. Among automatic vehicles, some manufacturers retain conventional-looking selectors because customers understand them and find them comfortable to use. And a few of those manufacturers who deviated are coming back to them.

The likely future is a mixture of approaches. Electronic shift-by-wire technology will remain in nearly all vehicles because it offers packaging flexibility and integrates readily with modern vehicle electronics. And is less likely to break. EVs will likely continue to use compact selectors, while performance cars and pickup trucks may preserve more traditional controls where they contribute to driver engagement.

The important distinction is between modernizing a control and needlessly complicating it.

Perhaps that’s what the industry has forgotten: The best automotive controls aren’t always the newest or the smallest. They’re the ones that do their jobs so well that the driver barely has to think about them.

We’ve tested our fair share of kitchen appliances over the years, and for our money, a good water filter is one of the most practical investments you can make. From removing tap water’s harsh taste and smell to catching invisible and unhealthy contaminants, countertop reverse osmosis systems make access to crisp, clean drinking water easy.

In our recent head-to-head testing of the best countertop water filters, the Bluevua Ropot countertop reverse osmosis water filter system earned the top spot. It wasn’t just the five-stage filtration that won us over—it was the combination of NSF- and WQA-certification, the no-installation setup, and the fact that the filters last up to 2 years, all wrapped in a design that won’t look out of place next to your coffee maker.

Performance is perhaps the most important aspect of a water filter, and the Ropot’s is excellent: water passes through a sediment filter, a pre-carbon block, a high-precision reverse osmosis (RO) membrane, a post-carbon filter, and a remineralization stage. Unlike some competitors, Bluevua backs this unit’s performance with actual NSF and WQA certification.

The downside of such thorough filtration is that the process takes longer than it would with a basic pitcher filter, meaning the Ropot isn’t for you if you’re not going to be diligent about refilling it in advance. But if you can get into the habit of refilling the reservoir after every couple of glasses, it’ll be well worth it. Not only will the five-stage filtration process remove contaminants (including sediment, chlorine, heavy metals, fluoride, PFAS, microplastics, pesticides, dissolved solids, and bad tastes and odors), but it goes the extra mile with a remineralization stage that adds beneficial minerals back in, like calcium and magnesium. In our taste tests against tap water, pitcher filters, and other RO systems, the Ropot’s flavor was easily one of the best.

While reverse osmosis systems are hard to beat in terms of filtration performance, they’re traditionally a bit rough when it comes to installation. But since the Bluevua Ropot is a countertop unit, there’s zero drilling or plumbing necessary. You just set it on the counter, plug it in, and fill the removable 1.77-liter tank. The digital panel shows live total dissolved solids (TDS) readings alongside filter-life indicators, so you know when it’s time to change them out. When that time comes, the cartridges twist out and in without tools.

We also loved the high-borosilicate glass pitcher. Some of the others we tested didn’t come with a collection chamber for the filtered water at all, and if they did, they were often plastic (which can absorb odors or degrade over time). Bluevua’s glass carafe keeps purified water fresh and fits neatly in the refrigerator if cold water is what you prefer.

In terms of downsides, the Ropot was one of the more expensive water filters we tested, and the slower flow rate and larger footprint are real considerations if speed or space are your priorities. But between the certified filtration, the 2-year filter life, and water that consistently tasted better than bottled, we think it’s worth it.

#7783. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, “Trump’s Transportation Department Makes Commonsense Updates to Vehicle Lighting Standards for AVs”

#7782. Weber Slate 22-Inch Griddle Review: A Rust-Resistant Tabletop Griddle With Precise Heat Control

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 12, 2026 6:44 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Flat top griddles are great for cooking all kinds of foods, including those you’d never throw on a standard grill, which is why they’re such great sidekicks for tailgating and camping trips. These smaller flat-top griddles are also ideal for those who want one but don’t have enough deck or patio space for a full-sized outdoor griddle.

I recently tested a new entrant in the portable griddle market: Weber’s 22-inch Slate griddle. While the Slate offers the rock-solid build quality and refined temperature controls we at Bob Vila have come to expect from Weber, it comes at a price, both in terms of cost and weight. The Slate is one of the most expensive and heaviest portable griddles we’ve tested. I’ve spent several months using the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle to cook a variety of foods and found it worth the weight and price thanks to impressive cooking performance and rock-solid build quality.

The Weber Slate 22-inch griddle is one of the largest portable tabletop griddles I’ve seen. With its 352 square inches of cooking surface, you can fit a lot of food on the griddle at once. And since it has two burners, you can create two large cooking zones. This came in handy when cooking meals that require two different temperatures, such as beef and peppers for fajitas or bacon and pancakes for breakfast.

While size and weight obviously matter a great deal when it comes to portable griddles, performance is also crucial. The Weber Slate heats the carbon steel cooking surface with two burners totaling 16,000 BTUs. That isn’t particularly impressive—for comparison, Blackstone’s 22-inch tabletop griddle puts out a whopping 24,000 BTUs—but Weber makes up for it with its smart design. The Slate’s burners sit very close to the cooking surface, so more heat is directly transferred to the carbon steel plate. It also has built-in wind guards that prevent heat loss, so the heat generated by the burners can build up under the cooking surface. And once the griddle gets going, the carbon steel plate retains heat exceptionally well.

During testing, it took about 10 minutes to reach 500 degrees Fahrenheit with the lid closed. While this isn’t as hot as other portable tabletop griddles I’ve tested, the Weber also offered great low-temperature control. I was able to keep it at under 300 degrees Fahrenheit, which is among the lowest consistent temperatures I’ve been able to maintain on any griddle. How did that translate while cooking? The Weber packed enough heat to sear restaurant-worthy smashburgers but still offered enough low-temperature control to fry eggs and cook pancakes without burning them.

We’ve come to expect top-notch materials and build quality with Weber’s grills, and the Weber Slate 22-inch griddle didn’t disappoint. Anyone who’s used a griddle knows how hard it is to keep the surface from accruing rust, even when stored in a dry shed or garage. Weber case-hardens the Slate’s cooktop, which makes its cooking surface rust-resistant. Most griddles I’ve tested developed rust on the cooking surface even when cleaned, oiled, and sitting in my garage. The Weber remained rust-free, even when I neglected to clean it after cooking for several weeks.

That said, there are a few trade-offs for that expansive cooking surface, multi-burner design, and solid build quality. One is its weight. At 53.5 pounds, it’s far heavier than other top tabletop flat top griddles. In fact, it’s about 20 pounds heavier than the Blackstone 22, which has a similar cooking surface, and more than twice as heavy as the Pit Boss two-burner griddle. While I was able to carry the griddle over short distances without help, I found myself having to lighten the load by removing the cooktop, which meant I had to make two trips when moving it.

The Weber Slate also comes with a steeper price tag. At $379, it’s far more expensive than other similarly sized portable griddles, including the Cuisinart 22-inch tabletop griddle ($290) and the Blackstone 22-inch tabletop griddle ($219). The price difference is significant, but its build quality, rust-resistant top, and exceptional performance make it worth the additional cost.

#7781. Defense attorney in Tupac Shakur murder trial discovered dead inside his Vegas home

Attorney Michael Sanft, in court last August during the trial of Duane “Keffe D” Davis, was found dead in his Las Vegas home on Friday. (Daniel Cole/Pool Photo via AP)

The lawyer who defended the man convicted of killing rapper Tupac Shakur was found dead Friday inside his Las Vegas home, a short time after filing an appeal in the case.

Michael Sanft, 55, was the attorney for Duane “Keffe D” Davis, who was found guilty Oct. 13 of first-degree murder in the killing of Shakur. Davis, 63, was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison for being the architect of the drive-by shooting targeting Shakur in 1996 when the rapper was 25 years old, according to the New York Post.

Sanft filed an appeal of the conviction on Oct 30. He had taken Davis’ case pro bono.

Sanft leaves behind two children. The cause of death is pending. Police said Sanft’s death doesn’t appear to be suspicious.

#7779. The Best Quiet Generators for a Peaceful Power Supply, Tested

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Mark Wolfe, Michelle Larson, Additional research provided by Bob Beacham

Updated Nov 13, 2026 3:10 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Quiet generators supply electricity for outages, jobsites, and camping trips without the racket associated with traditional models. But quieter engines raise an obvious question: Do they come at the expense of useful power? To find out, we researched more than 35 options and tested 10, running appliances, tools, and electronics and evaluating noise, ease of use, portability, and value to identify which backup generators are worth considering.

Based on our results, the best overall option is the Honda EU2200i inverter generator, which pairs low noise with a compact design and dependable performance. During testing, it powered a full-size refrigerator and handled an array of jobsite tools without tripping its breaker. But since different shoppers have different priorities, you’ll want to consider what you need to run, as well as fuel compatibility, portability, and noise level. Read on to learn more about these factors and how our picks for the best quiet generators performed in our tests.

Bottom line: These tested quiet generators provide efficient, low-noise power solutions for emergencies, camping, and more.

These generators made our list by providing power for various needs without creating ear-splitting noise. No matter your power needs, if you’re looking for a quiet way to generate electricity, one of these generators may very well fit the bill.

The Honda EU2200i inverter generator offers an excellent combination of portability, reliability, easy operation, and low noise, making it a great option for tailgating, camping, picnics, and other on-the-go outdoor events. Though it’s not a completely noiseless generator, its engine sound easily gets lost in the background.

This inverter generator has a Honda GXR120 commercial series engine that delivers 120 volts and up to 2,200 peak watts and 1,800 running watts. A 125V-20A duplex outlet allows users to plug in two electrical cords, just like a wall outlet at home. We used it to power a full-size refrigerator for 4 hours, burning about a half tank of gas. In another test, we plugged in a portable table saw and miter saw on a jobsite for a whole workday. The current was clean and consistent, and we didn’t trip the breaker once. We also added a USB hub to charge a phone and laptop.

This generator is compatible with the Honda My Generator mobile app for remote monitoring and is parallel ready for use with a second Honda EU2200i (connection kit sold separately). It also features a built-in carbon monoxide sensor and safety shutoff. Its molded plastic handle sits behind the fuel tank opening for balanced carrying despite its nearly 50-pound weight. Our only complaint was that there was no built-in USB port, so we had to unplug a three-prong extension cord on a tool that draws nearly 10A to charge a device using less than 3A.

What our tester says: “This unit’s mix of impressive features makes it a great option for camping, tailgating, or a jobsite. It’s easy to imagine it working for most users, which is why it’s our top pick.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Honda quiet generator at Amazon or Northern Tool + Equipment.

The Pulsar 2200-watt inverter generator is a great option for powering small tools and devices for up to 8 hours. With a 1.18-gallon fuel tank and the ability to run either gasoline or propane, the generator supplies up to 1,800 watts while running, peaking at 2,200 watts on startup.

Setup was a bit difficult at first. To access the oil fill port, we had to remove a side panel, and doing so required some manual force. Once we were able to pop the panel off, getting the generator ready to start for the first time took only a couple of minutes.

With just a couple of pulls on the recoil start, the engine came to life quickly. Our test rig included a couple of heat guns and hair dryers running at the same time on different high and low settings to vary the load. We found the generator handled 1,800 watts as advertised but noise levels were higher. Pulsar states that this generator runs at approximately 60 dB, about the sound level of conversation, but to us, it sounded about as loud as a vacuum cleaner.

Even though it was a bit louder than we hoped, we found that this generator is a great option, particularly at this price point, for light-duty power needs such as small DIY projects and powering a couple of household appliances during an outage.

Get the Pulsar quiet generator at Amazon.

It’s hard to beat Westinghouse’s 4,500-watt iGen inverter for power output, versatility, and portability. This gasoline-only generator has a 3.4-gallon tank that can run up to 18 hours. It operates at just 52 dB(A), which is quieter than normal conversation. This was a significant upside for us as travel trailer owners because RV parks are notorious for looking down on ear-splitting generators.

This quiet gas generator offers a variety of power ports, including a 30A outlet, two 20A outlets, and two USB ports. It’s not the most powerful model we tested, but it excelled in running grinders, saws, and the electric-based essentials in a travel trailer while also charging digital devices, which is exactly why we chose it as the best quiet generator for camping.

It weighs nearly 105 pounds without fuel, so it was challenging (but worth the effort) for just one of us to lift it into and out of the truck bed. Setting it up was a snap—we added oil and filled the tank with gas, and we were in business. While this would be a great emergency generator for home use, we think it’s also an ideal quiet generator for RV or jobstie use

Get the Westinghouse quiet generator at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Walmart.

Solar generators have come a long way in the past decade, and nowhere are the improvements more apparent than with the Generac. This solar-powered generator delivers up to 3,200 peak and 1,600 running watts via three AC ports, four USB ports, a 12V DC port, and a wireless charging pad. If you’re searching for a portable silent generator, this rechargeable power station is an alternative to consider for emergency backup, tailgating, and camping.

Although the Generac does not include solar panels, we paired it with our EcoFlow 400-watt portable panels. Using those, we charged the generator from 28 percent to 100 percent in just under 5 hours. Charging time may vary, of course, depending on the capacity of your panels and the amount of sunlight available on any given day.

Once charged, we powered several household appliances, including a fridge and lamps, multiple electronic devices, and even a miter saw. Unlike fuel-powered generators that constantly produce a set wattage, the Generac expends only as much power as you use, making it one of the most efficient generator models available.

Overall, we were impressed by this model, which was the quietest portable generator we tested. However, its 43-pound weight is worth noting. Carrying it over long distances can be cumbersome, but its rugged, nonslip handle makes short moves more manageable.

Read our full review: Generac GB2000 Portable Power Station

What our tester says: “It’s good for more than just energy assurance should the electricity go out—it provides off-grid power for tailgating, camping, or road trips. I ended up using the GB2000 to power a laptop and projector, and to my delight, was able to watch an entire movie projected on a rock wall.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Generac solar generator at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

Running on gasoline (6,800 peak and 5,100 running watts) or propane (6,000 peak and 4,500 running watts), the Wen DF680iX is a quiet dual-fuel generator that packs a lot of output into a relatively portable package. And because it produces clean, stable power (pure sine wave—similar to what you get from a wall outlet at home), this quiet portable generator is ideal for everything from electronics to small-to-medium home appliances.

We put the Wen’s capabilities to the test by powering a laptop, cell phone charger, and small refrigerator at the same time. We ran that setup on propane and then on gasoline, and each fuel kept the generator going for multiple hours without refueling. The Wen was also one of the lighter models we tested at just under 100 pounds, so it was easier to move around than you might expect for such a powerful machine.

The outlet lineup on this small quiet generator is generous as well. There are two 120V-20A outlets, a 120V-30A RV outlet, a 120V/240V-30A twist-lock outlet, a 12V DC port, and two USB-A ports—an array that lets you charge multiple devices and run heavier equipment from the same unit. And it measures about 64 dB at a quarter load, which is quiet enough to talk or listen to music.

Get the Wen quiet generator at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Wen.

If you’re comparing the best generators for backup power, the Champion is definitely a top contender, especially if you don’t want to be tied to one fuel. Not only does it run on gasoline, propane, and natural gas, but the hoses you need for all three come included—which is surprisingly rare for multi-fuel appliances. Peak output is an impressive 8,500 watts regardless of the fuel source, though running watts drop from 6,500 on gasoline to 5,850 on propane and 5,265 on natural gas. Because it’s an inverter generator, it’s safe for sensitive electronics.

Over more than 3 hours of testing, we used this quiet home generator to power our garage fridge, a microwave, a corded handheld random orbital sander, and multiple small electronic devices, and it didn’t struggle at all. We didn’t notice any dips when we switched between gasoline and propane, and we loved that the wireless remote let us start it from inside rather than stepping out into the cold.

The 132.3-pound weight was our biggest complaint since it made lifting a challenge, but we did appreciate that there’s a wheel kit for easy rolling. And at about 64 dB(A), it was on the loud side for this lineup, but that noise level felt totally reasonable since it’s also the most powerful option by far.

What our tester says: “The Champion puts out a lot of power for such a quiet-running generator—enough for a refrigerator. But my favorite feature was the remote start, which worked even when I clicked it looking out our front window. Add in the fact that you can use it with three different types of fuel and that it hits 8500 peak watts, and you have one pretty impressive whole-house generator.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Champion quiet generator at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Acme Tools.

Generators have a reputation for being loud, and in our experience it’s mostly deserved. Of the dozens we’ve tested for various guides, many have been as loud as gas-powered lawn equipment. But as technology improves, manufacturers are making them quieter and more efficient, with the quietest models using computer-controlled inverters. In addition to being quieter, inverter generators self-regulate to avoid wasting energy, which makes them among the most efficient options.

For this list, we researched more than 35 generators before selecting several top-rated models for hands-on testing. We considered some of the best generator brands, along with customer satisfaction, power output, cost, and noise level, and we focused on inverter models that run at 64 decibels (dB) or less, about the level of a normal conversation or a running dishwasher. We also looked at solar generators, which produce little to no noise at all.

For testing, we assembled each model, followed the instructions for fueling and safety, and powered them up. We plugged in a variety of tools, appliances, and other items, using an online wattage calculator to help estimate the correct wattage for each model. Noise got our closest attention, but we also assessed ease of use, power, portability, and overall value.

There are a variety of factors to consider when shopping for a quiet generator for home use. In this section, we take a closer look at these factors to help you find a model that provides enough power and portability at the lowest decibel levels.

Wattage is typically the most critical factor to consider when buying a quiet generator. While generators have different wattage ratings, here’s an important point to remember: The higher the wattage rating, the higher the power output. Higher wattages usually mean larger, more expensive units (with the largest being standby generators), but quiet generators are usually compact and small, providing moderate power output for laptops, smartphones, and other small devices.

Those in the 1,000- to 1,600-watt range are great for camping and minor jobsite use, but not for home backup. For that, a minimum of 2,000 watts is recommended (to run an oven or large refrigerator), although 3,000 watts or more will be needed to run several items concurrently. Every electrical device has a label with the wattage rating on it, which may help when deciding which generator to buy.

Quiet inverter generators typically use gasoline as a fuel source, and dual-fuel models can run on propane, too. This is a big advantage, as it allows you to choose fuel based on your specific needs, such as power output requirements, fuel availability in the area, and the fuel type available.

Inverter generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the generator fuel tank, the longer it will be able to provide gasoline-based power, but the size of the generator itself also increases.

Fuel capacity has no bearing on how much propane can be used with the generator (making propane generators worth a look for those who need versatility in these machines). Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

Quiet inverter generators are less noisy than large or open-framed models, often in the 50- to 60-decibel range. To better understand generator noise output, here are some common comparable sounds:

The quietest inverter generators also use sensors to detect how much power they need to expend, throttling down for smaller loads and producing lower noise levels.

We’ve included one solar generator on our list, although solar generators function differently from traditional generators. A solar generator is basically a portable power station that can be charged via solar panels, though some can also charge via an electrical outlet. Solar generators don’t produce as much energy, but they’re completely silent, eco-friendly, and can be used when no gasoline or propane is available. (Note that, like the Maxoak Bluetti above, they may make a small amount of noise when charging via an AC outlet.)

Physical size and weight are also worth considering, particularly if you intend to regularly transport the generator. Since these units are meant to provide power where it is needed, small inverter generators are usually top-handled or side-handled units that can be picked up with one hand and carried with relative ease, as they’re typically around 40 to 60 pounds.

Heavier units weighing up to 100 pounds come with wheel kits to make portability easier. Both constructions are compact enough to bring to the campsite, stow in the car, or keep in the garage for when backup power is needed.

Quiet generators may be equipped with features that make their operation as convenient as possible. These include:

Here are some of the most frequently asked questions we get from shoppers who are looking for the best generators for their homes.

A range of 50 to 64 decibels is considered quiet for a generator. Unlike many traditional generators, which operate at loud volumes, modern inverter models are much quieter.

Inverter generators don’t use alternators like typical open-framed models, which require the engine to work harder and produce more heat and noise. For that reason, inverter generator engines run more quietly. In addition, manufacturers can close them inside plastic housing for even better noise control without overheating.

Yes. Just like your car, a generator’s engine requires periodic maintenance. This includes routine oil changes, such as after 20 hours of use for a brand-new generator and every 100 hours of use afterward, cleaning the air filter after 100 hours of operation, and ensuring that it runs for 20 or 30 minutes at least once every 3 months. Manufacturer recommendations will vary depending on the machine.

Generally, no, but it depends on the type of generator. A small portable generator may need a break from running after 8 to 12 hours (check your owner’s manual), while a standby generator is designed to run continuously if needed. Operating a portable fuel-powered generator overnight may not be safe unless someone is awake to monitor it. While today’s manufacturers take precautions to make their generators as safe as possible, there is always a risk of fire if something flammable gets too near the generator. Additionally, fuel-powered generators produce carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that can be hazardous if inhaled. In addition to not running a generator overnight unmonitored, don’t run one in a basement, a garage, or any enclosed space. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions for safe operation.

A quiet inverter generator typically lasts 1,000 to 3,000 running hours, or 10 to 20 years of occasional use with regular oil changes and care.

Outdoors, on a flat, dry surface at least 20 feet from your home, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows, and vents.
