#7759. This $10 Hardware Store Staple Can Fix More Around the House Than You Think

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Donna Boyle Schwartz, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:32 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Caulk fixes myriad projects around the house, from outdoor maintenance to indoor decorating. What makes the material such a versatile DIY essential? The rubbery substance, available in a variety of formulations, including silicone, latex, acrylic, butyl rubber, polyurethane, and construction adhesives, can bond to almost any material, making it a wonderfully flexible material for projects indoors and out. With the right tube of caulk, you can solve just about any problem—including these common issues.

Caulking windows and doors is the best way to reduce drafts, cut home energy costs, enhance your house’s energy efficiency, and decrease your carbon footprint, according to the Consumer Federation of America. For this job, choose either acrylic latex or vinyl latex caulk. Acrylic latex caulk works best in dry environments and will perform well for up to 15 years, while vinyl latex can be used in damp areas and lasts about 5 years.

Concrete and mortar repair caulk is an excellent tool for sealing cracks and gaps in concrete, brick, stucco, stone, and metal. Similarly, it’s perfect for repairing small fissures in foundations and basement walls that allow insects, rodents, and other pests to enter your home. Designed for both interior and exterior use, concrete and mortar repair caulk has a textured finish and can be painted once it’s dry.

No matter how carefully you measure and cut, you often end up with little gaps between, above, and below moldings and baseboards. When you need to close the gap, acrylic latex caulk is one of the best caulks for baseboards, ideal for filling in those small spaces. The product dries quickly and can be painted as soon as 6 to 8 hours after application. Acrylic latex also comes in a variety of different pigments, so you can match the color to the surrounding material.

Over time, small spaces can open up between tiles, and in moist environments that’s an invitation for mold and mildew to grow behind the walls. Both 100 percent silicone caulk and siliconized acrylic caulk are ideal for wet environments and form a durable, watertight seal. Mold- and mildew-resistant silicone caulk is made for nonporous surfaces like ceramic, glass, and metal, while waterproof siliconized acrylic caulk works well on tubs, tile, glass, and ceramic tile surfaces. Gorilla silicone sealant is ideal to use since it is waterproof, and mold and mildew resistant.

Gorilla silicone caulk is flexible, adheres well, and creates a mold- and mildew-resistant barrier on bathroom surfaces. Read the review.

When you need to cover small holes and tiny cracks prior to painting, painter’s caulk, an acrylic latex compound, is just what you need. Painter’s caulk such as DAP Alex painter’s caulk adheres to wood, drywall, masonry, and other surfaces. Because it dries to a paintable texture in about an hour, it’s a good choice for busy DIYers.

Fire barrier sealant, a specialized type of caulk, does more than patch holes. It actually helps make your home safer by preventing fire from moving through open spaces within a structure. Fire barrier sealant can be used to seal holes, gaps, and cracks around holes in interior framing, especially around plumbing or electrical conduits.

When a length of molding falls off, a corner of carpet comes up, or a tile comes loose, all-purpose caulk can often fix it. Dab a little caulk behind the loose piece, then stick it back into place. You can even use an all-purpose caulk like GE all-purpose silicone caulk to install wood wall paneling without nails.

To keep wallpaper from pulling up as it dries, run caulk along all trimmed paper seams, especially in the corners, then smooth with a wet sponge or finger to remove any surface imperfections. For wallpaper that is peeling, lift up the loose section of paper, apply adhesive under it, then smooth the paper back against the wall. Once the adhesive dries, apply a continuous bead of caulk along the seam to keep it from peeling up again.

With the right caulk, you can even repair a roof! Roof repair caulk, like Roofers Choice Roof Cement Caulk, can be used to seal small cracks or gaps along roof edges, between shingles, and around skylights or flashing. As you might expect, roof repair caulk is completely weatherproof and waterproof, and can be used in wet areas or on dry surfaces.

As your home’s gutters age, they can develop cracks and gaps, especially around joints and downspout junctions. Butyl rubber caulk, a strong waterproof sealant, can be used to seal joints in those damaged gutters. Dab a little onto the cracks to keep your gutters leak-free—and keep rainwater flowing out and away from your home.

Painter’s caulk (or decorator’s caulk) is used, as its name suggests, just before decorating and painting. It’s the right choice for sealing crown molding, chair rails, and baseboards because it’s flexible and hides gaps between the wall and the finishes.

Whether you’re repairing a small hole or a sizable tear in your home’s vinyl siding, siding caulk can help. Simply choose a shade of exterior caulk that matches the hue of your exterior (even black caulk is available), and use a small dab to seal minor punctures, like nail holes. Cover larger holes or tears by applying caulk to the back of a scrap piece of siding, and covering the hole with the scrap piece.

Caulking between a countertop and a tile backsplash in the kitchen doesn’t just give your work space a “finished” look. It keeps crumbs, food items and worse yet, water, from getting behind your countertop and cabinets. Silicone caulk, which is moisture and mildew resistant, is the best caulk for the job. While you have your caulk gun out, make sure there’s a sturdy seal between your countertop and kitchen sink, too!

When you don’t have any fluffy furniture pads on hand to stick on the undersides of flower pots and other decorative items, caulk can help. Turn your pots on their sides and apply a few dabs of silicone caulk to the bottoms of the pots. Allow the caulk to dry so the pots won’t stick to your floors. When they’re set, the silicone pads should keep the pot from scratching your hardwood.

One of the easiest ways to keep your asphalt or concrete driveway in good condition is to attend to cracks as soon as you notice them. The longer you wait, the better the chance that moisture will seep into the cracks, and make an even more fractured-looking mess of your driveway. Load your caulk gun with a quality, water-resistant asphalt crack sealant. Acrylic formulas are flexible and should fit into just about any nook or cranny.

#7758. What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

“TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

#7757. Help set the ABA’s new advocacy agenda in D.C.: Take the Legislative Priorities Survey

The ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey. (Al Drago/Bloomberg)

The historic November midterm elections have rewritten the political landscape in Washington, D.C., setting the stage for Democratic control of both chambers of Congress and a potentially consequential legislative agenda.

The 120th Congress convenes in early January to confront the challenges of governing in a divided government. It is important that the American Bar Association is ready to engage and to have a strong voice at the table on issues affecting the legal profession and the administration of justice. As a new balance of political power takes shape during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office, the ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey.

Participation in the survey is available exclusively to ABA members. By participating in the survey, you have the opportunity to have your voice heard on issues that matter most to the legal profession and the justice system.

The survey opened Nov. 6 and will close on Dec. 4. Most ABA members have received an email with a personalized link to the survey. But any member can access the survey at ambar.org/priorities. Members can also expect an invitation from ABA President Barbara Howard, and the link will be distributed via the ABA’s social media. With a new political landscape taking shape in Washington, the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey will play an important role in ensuring that the association’s advocacy efforts reflect the concerns and priorities of our members.

The 2026 survey has an even more streamlined ranking system than the last priorities survey. Members are being asked first to prioritize issues aligned with the ABA’s current priorities and policies. Members then respond to open-ended questions designed to identify additional policy issues the ABA should consider prioritizing, including those that might require the development of new policies.

The survey takes less than 10 minutes to complete, and your input will be indispensable to informing the ABA’s legislative priority-setting process.

The survey results will be presented to the Board of Governors at the ABA Midyear Meeting in early 2027. The Board will consider ABA member input, along with the following criteria, to determine whether an issue should be made a priority:

• Breadth and strength of the ABA interest • Importance to the practice of law • Public perception of the profession • Opportunity for impact • Potential for achievement • Timeliness of issue • Expertise of lawyers on the issue • Importance to society • Importance to the administration of justice

The 120th Congress presents new opportunities for the ABA to advance policies important to our members and our legal profession and to work with policymakers as they contend with issues that could have far-reaching consequences for our nation.

Please take a few minutes to complete the survey now. Your input will help strengthen the ABA’s voice in Washington, ensuring that the legal profession’s priorities are heard and its commitment to the rule of law amid the new political realities in Washington, D.C., remain a powerful force in our nation’s capital.

This report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to issues being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

#7755. Arkansas S. Ct.: Legislature May Revive Cases Barred by Statute of Limitations

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court reverses its precedent, dating back to 1846, that held such revival unconstitutionally restricted the defendant's "vested rights" not to be sued, which had been created by the earlier statute of limitations.

From H.C. v. Nesmith, decided last week by the Arkansas Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Nicholas Bronni, joined by Justices Courtney Rae Hudson, Cody Hiland, and Rhonda Wood (note that other state courts are split on this question, see, e.g., this post and this one):

This case presents a particularly important question: Can the General Assembly extend the statute of limitations in cases where it has already run and afford child-sex-abuse victims an opportunity to hold their abusers accountable? … [T]his court's vested-rights precedent … categorically bars "expand[ing] a limitation period so as to revive a claim already barred." …

Revisiting our vested-rights precedent, we conclude that it lacks any constitutional basis and, as such, cannot stand. We therefore overrule our prior cases prohibiting the legislature from expanding a limitations period and thereby reviving time-barred claims [and] uphold the Vulnerable Victims of Sex Abuse Act against Nesmith's constitutional challenge ….

[Under] our vested-rights precedent …, "the legislature cannot expand a statute of limitation so as to revive a cause of action already barred." That doctrine rests on the assumption that when a civil statute of limitations runs, a tortfeasor has a vested right to the property that could have been the subject of a potential claim….

[But] our cases do not cite any constitutional basis for that doctrine. Far from it, when we first employed that principle to strike down legislation in 1933, we instead relied on a single legal encyclopedia published in 1915 assuring us that—at that sole moment in time—most jurisdictions held that legislatures could not revive a claim after a statute-of-limitations defense had run. Or, perhaps more generously, we relied on that legal encyclopedia plus an unreasoned extension of this court's prior case law suggesting that to retroactively alter an applicable statute of limitations, the legislature needed to speak clearly and show it had considered the consequences. That approach, unbound by actual text or constitutional history, is not consistent with our constitutional role….

To be sure, some later cases—perhaps recognizing that our earlier cases do not cite any constitutional language supporting our vested-rights precedent—suggest that precedent rests on due-process principles…. [But] that label does not work because the expiration of a statute-of-limitations period does not confer a property right—or any other right for that matter.

As the Supreme Court has explained in rejecting similar arguments under the federal due process clause, a statute-of-limitations period merely governs the time within which a claim must be brought, see Chase Sec. Corp. v. Donaldson (1945); it does not reflect a legislative judgment "that [a] defendant should 'be free from liability after the legislatively determined period of time.'" Instead, these limitations "are by definition arbitrary" and rest entirely on legislative judgments about how best to encourage plaintiffs to diligently pursue claims and avoid litigation "after memories have faded, witnesses have died or disappeared, and evidence has been lost."

As such, they "represent a public policy [choice] about" how to balance those interests and exist only by "legislative grace." Altering that period and establishing a different, equally "arbitrary" date does not—contrary to our prior case law's unfounded assertion—deprive a defendant of any vested property right. Rather, balancing competing interests and "resolv[ing] the debate" about when a claim should be time-barred is precisely the kind of thing that our constitution leaves "to the legislature."

We therefore hold that the court's vested-rights precedent has no basis in law, and we overrule our prior cases categorically barring the legislature from expanding the limitations period and thereby reviving claims. Indeed, as we recently reaffirmed, "we are bound by constitutional text," not precedent that "treats our constitution not as a written document but as a set of civic values and norms determined by judges." And we now restore to the General Assembly its constitutional power to decide how long is too long to bring a claim….

Recognizing the vital importance of stare decisis, I nonetheless conclude that this is an exceptional case that warrants breaking with our precedent. Before the General Assembly enacted the Justice for Vulnerable Victims of Sexual Abuse Act, victims of sexual abuse who were under age twenty-one generally had until three years after attaining full age to file suit. Yet childhood sexual abuse presents a unique problem in that—by its very nature—it often prevents victims from bringing timely claims. This consideration leads me to conclude that great injury and injustice will result if we continue to follow our vested-rights precedent in this case….

In recent years, research has revealed the prevalence of childhood sexual abuse and some of the reasons for delayed reporting. For example, we now know that at least one in four girls and one in twenty boys in the United States experience child sexual abuse. Even still, childhood sexual abuse is vastly underreported, and when it is reported, often years or decades have passed. Victims may be reluctant to come forward due to the negative repercussions of disclosure, such as disruptions in family stability, loss of close relationships, or involvement with the authorities; fear of not being believed; and psychological obstacles such as shame and self-blame….

I disagree with the majority's decision to upend 180 years of this court's precedent prohibiting legislative attempts to revive expired statutes of limitation…. In my view, applying our vested-rights precedent to the present case, … the legislature lacked the power to revive the expired statute of limitations applicable to Nesmith, and therefore, the claims against Nesmith were time-barred.

[I]n 1846 this court in Couch v. McKee treated the completed bar [of the statute of limitations] as a property interest that cannot be removed by later legislation. When the statute has run, the defendant's right to be free from the claim becomes part of his or her protected legal estate, an interest the State cannot simply reassign by retroactive enactment. Our later cases have repeatedly applied that same rule, holding that revival statutes cannot constitutionally divest a defendant of a vested limitations defense.

Nor, contrary to the majority's assertion, is our vested-rights jurisprudence untethered from constitutional text. The Arkansas Constitution reflects a longstanding hostility toward retroactive laws impairing settled rights. See Ark. Const. art. 2, § 17 (prohibiting ex post facto laws and laws impairing contractual obligations); id. § 21 (protecting due process). Consistent with those principles, this court has repeatedly recognized that retroactive legislation may not constitutionally disturb vested substantive rights….

That rule is not a mere formalism. Statutes of limitation serve an important public function. They encourage the prompt filing of claims so that the truth-finding process is not impaired by faded memories, lost documents, unavailable records, and deceased witnesses. Those concerns are not hypothetical. The amicus brief filed in this case illustrates the serious prejudice that can result when claims are revived decades after the fact.

Ms. Shirley Suhl, an eighty-seven-year-old retired widow, represents that she is defending claims in federal court arising from alleged events at a facility that ceased operating around 2006 and from conduct dating back nearly forty years. She is not alleged to have personally committed sexual abuse; rather, she is alleged to have known of or been complicit in abuse by others. According to her brief, relevant facility records no longer exist, potential witnesses are elderly or deceased, and one named former employee accused of abuse is now in his nineties. Whether those allegations ultimately have merit is not before us. The point is more basic: the passage of decades can make a fair defense difficult, sometimes impossible.

This is precisely why Arkansas law has treated an accrued limitations defense as vested. Once the limitations period has run, the defendant is entitled to repose, not because the underlying allegations are unimportant but because the law recognizes that, at some point, the defense of stale claims becomes too impaired to permit reliable adjudication. The majority treats the limitations bar as a revocable act of legislative grace. Our cases have treated it differently. They have recognized that once the bar attaches, it becomes a substantive right to resist enforcement of the claim. That rule does not deny the gravity of child sexual abuse. It enforces the constitutional limit on retroactive legislation that destroys vested rights.

In this instance, stare decisis carries particular force. The rule the majority abandons today is not isolated or recently decided precedent. It can be traced back to this court's earliest jurisprudence and has been reaffirmed across generations of cases. Litigants, lawyers, and the General Assembly have long operated against that settled backdrop. Yet today, the majority discards nearly two centuries of precedent. Stability in the law matters, especially when the court alters longstanding rules governing substantive rights and retroactive legislation….

{While many judges and justices pledge full allegiance to the doctrine of stare decisis, even to the point of perpetuating clear errors of constitutional interpretation, I am not one of them. And while it is an important piece of our judicial system, I have frequently noted that "[t]his court "should not invoke stare decisis to uphold precedents that are demonstrably erroneous." Here, however, our two centuries of case law on the subject are rooted in the Arkansas Constitution as article 2 section 21 supports our precedent. Accordingly, I would follow it.

Joshua D. Gillispie (Gillispie Law Firm) and Brian G. Brooks represent plaintiffs.

#7754. Elon Musk Is Pulling the Plug on Cybertrucks to Focus on Something New

Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The company’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

For anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

Tesla hasn’t said which customers will receive their trucks or how it plans to handle the remaining orders.

The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The company plans to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

Musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He says the company can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

#7753. It’s Not Too Late to Do the Lawn Maintenance You’ve Been Putting Off

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:11 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Many people assume lawn care ends when summer does, but autumn is when you’re laying the groundwork for next year’s success, says Allison Koenig, lawn and garden expert at Tractor Supply Company. “The work you do before winter, from mowing and fertilizing to leaf management and soil care, has a much bigger impact on spring performance than most homeowners realize,” she says. We spoke to Koenig and other lawn care experts to learn which fall lawn maintenance tasks you can still do even into early winter to improve the health and appearance of your lawn next spring, and what should be put off because it’s too late.

Earning perfect scores for ease of use, accuracy, and value in our hands-on test, this simple kit can help inform your fall lawn care routine.

The biggest misconception about fall lawn maintenance is that the lawn is dead because of cooler temperatures and doesn’t need attention anymore, says Koenig. But this isn’t true; the lawn is just dormant, which is a big difference. “A dormant lawn is still relying on the roots and reserves it built up in fall,” says Koenig. “Treat it like it’s done for the year and skip the prep work, and you’ll feel that mistake in spring.” Just be mindful that once the ground freezes or grass is fully dormant, it’s best to avoid aggressive projects like aerating, heavy raking, and major repairs. Winter is better spent protecting the lawn rather than trying to renovate it.

Pay a little attention to your lawn in fall and gain the rewards come the busy spring season. Experts suggest the following:

One of the simplest yet most important tasks in fall and winter is to keep your lawn free of debris, says Theresa Smith, senior vice president at NaturaLawn of America in Frederick, Maryland. “Fallen leaves and sticks can smother the grass, block sunlight, and trap moisture, leading to the grass becoming weak and susceptible to disease.” Regularly rake, mulch, and remove any large debris from the lawn to allow your grass to breathe and absorb as much sunlight as possible.

Mowing the lawn to the right height before winter arrives is an essential fall lawn task for preventing damage, says Smith. “Avoid cutting the grass too short, as this can lead to scalping and weakening the much-needed root system that it needs to survive winter,” she explains. “On the other hand, leaving the grass too long can also damage a lawn if it gets matted down with snow and ice, which can lead to disease and dying off.”

Fall is one of the most effective times for weed control because many weeds are moving nutrients into their roots as they prepare for winter, which makes them more susceptible to treatment, says Brian Feldman, lead agronomist and senior director of technical operations at TruGreen. Consider the timing and the type of lawn, though. “For cool-season lawns, the ideal window is generally October through early November, while warm-season lawns can still benefit from treatment later in the fall, particularly for certain winter annual weeds,” says Feldman.

Before you put down any fertilizer or aerate, Wells Westmoreland, co-founder of Tomball Lawn Care Service in Tomball, Texas, recommends getting a soil test first. “The results tell you exactly which nutrients your lawn is missing (or has too much of), so when you go to buy fertilizer or hire someone to apply it for you, you’re getting the nutrients your yard actually needs,” he explains.

Fall can be a great time to aerate and overseed your lawn; however, the best time of year depends on the type of grass you have. “Cool-season grasses, such as Kentucky bluegrass or tall fescue, should be aerated and reseeded in late summer through fall, or mid-August to mid-October,” advises Smith. On the other hand, warm-season grasses, such as zoysias and Bermuda grasses, should be aerated when they are more actively growing, usually during late spring or early summer.

After a hot and dry summer, lawns begin to recover in the early fall, making it an ideal time to apply fertilizer in support of its growth, says Smith. “Since daylight hours are shorter, the grass produces less top growth and directs the nutrients in the fertilizer toward root development, which helps keep the lawn healthy during colder months and helps yards that were fertilized to green-up quicker come springtime.” Some states have specific fertilizer restrictions in the late fall months, so be sure to check your state’s regulations before applying fertilizers.

Although winter typically reduces pest activity, some issues can still arise. Mice, voles, and other small mammals may take refuge in your lawn during the colder months, causing damage by burrowing or feeding on grass roots, warns Smith. “Check for signs of pest damage and act, such as using traps or deterrents if necessary,” says Smith. “Similarly, look for any patches where the grass has turned brown and may be holding disease spores. Rake up the dead grass and bag it so it doesn’t spread before winter temperatures arrive.”

Your grass doesn’t need nearly as much water this time of year, so decrease the frequency with which you water it. While you don’t need to stop, it’s a good time to pull back to avoid overwatering, which can cause large patches of your lawn to die off and invite fungus, disease, and root rot, says Westmoreland. “We see this a lot when sprinkler systems are still running on their summer schedule, so be sure to check your timer.”

It’s critical to avoid sodding during colder months. “You’ll likely spend several hundred dollars or more hiring a contractor, and the new sod has a very low chance of taking root because it can’t establish itself in the cold,” warns Westmoreland. Instead, wait until spring and you’ll get a much better return on that investment.

Adding a lot of nitrogen right before the cold months encourages new growth to pop up. “The problem here is that new growth gets hit harder by the cold than more established turf, so nitrogen can end up killing off a big chunk of your lawn,” explains Westmoreland. “Save the nitrogen for when things warm back up; then, the new growth will be supported.”

If you have a warm-season grass like St. Augustine, Bermuda, or zoysia, hold off on aeration and dethatching. These types of grasses only benefit from these processes when temperatures are much higher, as they’ll actively be growing during that time, says Westmoreland. “In the cold, the root zone on these grass types goes dormant, so aeration will just open up the turf to damage from the cold since the roots won’t be spreading as quickly.” However, if you have cool-season grass like fescue or ryegrass, you can still move forward with these tasks.

Once soil temperatures have dropped and winter conditions have arrived, it is most likely too late to overseed cool-season lawns, says Feldman.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7752. What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

Should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the New World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

How many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

Definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” says Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”

It’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”

One option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she says, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”

For a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” says Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”

This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

The danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

Before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

Composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they quickly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”

It’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

If you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

#7751. The Best Cordless Drills for Home Repairs and Heavy-Duty Projects

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Glenda Taylor, Bob Beacham, Mark Wolfe

Published Nov 13, 2026 4:52 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Cordless drills make it easier to bore holes and drive screws without a cord restricting movement. Among the most useful battery-powered tools, they serve everyone from occasional DIYers to busy renovation pros. To find the best cordless drills for different projects, we tested 14 highly rated models, from heavy-duty hammer drills to compact drill/drivers.

Choosing a quality drill means finding the right balance of power, control, and comfort for the work ahead. We evaluated cordless electric drills for quality, torque, ease of use, and power, testing each function to identify where every model excelled. Our top recommendation is the Bosch GSB18V-65B12 18-volt ½-inch hammer drill driver, which is well-balanced, highly maneuverable, and offers great cost value.

Whether you need extra muscle for demanding work or a smaller tool for crafting and household repairs, a good cordless drill should suit your projects and budget. Our tested picks cover a range of needs.

The following cordless drills represent many of the drill brands known for reliability and value, and we tested each one. We tested each tool to determine its power, durability, battery life, and overall quality. For shoppers comparing DeWalt vs. Milwaukee, the battery platform and available tools are also worth considering.

The Bosch GSB18V-65B12 earned our Best Overall cordless drill award for its compact build and outstanding performance across a wide range of drilling and driving tasks. This lightweight cordless drill proved comfortable for extended daily use and powerful enough for occasional heavy-duty work.  The kit includes the drill with a pre-installed belt hook, a 2.0 amp-hour battery, charger, and tool bag.

This pro-quality model was smaller and lighter than the other 18-volt drills we tested, making it easier to maneuver in confined workspaces. Pound for pound, it was stronger, too. Its 575 inch-pounds of maximum torque handled hardened steel, concrete, and brick without binding and drove heavy-duty construction screws and lag bolts with ease.

Even in concrete and brick, we found hammer mode unnecessary: Low speed and firm downward pressure were enough. However, when the bit reached about an inch deep, its straight shank began slipping in the chuck. Retightening allowed us to finish the hole, but slippage occurred three times during testing. The drill had ample power, but three-flat-shank bits may provide a more secure grip.

What our tester says: “I really liked how the new Bosch hammer drill/driver felt—light, comfortable, and capable. In terms of comfort, as well as speed and torque, I preferred it over all of the other drills that I tested.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Bosch 18V cordless drill at Amazon or Acme Tools.

The Black+Decker 20V MAX PowerConnect brushless drill/driver combines affordability with useful power and features for home projects. For buyers seeking a cordless drill with battery and charger, this kit includes both, along with a double-ended screwdriver bit and belt clip. The 2.0 amp-hour battery also works with other compatible Black+Decker PowerConnect tools.

The brushless motor delivers up to 486 inch-pounds of torque, while the ½-inch keyless metal chuck accepts larger-shank bits than the ⅜-inch chucks on some entry-level drills. Two speed ranges—0 to 450 and 0 to 1,900 RPM—cover screwdriving and drilling tasks. We found the ten clutch settings prevented overdriving fasteners when assembling furniture or installing hardware, and a separate drilling position provides access to full power.

We like its compact body, soft-grip handle, and built-in LED—they make the drill a good option for working inside cabinets and other confined spaces. The magnetic bit holder keeps a spare bit within reach, while the battery indicator displays remaining charge. Starting screws may require a light touch on the variable-speed trigger, so the lower gear is useful for more controlled driving. The single included battery suits intermittent household projects, though a spare would help keep longer work sessions moving.

Get the Black+Decker cordless drill at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Black+Decker.

The DeWalt DCD1007WW1 is a heavy-duty drill with an efficient brushless motor that produces up to 1,530 watts. Although it was among the more expensive drills we tested, its rugged construction and heavy-duty performance help justify the investment. The kit includes a ½-inch three-speed hammer drill, removable side handle, belt hook, 8-amp-hour battery, charger, and tool bag.

We pushed this drill harder during testing, and it delivered. It drilled ½-inch holes in wood faster than any other model we tested, with similarly strong results in steel, brick, and concrete. It also drove every ½-inch lag bolt flush without a pilot hole, then finished driving bolts another drill had left halfway in. After these initial tests, the battery indicator still showed a full charge. DeWalt claims up to 275 holes per charge.

This cordless hammer drill was also surprisingly maneuverable thanks to its short motor-and-chuck assembly. Although slightly heavier than the older DeWalt DCD996 we compared it with, it was about an inch shorter. That compact shape helped it fit tighter spaces and feel more balanced when working at different angles. Still, at roughly twice the weight of many 18-volt drills, it is best suited to demanding projects that warrant the extra power.

Another useful feature is the adjustable LED at the base of the handle. Unlike lights that operate only with the trigger, this one pivots to three positions and can stay on independently for up to 20 minutes. It is brighter than a smartphone flashlight and offers a practical alternative to putting a phone within reach of a dimly lit repair.

What our tester says: “The DeWalt 20-volt hammer drill felt like it could do anything, and the shorter nose allowed it to do quite a bit more than its predecessors. It’s incredibly powerful for a cordless drill, and it held a super strong grip on the bit shaft.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the DeWalt cordless drill at Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Acme Tools.

The standout feature of the Makita 7.2V cordless driver-drill is its hinged body, which converts from a pistol grip to an in-line configuration like an electric screwdriver. We were especially interested in how the straight grip would improve access when using this small cordless drill.

We began testing with a fully charged battery, the pistol grip, and a small hex-shank paddle bit. The chuck doesn’t accept round-shank bits, which limits bit compatibility. As expected, this 7.2V model lacked the power of the larger drills we tested, but it isn’t intended to compete with a professional 20V drill. It’s designed primarily for drilling wood and drywall, and it handled those tasks well.

The in-line grip proved most useful when installing fasteners in tight spaces, such as cabinet slides and hinges. In that configuration, the Makita worked like a cordless screwdriver with extra power. Its 21-setting clutch let us adjust the torque to suit different fasteners before disengaging, while two speed settings added versatility.

If we could keep only one drill/driver for everyday household tasks, we’d choose this Makita. It isn’t a construction drill, but its ability to reach awkwardly positioned fasteners makes it especially useful around the house. It ran for nearly 30 minutes before the battery needed recharging. The LED illuminated the work area and flashed to alert us when the charge ran low.

Get the Makita DF012DSE cordless drill at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Acme Tools.

The Ryobi PCL206K2 carries on the brand’s reputation for affordable, dependable tools. This 18V cordless drill has a ½-inch chuck, a maximum speed of 1,750 RPM, and 515 inch-pounds of torque, offering specifications comparable to many higher-priced models while weighing slightly more than 2.5 pounds. The kit includes two 1.5 amp-hour batteries and a charger.

In testing, the Ryobi delivered impressive drilling and driving speed and power. It bored effortlessly through a 2×4 with a ⅛-inch twist bit, then made a clean, precise hole with a spade bit in just 4 seconds. It was equally quick and effective at driving 3-inch deck screws. Performance nearly matched that of similarly sized brushless drills. We suspect its brushed motor would drain batteries faster, but it held its own in our drilling and driving tests.

The brushed motor and plastic chuck help explain the lower price. Professional-grade models typically use brushless motors and all-metal chucks for better battery life and durability. For weekend DIYers, though, this standard ½-inch drill delivers ample power and speed at an excellent value.

Get the Ryobi cordless drill at The Home Depot.

The Milwaukee M12 right-angle drill combines useful power with easy access to tight spaces. We tested the kit version, which includes a battery and charger, but those who already own Milwaukee M12 tools can purchase the tool-only model and use their existing batteries.

Weighing just 2.03 pounds, this compact drill slipped easily into confined spaces and was comfortable to operate with one hand. It lacked the power of some larger models we tested, making it better suited to furniture assembly and drilling small holes than heavy construction work. The built-in LED helped illuminate the work area, although we needed an additional work light in darker spots.

A welcome feature was the clutch, which helps prevent stripping screw heads when driving fasteners. The elongated trigger also let us shift our grip higher or lower on the handle without losing easy access to the control. For electricians, HVAC technicians, and plumbers who need controlled screwdriving or small-hole drilling in tight spaces, this Milwaukee is a useful option.

Get the Milwaukee right-angle drill at Amazon (tool only), Ace Hardware (tool only), or The Home Depot.

Small but mighty, this Bosch cordless drill came with several quick-change attachments that allowed us to drill holes and insert screws in various settings. We quickly discovered why this Bosch drill features what the manufacturer calls the FlexiClick system: The attachments connect via a simple push-and-click movement that locks them firmly in place. The drill has a standard attachment with a ⅜-inch chuck that accepts most drill and screw bits. It also has an offset attachment that allowed us to adjust the position of the bit to fit in hard-to-reach spots and an angle attachment that gives the Bosch drill a multiposition head for drilling at various slants.

While this is just a 12-volt model, we found it had ample power and torque to drill holes in dimensional lumber using even a paddle bit. We also found the 20-position clutch helpful for adjusting the torque to keep from stripping out screw heads in both hardwood and softwood.

The LED guide light isn’t as bright as it could be—it may help slightly, but you will probably want to use a supplemental work light if you’re drilling in low-light situations. The belt clip on this tool is located at the back of the head, which we liked better than the drills with clips located at the base of the handle. It was easier to slip on and off our tool belts. This little drill won’t replace a full-power drill/driver, but it’s an excellent pick for tackling tasks in tight spots.

Get the Bosch 12V cordless drill at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or Acme Tools.

We spent 27 hours testing 14 highly rated cordless drills, drilling more than 500 holes and installing 200 screws and bolts. We evaluated drilling speed and power in materials such as wood, steel, brick, and concrete, along with screwdriving control and the ability to seat larger fasteners. We also assessed chuck security, grip comfort, weight, maneuverability in confined spaces, and the usefulness of features such as work lights, speed controls, and adjustable clutches.

Features such as battery performance and included accessories also informed our value assessments. Each drill received scores from 0 (lowest) to 5 (highest) for build quality, ease of use, performance, and value. We then compared cumulative scores within each voltage range and selected the strongest performers for different users and project types.

When choosing from different types of drills, start by matching their features to the needs of your projects. The most powerful cordless drill isn’t necessarily the best fit for occasional repairs, especially if its weight makes it tiring to use. As with all the best cordless tools, the ideal tool for the job tends to balance versatility, comfort, and value. Understanding how to use a drill also helps users get the most out of whatever drill you choose.

Battery voltage helps indicate a cordless drill’s capabilities, but it doesn’t measure power on its own. Motor design, gearing, and battery performance also matter. When choosing a battery-powered drill, consider the work you plan to tackle rather than voltage alone.

The distinction between 18V and 20V MAX can be confusing. These labels describe the same voltage class: 20V is the maximum initial battery voltage measured without a workload, while 18V is the nominal voltage. The difference isn’t a startup surge, nor does a 20V MAX label guarantee more power than an 18V model. Similarly, many drills marketed as 12V use batteries rated at 10.8V nominal.

Use these categories as a starting point:

For masonry projects, knowing how to drill into concrete will help you select the appropriate tool, bit, and technique.

Battery capacity, measured in amp-hours (Ah), also matters. At the same voltage, a higher Ah rating generally means longer runtime, though actual results depend on the drill and workload. Smaller packs keep the tool lighter, while larger packs support longer work sessions but usually add weight and cost. A higher Ah rating alone doesn’t guarantee more drilling power. For occasional projects, a compact battery may be sufficient; for extended use, consider a larger pack or a spare.

Torque is the twisting force a drill delivers, while speed, measured in revolutions per minute (RPM), describes how quickly the bit turns. A lower gear generally provides more torque for driving fasteners and drilling with larger bits. Higher speeds suit many smaller-bit drilling tasks, though the appropriate speed depends on the material and bit.

Most drills have an adjustable clutch that limits the torque transmitted to the chuck. When resistance reaches the selected setting, the clutch disengages to help prevent overdriving screws or stripping their heads. It responds to resistance rather than a preset screw depth, so choosing the right setting helps maintain control. Knowing how to change a drill bit also helps ensure the bit is properly seated and secured.

Look for at least 10 clutch settings to accommodate different fasteners and materials. A drilling machine with two gear settings offers more versatility, while a variable-speed trigger lets you fine-tune speed within the selected range.

A drill’s size and weight affect comfort, especially during extended use. Lightweight models can weigh about a pound, while heavy-duty cordless hammer drills may exceed 8 pounds. Extra power often adds weight, so choose a tool that balances capability with comfortable handling. Check whether the listed weight includes the battery, which can make a noticeable difference.

A compact drill is easier to maneuver in confined spaces, and a smaller body doesn’t necessarily mean less power. Consider both weight and overall dimensions when comparing models.

Most cordless drills have keyless chucks for quick bit changes. Chuck capacity determines the largest bit-shank diameter the tool accepts, rather than the size of hole it can drill. Many general-purpose models have ⅜- or ½-inch chucks, while some compact drill/drivers use ¼-inch hex holders that accept only compatible hex-shank bits.

The best drill bits for a project must suit both the material and the drill’s chuck. Check compatibility before buying a bit set.

Corded drills sometimes come with a brushed motor. They are cheap and reliable, but the brushes eventually wear down and require replacement. Another challenge with brushed motors is that they create friction, which drains the battery faster in cordless models.

The best cordless power drills often use a brushless motor. These virtually maintenance-free motors use the battery much more efficiently. However, brushless motors cost more. As a result, many budget cordless drills still use brushed motors.

For a typical DIYer, the difference is probably negligible. Those who want to maximize performance and runtime, particularly professional users, often choose a brushless cordless drill.

Like most modern battery-operated drills, the models in this guide use rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. Runtime depends on battery capacity and workload, while charging time varies with the battery and charger. For extensive drilling, a kit with a spare battery lets you keep working while the depleted pack charges.

Note that manufacturer runtime claims often factor backup batteries into their runtime estimates. For instance, the specs on a drill that comes with two batteries, each lasting 1 hour, may list a 2-hour runtime.

Additionally, many cordless drills include a smart charger that replenishes the battery faster, usually within 15 to 60 minutes. A charge indicator allows you to monitor battery capacity.

Depending on your projects, these extras can improve comfort and convenience:

A refurbished cordless drill can help you save money or afford a higher-quality model while reducing waste. Unlike ordinary secondhand tools, refurbished models usually undergo inspection, repairs, and testing before resale. Standards vary by seller, however, so check what “refurbished,” “reconditioned,” or “renewed” means for the listing.

These tools may come from customer returns or have sustained shipping or warehouse damage. Don’t assume they were barely used or restored to like-new condition. You can browse refurbished drills at Amazon.

Walmart and other retailers also offer refurbished options. Keep these considerations in mind:

Buy from a reputable source and inspect and test the drill promptly after delivery. If something is wrong, you’ll have time to request a return.

Our in-depth investigation of technologies and specifications above may have you feeling better equipped to choose the best power drill for your needs. That valuable information is underlined by examples of some of the top cordless drills currently available. Still, with so many options available, a few questions might remain. The following are answers to some of the most common questions.

The primary use of a cordless drill is for drilling holes and driving screws. However, you can also get numerous attachments, which are sometimes included in cordless drill sets. Stirrers, for example, can mix paint and other liquids. You can also attach a sanding drum, a wire brush for rust removal, or a polishing bonnet. Our guide covers more uses for your cordless drill/driver.

Corded models were once more powerful tools. But today, equally powerful cordless models rival them. However, cordless models lose some of their power over the course of the charge, while corded models perform at a consistent level for as long as they’re plugged in.

An electric screwdriver is usually much smaller, has less power, and cannot drill holes. The cordless drill can drill holes and also drive screws.

New and improved models enter the market all the time, so it’s difficult to name one brand as the best overall. Bosch, DeWalt, Makita, and Milwaukee all offer tools for different needs and budgets. Comparing individual models—including the best DeWalt drills—is more useful than choosing by brand alone.

It very much depends on the amp hours of the battery and how hard the drill is working. A battery can last as little as 15 minutes, though many will run between 30 minutes and 1 hour. Buying a spare battery for your rechargeable drill lets you swap it out and keep working while the other charges.

Brushless electric motors are more efficient and powerful than brushed motors. They often last longer, too. But higher performance also comes at a higher price. For occasional light-duty drilling, brushed cordless drills are more cost-effective.

The best voltage depends on the user’s needs. For instance, 12-volt drills are inexpensive and perfectly capable of light-duty drilling and driving, while 18-volt drills deliver the higher torque and faster RPM needed for medium- and heavy-duty projects.

Glenda Taylor is a product tester and writer specializing in construction, remodeling, and real estate. She tests a wide range of power tools as well as other home improvement, household, and lawn-and-garden products.

#7749. Russell Brand sentenced to 10 years following rape and sexual assault conviction

British comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London during his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. He was convicted and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. (Photo from Shutterstock)

British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced in London on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison following his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand, 51, as a sexual predator who used his public standing to shield himself from accountability before women came forward following media reports in 2023, Courthouse News Service reports.

Brand will likely serve two-thirds of his sentence before being released on parole, the judge said. The sentencing followed a four-week trial in which jurors found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Before the sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women, who described the lasting effects of the attacks on their confidence, relationships and ability to feel safe.

The judge considered Brand’s charitable work, including helping people struggling with addiction by funding treatment. However, he said good character and exemplary conduct would not normally justify a significant reduction in a prison sentence.

#7748. Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

What makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

Unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can quickly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”

Vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can quickly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception issue if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes says.

Broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty says. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”

Fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be new to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker says. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”

Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker says. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”

While low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes says.  But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

“There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty says. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland says. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

“A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland says. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our new neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty says. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.
